title: Too Dumb To Improve The App

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have any suggestions for improving the app?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but you are far too dumb to implement any of them, so I won't bother.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: At least tell me where the problems are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The big ones are all in this big bag of skin.

setting: Office hallway near an elevator or door
situation: A coworker in a face mask asks Dilbert, who is also masked, for suggestions to improve their app. Dilbert bluntly refuses because the coworker is too dumb to implement anything. When the coworker asks at least to be told where the problems are, Dilbert points at him and says the biggest ones are inside his own body.
punchline: Dilbert insults the coworker by saying the biggest problems with the app are the coworker himself, the 'bag of skin' who develops it.
summary: Asked for app improvement ideas, Dilbert declines on the grounds of the asker's stupidity and then identifies the asker himself as the main flaw.

title: Faking COVID Symptoms to Skip Meetings

transcript.speaker: Person in hazmat suit
transcript.text: You reported COVID-19 symptoms, so we have to quarantine you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't have symptoms. I just said I did to avoid a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Person in hazmat suit
transcript.text: Well, you probably have it now. I haven't washed this hazmat suit in five months.

setting: Office break area during the COVID-19 pandemic
situation: A safety officer in a yellow hazmat suit tells a masked employee holding a coffee that he must be quarantined for reporting COVID-19 symptoms. The employee admits he lied to get out of a meeting. The officer replies that the employee has probably caught the virus anyway, because the suit has gone unwashed for five months.
punchline: The employee's lie to dodge a meeting backfires, since the filthy hazmat suit of the person sent to quarantine him has likely given him the very illness he faked.
summary: A worker who falsely claims illness to skip a meeting ends up exposed to real infection by an unwashed protective suit.

title: What Generalists Actually Do All Day

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, can you help me on this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I'm more of a generalist than a subject matter expert.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What kind of work do generalists do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You just saw it.

setting: Office, with both people wearing face masks (2020)
situation: A coworker holding papers asks Wally for help on a task. Wally sits with a coffee and declines, claiming to be a generalist rather than a subject matter expert. When the coworker asks what generalists actually do, Wally replies that they just watched it, meaning nothing.
punchline: Being a 'generalist' is Wally's excuse for avoiding work, and the work a generalist does is simply refusing to help.
summary: Wally dodges a request for assistance by hiding behind a job-title label that supposedly excuses him from doing anything useful.

title: Boss Debunks Wally's Brilliant Idea

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you see my brilliant product idea I emailed to you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, I already debunked it in my mind.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Perhaps you could share your reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it's such a great idea, why isn't someone else doing it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And if someone is already doing it, we are far too late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In order for your idea to be good, I would have to think you are smarter than everyone in the industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And seriously, just look at you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyone else have an idea?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Never.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Nope.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Wally asks the boss whether he saw the product idea he emailed. The boss explains that he already rejected it mentally, using circular reasoning that the idea is either unoriginal or too late, and then insults Wally personally. The boss then asks if anyone else has an idea, and everyone in the building says no.
punchline: The boss's catch-22 logic dismisses every possible idea and insults the proposer, so he successfully teaches the whole company never to suggest anything.
summary: A manager shoots down an employee's pitch with unwinnable logic and a personal insult, then wonders why nobody else offers suggestions.
keywords: why isn't someone else doing it

title: Trick Interview Question Gets Candidate Dismissed

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We added the following trick question to our interview process. . .

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do Black lives matter?

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: Yes, of course.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: I think ALL. . .

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Dismissed!

setting: Interview room in an office, with both people wearing face masks
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells a masked job candidate that the company has added a trick question to its interviews and asks whether Black lives matter. The candidate agrees, then starts to qualify the answer when prompted to elaborate. Catbert cuts him off and dismisses him the moment he begins saying 'all'.
punchline: The 'trick question' is rigged so that the common deflecting response 'all lives matter' immediately disqualifies the candidate, showing Catbert's cruel, gotcha style of hiring.
summary: A malicious HR interviewer springs a loaded question on a job applicant and rejects him the instant he starts to deflect.

title: Skip The Bribed Experts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't approve your plan until I know what the experts say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can save us some time by talking to the people who bribe the experts. I'll get the same answer, but faster.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ouch! The truth hurts!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Take a deep breath. It will pass.

setting: Conference table in an office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: The Boss refuses to approve Dilbert's plan until outside experts have weighed in. Dilbert offers to shortcut the process by asking the people who bribe the experts, since the answer would be the same. The Boss winces at the accusation, and Dilbert calmly tells him to breathe and wait for the discomfort to pass.
punchline: Dilbert implies that expert opinions are bought and predetermined, so consulting them adds delay but no real independent insight.
summary: An employee points out that waiting for paid-off experts is a slower way of getting an answer that could be had from their sponsors right away.

title: Court Orders Dilbert to Read Minds

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Court of Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: The court rules that Dilbert should magically know what his boss wants at all times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not a mind-reader!

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Prove it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I prove I can't read minds?

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Easy. Tell me what I'm not thinking.

setting: A courtroom labeled the Court of Stupidity
situation: A judge rules that Dilbert must magically know what his boss wants at all times. Dilbert protests that he is not a mind-reader, and the judge demands he prove it. When Dilbert asks how to prove a negative, the judge offers an impossible test: tell him what he is not thinking.
punchline: The judge's 'easy' test is logically absurd, since there are infinitely many things he isn't thinking, which mirrors how managers set impossible expectations and make employees prove they can't meet them.
summary: A mock court forces an employee to prove he lacks psychic powers, using a test that cannot reasonably be passed.

title: The Time-Wasting Fool Isn't Muted

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: We've been going for two hours, so let's wrap up...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a new topic...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Why is there always one time-wasting fool on every Zoom call???

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why? Why?

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: Dilbert, you're not on mute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. Did you hear my TV? I'll turn it down.

setting: Home offices during a Zoom video call
situation: A two-hour video call is finally being wrapped up when Dilbert pipes up with a new topic. A frustrated coworker, who believes he is muted, rants about the one time-wasting fool on every Zoom call. Dilbert's voice then reveals the coworker was not on mute, but Dilbert misunderstands and offers to turn down his TV.
punchline: The coworker's rant about the time-wasting fool was broadcast to everyone, and Dilbert, the obvious target, obliviously thinks the complaint is about his TV noise.
summary: A man fuming about a meeting-prolonging colleague forgets his microphone is live, and the colleague fails to grasp that he was the target.

title: Desperate Meeting Attendees Dread Questions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, that's all for today unless anyone else has a question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert and coworkers (thought)
transcript.text: Please let it end. Please let it end. Please let it end.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: What's the company vision?

transcript.speaker: Office building
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with masked attendees; final panel shows the office building exterior
situation: The Boss wraps up a meeting by asking if anyone has a question while three masked attendees silently pray for it to end. In the final panel, someone off-panel asks about the company vision, and the whole office building screams in anguish.
punchline: Someone asking a question at the end of a meeting is so dreaded that the entire building screams in despair, with the question itself being the most vague, time-consuming one possible.
summary: Everyone silently begs for a meeting to finish, only for one person to ask a broad question that makes the whole building cry out.

title: Terrific Attitude About Disliking Coworkers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your work has been exceptional, but people are complaining about your attitude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aren't the people who are doing the complaining usually the ones with bad attitudes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They think you dislike them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I do, but I have a terrific attitude about it.

setting: Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that although his work is exceptional, coworkers are complaining about his attitude. Dilbert points out that complainers usually have bad attitudes themselves. When the Boss explains they think Dilbert dislikes them, Dilbert admits he does but insists he feels great about it.
punchline: Dilbert cheerfully admits he dislikes his coworkers, claiming his positive attitude about disliking them makes his attitude fine.
summary: A boss relays complaints about an excellent employee's demeanor, only to have the employee candidly confirm the dislike while praising his own cheerful outlook on it.

title: Quarantined Management Says Stop Working

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The entire management team has contracted coronavirus and is quarantined.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They asked me to tell you to stop working, because without their wisdom, you idiots will ruin everything.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I think you covered the main themes.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to masked employees at a conference table that all of management has caught coronavirus and is quarantined. He then relays management's message that everyone should stop working because the staff would ruin everything without managers' wisdom. When he asks for questions, Dilbert dryly says the message already covered the main themes.
punchline: Management's message boils down to insulting employees and telling them to do nothing, and Dilbert sarcastically notes that the insult and the pointless instruction were all there was to say.
summary: An HR cat delivers a pandemic-era memo from sick executives that condescendingly tells staff to halt all work, and one employee deadpans that the point has been made.

title: Cross-Training Replacement Plan Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss told me to ask you to cross-train me on your job functions.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: That sounds exactly like he plans to fire me as soon as you can do my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my defense, he assured me you would be too dumb to realize that.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert asks a co-worker to cross-train him on the co-worker's job, saying the Boss told him to. The co-worker immediately realizes this means he will be fired once Dilbert can do his job. Dilbert admits the Boss had told him the co-worker wouldn't figure it out.
punchline: Dilbert's 'defense' is that the Boss thought the co-worker was too dumb to notice the scheme, which insults the co-worker while also confirming he's being set up for firing.
summary: A man asked to teach his job to a colleague instantly guesses he's being phased out, and the colleague sheepishly admits the boss counted on his obliviousness.

title: Safety Concerns Raised Too Late

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And we can get that all installed in thirty days.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Why do you not care about safety?

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: Literally everyone cares about safety.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Then why didn't you mention it?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Blah, blah, safety. I happy?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office meeting room, with the exterior of an office building in the last panel
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, presents a diagram of a system installation that can be done in thirty days. A masked coworker in a blue shirt asks why he doesn't care about safety, and Dilbert insists everyone cares about it. The coworker asks why he never mentioned it, and Dilbert sarcastically recites a token mention of safety to satisfy him.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic 'Blah, blah, safety. I happy?' shows that a required token mention of safety is just box-ticking rather than genuine concern.
summary: A presenter is pressed by a coworker to bring up safety and responds with a mocking, perfunctory nod to the topic.

title: Silencer Installed in Boss's Mask

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now he's the only one who can hear himself talk, but he doesn't know it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here he comes. Play along.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-huh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, thanks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I can do the same thing to the face mask of anyone else who bores me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-huh.

setting: Office break area during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has secretly installed a silencer in the Boss's face mask, so only the Boss can hear himself talk. When the Boss approaches and speaks, Wally and Dilbert nod along while hearing nothing, and the Boss leaves satisfied. Wally then says he could do the same to anyone else who bores him, and the final panel shows him giving a bored 'uh-huh' to another speaker whose words are silent.
punchline: Wally's silencing trick works so well on the Boss that he applies the same lazy tune-out to everyone else, implying he may have already silenced someone else's mask.
summary: A trick that makes a manager's rambling inaudible lets his coworkers nod politely while hearing nothing, and the prankster hints he can mute anyone dull.

title: Confidently Wrong Hire Insults The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a guy who is always wrong, yet he is inexplicably confident.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why? We already have one of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what you meant by that, but I am confident it is wrong.

setting: Office meeting table, with both wearing face masks
situation: The Boss tells Alice he has hired someone who is always wrong but inexplicably confident. Alice points out that the company already has one of those, meaning the Boss himself. The Boss fails to grasp the insult but confidently declares that it must be wrong.
punchline: The Boss proves Alice's point by being confidently wrong about her insult without even understanding it.
summary: A manager brags about recruiting an overconfident blunderer, and when a colleague mocks him as the existing example, he dismisses the jab without comprehending it.

title: Wally Admits He Did Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I didn't do any work because there is no point in trying.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the unlikely event I did something useful, it would be ruined by the massive incompetence of my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I pay you to act as if you are trying.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh. In that case, I worked hard this week.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a weekly meeting, Wally announces he did no work because trying is pointless, and that any useful output would be ruined by his incompetent co-workers. The Boss responds that he is paid to act as if he is trying. Wally then happily claims he worked hard that week.
punchline: The Boss only cares about the appearance of effort, so Wally can honestly claim to have worked hard by simply pretending, which exposes how hollow the workplace expectations are.
summary: A lazy employee confesses to doing nothing all week, and his manager's only complaint is that he should have faked effort, which he cheerfully says he did.
keywords: act as if you are trying

title: Watching Over Your Shoulder for Mistakes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a feeling you are doing something wrong, but I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you mind if I watch over your shoulder and look for mistakes as you make them?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You don't have any friends, do you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like to travel light.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells an employee seated at a computer that he suspects something is wrong with the work but cannot say what. He then asks to stand behind the employee and watch for mistakes as they happen. The employee asks if he has any friends, and the Boss replies that he likes to travel light.
punchline: The Boss responds to a pointed insult about his lack of friends by cheerfully reframing his social isolation as a lifestyle choice, showing he is oblivious to how intrusive and unwelcome his micromanagement is.
summary: A manager with only a vague suspicion of error offers to hover over a worker's shoulder, and shrugs off a barbed remark about his friendlessness.

title: Contact Tracing Reveals Dilbert's Love Life

transcript.text: We need to do contact tracing to determine who else you might have infected with cooties.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: How many women have you had physical contact with in the past two weeks?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd rather not say.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'll put you down for zero.

setting: A doctor's office during the pandemic, with both wearing face masks
situation: A masked doctor tells Dilbert they need to do contact tracing to find out who he may have infected with cooties. When asked how many women he has had physical contact with in the past two weeks, Dilbert evasively says he'd rather not say. The doctor calmly writes down zero.
punchline: Dilbert's reluctance to answer is read as embarrassment, and the doctor correctly assumes that he has had no physical contact with any women, mocking his lack of a social life.
summary: A doctor tracing the spread of a childish ailment quickly deduces from a patient's evasiveness that he has no one to report.

transcript.text: It is the opposite of work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you have to do is sit in one place and think of nothing in particular.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I drink coffee at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is not recommended.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In other words, meditating is what I already do, but without the advantage of coffee?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you have already achieved enlightenment.

transcript.speaker: Wally

setting: Office conference table
situation: Dilbert suggests to Wally that he try meditating. Wally assumes it sounds like work, and Dilbert explains it is just sitting and thinking of nothing. Wally realizes that this describes what he already does all day, minus the coffee.
punchline: Wally's usual workday of sitting around doing nothing while sipping coffee is effectively meditation, so he may already be enlightened.
summary: A coworker pitches meditation to the famously idle Wally, who discovers he has been practicing it all along.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: At a staff meeting, the Boss announces that performance reviews are being scrapped. Instead, employees will be ranked on how acceptable their political and social opinions are. Dilbert asks for a list of acceptable opinions and the Boss refuses to give any guidance.
punchline: Employees are being judged on opinions they are not allowed to know in advance, making it impossible to comply and easy for management to punish anyone arbitrarily.
summary: Management swaps job evaluations for a secret test of employees' beliefs, offering no clue what answers are approved.

title: Doctor Diagnoses Cooties Via Skepticism

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: In my professional opinion, you have a bad case of cooties.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: We don't have any tests for cooties, but the main symptom is skepticism, and you have that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cooties are not real.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Diagnosis confirmed.

setting: Doctor's examination room
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, sits on an exam table while a masked doctor tells him he has a bad case of cooties. The doctor explains there is no test, but the main symptom is skepticism. When Dilbert protests that cooties aren't real, the doctor takes that as proof and confirms the diagnosis.
punchline: The doctor's circular logic makes any denial of the diagnosis count as evidence for it, so the patient can never be proven healthy.
summary: A physician declares a patient infected with an untestable made-up ailment and treats his disbelief as the proof.

transcript.text: Is that the one on the server rack?

situation: Catbert, acting as an HR-style authority, announces that common workplace words are racist or sexist and must be replaced. He gives the example of the "master switch" on the server rack, which Dilbert asks about. Catbert replies that such switches are now called "shelves," a nonsensical replacement term.
punchline: The mandated replacement for the offending term is absurd and unhelpful, mocking performative word-policing that creates confusion instead of real improvement.
summary: An HR cat orders staff to drop supposedly offensive jargon and offers a ridiculous substitute for a piece of server equipment.

The final panel shows a smirking administrator sitting on a cloud at a computer, gleefully mocking someone's browser history.
punchline: The people entrusted with guarding your cloud data are actually snooping through it and laughing at your private browsing habits, proving the worrier right.
summary: A reassurance that cloud custodians can be trusted is undercut by a gleeful admin ridiculing a user's personal browsing records.

title: Testing It Anecdotally

transcript.text: Well played.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: In a meeting, a masked manager asks Dilbert whether he has tested his proposal to be sure it will work. Dilbert answers that he tested it 'anecdotally,' and the manager privately thinks he doesn't know what the word means. Wally, seated nearby, compliments Dilbert's answer.
punchline: Dilbert uses a fancy-sounding word that really means he did no real testing at all, and the manager's ignorance of the word lets him get away with it, earning Wally's admiration.
summary: A boss demands proof that an idea works and gets fobbed off with an impressive-sounding word that conceals the absence of any real testing.

title: Sadist or Idiot Slide Deck

setting: Office hallway with a door in the background
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to review his 32-page slide deck and give feedback. Dilbert bluntly says only a sadist or an idiot would create such a long deck. The coworker teasingly says Dilbert will never guess which one he is, and Dilbert replies that he feels he could.
punchline: Dilbert's honest feedback insults the coworker, and when invited to guess whether the coworker is a sadist or an idiot, he sarcastically implies he already knows the answer.
summary: A colleague seeking feedback on an enormous presentation gets a brutally candid insult and then an invitation to guess his flaw, which Dilbert is happy to accept.

situation: Both wearing face masks, the Boss tells Dilbert how he insisted a vendor wear any face covering at all. The offended vendor went to his car and wrapped the plastic wrap from his sandwich around his head, suffocating himself. Dilbert notices the Boss eating the vendor's sandwich.
punchline: The Boss callously helped himself to the dead vendor's sandwich because it would otherwise have gone to waste, showing his total lack of empathy.
summary: A boss recounts how a vendor died by turning his sandwich wrap into a mask, then casually eats the leftover lunch.

setting: Office, in front of a plain background
situation: Alice notices Dilbert staring at his phone while she answers his question. Dilbert explains that her answer is unrelated to what he asked and he was too polite to interrupt. Alice insists she is providing important context, and Dilbert tells her to text him when she gets to the relevant part.
punchline: Dilbert politely sidesteps a long-winded, off-topic answer by asking to be texted when the actual answer arrives, implying her 'context' is just rambling.
summary: A coworker who rambles through a tangential reply gets told her listener would rather check his phone until she reaches the point.

transcript.text: I need you to be my lawyer and handle my appeal to the Court of Stupidity.

transcript.text: Court of Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The court rules in favor of the bailiff.

setting: Conference room, then a courthouse exterior
situation: Dilbert sits at a conference table with Dogbert and complains that his boss blames him for not knowing what the boss was thinking. He asks Dogbert to act as his lawyer in an appeal to the 'Court of Stupidity.' The final panel shows a courthouse, where the court absurdly rules in favor of the bailiff, someone who had nothing to do with the case.
punchline: The Court of Stupidity hands its verdict to a completely irrelevant party, the bailiff, showing that decisions in a stupid system make no sense and Dilbert's grievance will never be properly resolved.
summary: Blamed for failing to read his manager's mind, an engineer appeals to a tribunal of idiocy that promptly sides with a random court employee.

title: Astrology Filter Decodes Technology Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your strategic technology plan was incoherent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to run it through an astrology filter to make sense of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says you are "full of Taurus" and your plan "is a cancer."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds right.

setting: Dilbert's desk, during a video call
situation: Dilbert tells his boss, who appears on his laptop screen in a video call, that his strategic technology plan made no sense. He says he ran it through an astrology filter to interpret it, and reports the results, which are insults disguised as zodiac terms. The boss agrees with the assessment.
punchline: The astrology filter's output is a pun-based insult ("full of Taurus" sounding like "full of bull"), and the boss cheerfully accepts that it sounds right, showing he cannot tell nonsense from sense.
summary: An engineer uses horoscope software to translate a muddled management plan and gets blunt, pun-laden verdicts that the manager blithely endorses.

title: Slide 27 Might Contain Point

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you think of my slide deck?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reviewed all 26 of your slides, and I can't figure out what your point is.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I could put the point on slide 27.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or just give up.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A coworker in a blue shirt asks Dilbert for his opinion of a slide deck. Dilbert, seated at his laptop, says he read all 26 slides and still can't tell what the point is. The coworker suggests adding the point on a 27th slide, and Dilbert recommends he give up instead.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically dismisses the idea that yet another slide will fix a presentation that already fails to make its point, suggesting the effort is hopeless.
summary: After wading through a long presentation without finding its message, Dilbert tells the author that adding more slides won't help and quitting would be wiser.

title: Mandatory Zoom Happy Hour Drunk

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We're going to start having Zoom happy hour every weekday to boost morale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the only one in the entire department who drinks alcohol.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (via laptop)
transcript.text: You're all looshers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you already start drinking?

transcript.speaker: Coworker (via laptop)
transcript.text: I love you!

setting: Remote work video call; each person at a home desk with a laptop
situation: A manager announces daily Zoom happy hours to lift morale. Dilbert points out that the manager is the only one in the department who drinks alcohol. The manager, already visibly drunk on the video call, slurs that everyone is a loosher and professes love, and Alice asks if he has started drinking already.
punchline: The manager's plan for morale-boosting happy hours is really just an excuse for his own drinking, and he is already drunk during the meeting where he announces it.
summary: A boss proposes daily virtual cocktail hours for team spirit, but his slurred speech reveals he's the only drinker and has already started.

title: Promotion Offer Is Disguised Dismissal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear there's a great job opening in Operations for someone with your background.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Big salary, private office. Looks like a great opportunity for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you trying to get rid of me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not in a way you are supposed to notice.

setting: Office desk or meeting table
situation: The Boss approaches an employee who is sitting with his phone and coffee, and enthusiastically recommends a job opening in Operations with a big salary and private office. The employee suspects an ulterior motive and asks if he is being pushed out. The Boss admits it, saying only that he wasn't supposed to be obvious about it.
punchline: The Boss confirms he is trying to get rid of the employee, merely noting that the employee wasn't supposed to notice, which undermines the pretense of a friendly offer.
summary: A manager dangles a lucrative transfer in front of a worker, then lets slip that the real goal is to push him out of the team.

title: Fake Analysis After the Decision

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put some numbers on this decision so it looks as if we thought about it longer.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Are you seriously telling me to do the analysis AFTER the decision?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need help, talk to one of the experienced liars in the department.

setting: Boss's office, with both wearing face masks
situation: The boss hands an employee a paper and asks him to attach numbers to a decision that has already been made, so it appears to have been carefully considered. The employee is incredulous that the analysis is supposed to come after the decision. The boss casually suggests he get help from the experienced liars in the department.
punchline: The boss openly admits the analysis is fabricated after the fact and treats lying as a normal, even skilled, department expertise.
summary: A manager wants fabricated data to make an already-made choice look well studied, and recommends the office's seasoned fibbers as helpers.

title: Assignment Dodges Complaints by Complaining Later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to give this assignment to Alice, but I know she would complain about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want it either.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you plan to complain about it later?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not to your face.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Problem solved.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an assignment, explaining he didn't give it to Alice because she would complain. Dilbert says he doesn't want it either, and the Boss asks if he'll complain later. Dilbert promises only not to complain to the Boss's face, which the Boss accepts as a solution.
punchline: The Boss only cares about not hearing complaints, so Dilbert's promise to complain behind his back counts as a solved problem.
summary: A manager assigns unwanted work to the employee who will grumble where he can't hear it, treating hidden complaints as no problem at all.

title: Good Ideas Need a First Try

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why should we do what you are suggesting when literally no one has ever tried it before?

transcript.speaker: Bald man
transcript.text: Because everything good and amazing had to be done by someone for the first time.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Will this be good and amazing?

transcript.speaker: Bald man
transcript.text: Let's keep this on the concept level.

setting: Office meeting table, with both people wearing face masks
situation: A woman holding a document challenges a bald colleague, asking why the company should adopt his proposal when nobody has ever tried it. He replies that every good and amazing thing had to be done first by someone. When she asks whether his idea will actually be good and amazing, he dodges and says to keep the discussion at the concept level.
punchline: He offers an inspirational argument for trying something new but refuses to commit to any claim that his own idea will work, exposing that his pitch has no substance beyond the concept.
summary: A man defends an untested proposal with a lofty argument about innovation, then evades when asked if his idea is actually any good.

title: Hire Smart People, Then Sabotage Them

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The secret to being a great manager is hiring people who are smarter than you are.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Then you have to take credit for their successes so they don't take your job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I also find it helpful to start rumors that they steal.

setting: Office, at a desk
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, gives management advice to the Pointy-Haired Boss across a desk. He starts with the sensible-sounding tip of hiring people smarter than yourself, then explains how to neutralize them by stealing their credit and spreading false rumors about them.
punchline: The seemingly wise management advice quickly turns into a cynical recipe for undermining talented employees to protect your own position.
summary: A malicious feline HR chief coaches a manager on recruiting brilliant staff and then quietly destroying their reputations to stay on top.

title: Budget Ratio Too High, Says Who

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need to reduce our expense budget to 40% of our capital budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do we need to do that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Because the ratio is too high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying we can't afford it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. I'm saying the ratio is too high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but by what standard is it "too high"?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: By historical standards. It has never been this high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think we want to start using an irrelevant ratio to manage the department.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: To be fair, this is just the first time you noticed.

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting, with attendees wearing face masks
situation: In a budget meeting, a coworker insists the expense budget must be cut to 40% of the capital budget because the ratio is too high. Dilbert keeps asking why, whether it's about affordability, and by what standard the ratio is judged. The answers stay circular, and Dilbert argues it's an irrelevant measure for managing the department.
punchline: The ratio is only considered a problem because Dilbert just noticed it, implying the metric has always been meaningless and nobody cared until now.
summary: A meeting demands a budget cut based on a ratio that nobody can justify beyond the fact that it has gotten bigger.

title: Three Quotes From Two Vendors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Purchasing Manager

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: You need three vendor quotes, or I can't approve it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are only two vendors in that market.

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: Come back when something changes.

setting: Purchasing manager's office, at a desk
situation: A dinosaur-like purchasing manager tells Dilbert he must provide three vendor quotes before a purchase can be approved. Dilbert points out that only two vendors exist in that market. The purchasing manager rigidly tells him to return only when the market changes.
punchline: The purchasing manager's rule-following is so inflexible that he expects the real-world market to change to fit the policy instead of adjusting the policy.
summary: A stubborn procurement official refuses a request because policy demands a third bid that cannot exist.

title: Insulting Distracted Phone-Using Coworker Unnoticed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you listening to me? It looks as if you are using your phone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can do two things at once.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll bet you can't even hear me, you ridiculous moron.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Go on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You smell like old socks, and your brain is made of cheese.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert notices a masked coworker staring at a phone while he talks to her. She claims she can multitask, so Dilbert tests her by insulting her. She keeps saying 'uh-huh' and tells him to go on, proving she isn't listening, so he piles on more insults.
punchline: The coworker's absent-minded 'uh-huh' responses show she really isn't listening, and Dilbert gets to insult her freely without consequence.
summary: A man tests whether his phone-absorbed colleague is truly paying attention by hurling insults at her and getting only mindless agreement in return.

title: Overselling a Coronavirus Sick Leave

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My throat has a tickle, so I'd better take a month off of work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The coronavirus tests can have some false negatives, and I love you too much to put you at risk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did it work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I sold it too hard.

setting: Office, during the coronavirus pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: Wally tells a coworker at a desk that a tickle in his throat means he should take a month off, then lays on an over-the-top claim about loving her too much to risk infecting her. Afterward he tells Dilbert that the pitch failed because he oversold it.
punchline: Wally's transparent attempt to use a minor symptom and fake concern for others to score a month off was so exaggerated that it was rejected.
summary: A lazy employee dresses up a trivial symptom as a noble sacrifice to win extra time off, but his excessive sales pitch backfires.

title: Judging Candidates By Old Tweets

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I'd like to offer you a job, but ten years ago you said something offensive on social media.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm not the same person I was ten years ago. You are judging me by the actions of someone who literally no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I get your point, but if I go back to the old way of judging people by their looks, we still end up in the same place.

setting: Office interview room
situation: A hiring manager tells a job candidate that an offensive social media post from ten years ago is holding up the job offer. The candidate argues that he is a changed person and should not be judged by the actions of his past self. The interviewer replies that judging him on appearance instead would lead to the same rejection.
punchline: The interviewer says that even if he abandons the cancel-culture approach and goes back to judging people by their looks, he would still reject the candidate, which insults the man's appearance.
summary: A man's plea to be judged as a new person is shot down when his interviewer admits he'd turn him away on appearance alone.

title: Omitting Context Isn't Lying, Boss Says

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you write the project summary, make it seem as if we didn't make any mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You want me to lie? That would be a massive ethical violation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no. I only want you to omit important context.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why does my stomach hurt?

setting: Conference room or office with a desk, both wearing face masks
situation: The boss asks an employee to write a project summary that hides the team's mistakes. When the employee objects that this would be lying and unethical, the boss reframes it as merely leaving out important context. The employee, now sweating and queasy, realizes the ethical problem is still there.
punchline: The boss tries to redefine deception as 'omitting context' to sound ethical, but the employee's physical sickness shows it's the same dishonesty.
summary: A manager asks for a whitewashed report and renames the dishonesty as leaving things out, leaving the worker feeling physically ill.

title: Dogbert Profits From Private Cloud Data

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The only reason I took a job managing cloud data is so I could laugh at people's private information.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I discovered a robust market for selling that kind of stuff, so it's a twofer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to talk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. Just email your thoughts to a friend, and I'll probably read them.

setting: Outdoors beside a low stone wall
situation: Dogbert, walking beside Dilbert, cheerfully admits he took a job managing cloud data just to laugh at people's private information. He then adds that he found a lucrative market for selling that data. When Dilbert says they need to talk, Dogbert suggests he email his thoughts to a friend, since Dogbert will probably read them.
punchline: Dogbert's cheerful admission that he reads and sells everyone's private cloud data means that even Dilbert's private email to a friend is not safe from him.
summary: A smug Dogbert reveals he snoops on and sells the private data he manages, then warns his friend that any message he sends will be read.

title: Working From Home Descends Into Fort

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day one of working from home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting a lot done.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day two of working from home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I goofed off a little, would anyone know?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day three of working from home.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lame fort.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's version 1.0.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert works diligently on a laptop on his couch on day one of working from home. By day two he is lying down wondering whether anyone would notice if he slacked off a little. By day three he has built a blanket fort over the couch, and Dogbert dismisses it as lame.
punchline: Working from home deteriorates in three days from productivity to slacking to building a childish blanket fort, and Dilbert defends it with software-version jargon.
summary: A remote worker's discipline collapses over three days, ending in a half-hearted blanket fort that he excuses as an early release.

title: Sneeze Gets You Slapped Now

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ah-choo!!!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The pundits were right — everything is different now.

setting: Office meeting table during the COVID-19 pandemic
situation: Dilbert sits wearing a face mask and looking at his phone while Wally, beside him, sneezes without covering his mouth. Wally's mask flies off his face, and in the next panel someone slaps him so hard that he is knocked off his chair, leaving only his feet visible above the table. Dilbert calmly comments on how things have changed.
punchline: In the pandemic era, an uncovered sneeze at work now provokes violent social punishment, which Dilbert wryly cites as proof of the pundits' claim that everything is different now.
summary: A coworker's careless sneeze during the pandemic earns him an instant physical rebuke, illustrating how drastically office norms have shifted.

title: Parachute Ready For Window Jump

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I have to listen to you repeat that same point one more time, I'm going to jump out a window.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds like a bluff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I packed a parachute.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...Anyway, to reiterate...

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with masks worn
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker across the table that he will jump out a window if he has to hear the same point repeated again. The coworker calls it a bluff, so Dilbert produces a backpack with a parachute in it. The coworker keeps repeating himself, and in the final panel Dilbert has smashed through a window and floats away under a parachute.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to escape the repetitive meeting was not a bluff, since he came prepared with a parachute and followed through while the speaker carried on regardless.
summary: A man fed up with a colleague's endless repetition carries out his threat to leap from the window, equipped for a soft landing.

title: Mandatory Ethics Class Won't Stick

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You are all required to complete a class in ethics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make us the only ethical organization in our industry and create a competitive disadvantage that leads to our demise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop your worrying. The class is required, but I'm not expecting any of it to stick.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The boss tells everyone at a meeting that they must complete an ethics class. Dilbert worries that becoming the only ethical company in the industry would put them at a competitive disadvantage. The boss reassures him that the training is only a formality and nobody is expected to actually absorb it.
punchline: The company mandates ethics training for appearances while privately expecting and wanting no real change in behavior, implying that unethical conduct is part of staying competitive.
summary: A manager orders compulsory ethics training but calms a worried employee by admitting the lessons aren't meant to change anyone's conduct.

title: Medical-Grade Coffee Improves Lying

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've been highly productive since switching to medical-grade coffee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I finished all of my projects and did an excellent job on every one.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So that stuff actually makes you more productive?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, but it does make me lie better.

setting: Office conference room, then a hallway
situation: At a meeting table, Wally brags to Dilbert and Alice that medical-grade coffee has made him hugely productive, claiming he finished all his projects excellently. Alice is impressed. Afterward Dilbert asks if the coffee really boosts productivity, and Wally admits it only improves his ability to lie.
punchline: Wally's supposed productivity boost is a fabrication; the coffee has only made him a more convincing liar about work he never did.
summary: A slacker coworker's claims of coffee-fuelled achievement turn out to be nothing but a better-polished fib.

title: Blaming Climate Change for Lateness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. My alarm didn't go off because my town lost power and my phone battery died.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And we lost power because the state closed down the last coal power plant to reduce CO2 emissions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So really, the fault lies with climate change, not me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Slow clap.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Wally arrives late to a meeting holding his coffee mug and explains a chain of events: a power outage killed his alarm and phone, caused by the state closing its last coal plant. He concludes that climate change is to blame rather than himself, while Alice and Dilbert listen, and Dilbert responds with a sarcastic slow clap.
punchline: Wally stretches a convoluted causal chain so far that he can blame global climate change for his own tardiness, and Dilbert sarcastically applauds the absurd excuse.
summary: A late-arriving coworker traces his missed alarm back through a blackout and a closed power plant to pin the blame on the planet's climate.

title: Gaslighting Wife Skips Birthday Present

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's the name of the month that comes after October?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: November.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's what I thought. My wife is trying to gaslight me so she doesn't have to buy me a birthday present.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long has she been doing that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought I was 26 years old until just now.

setting: Office conference table, with both men wearing face masks
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert which month follows October, then claims his wife is gaslighting him so she can avoid buying a birthday present. Dilbert asks how long she has been doing this, and the coworker reveals he believed he was 26 until just now, implying she has been fudging his age for years.
punchline: The man's real age has apparently been hidden from him for years, so he is probably the one who is confused rather than a victim of gaslighting.
summary: A masked coworker blames his wife's trickery for a missing birthday gift, only for it to emerge that he has been wrong about his own age for ages.

title: Tracker Reveals Restroom Stall Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to my employee tracker, you spent 45 minutes in stall four of the men's room today.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I thought you said the purpose of tracking us was to ensure social distancing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you have to accept some responsibility for believing it.

setting: Office, during the COVID-19 pandemic (both wearing face masks)
situation: A masked manager checks his phone and confronts a seated employee about spending 45 minutes in a men's room stall, according to the employee tracking system. The employee points out that the tracker was supposedly introduced to enforce social distancing. The manager replies that the employee is partly to blame for believing that explanation.
punchline: The manager openly admits the tracking was really for surveillance and blames the employee for being gullible enough to believe the pandemic-safety excuse.
summary: A boss uses his pandemic distancing tracker to monitor a worker's bathroom breaks, then shrugs off the deception by saying the worker was foolish to trust him.

title: Basing Decisions on Career of Errors

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you're wrong.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What error did I make?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm basing my decision on your entire career of being wrong about everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope I'm not the first person to point that out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Give me a minute to reassess my entire life.

setting: Office meeting table, with both men wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert tells a masked coworker across the table that he thinks the coworker is wrong. When asked what mistake was made, Dilbert explains that his judgment rests on the coworker's whole career of being wrong about everything. The stunned coworker says he needs a minute to reassess his entire life.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt insult implies the coworker has never been right, and the coworker's reaction shows he is genuinely shaken into questioning his whole existence.
summary: A man's disagreement with a colleague turns into a devastating verdict on the colleague's entire professional record, leaving him questioning everything.

title: Threatening to Cancel Gets Easier Paperwork

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Just fill out these five pages of information, and we're good to go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cancel the order, and I'll find an easier vendor to work with.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: In that case, all I need is your signature.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That worked?

setting: Office meeting table, both wearing face masks
situation: A vendor's salesman asks Dilbert to fill out five pages of information to complete an order. Dilbert refuses and threatens to cancel and go to an easier vendor. The salesman instantly drops the paperwork requirement and asks only for a signature, surprising Dilbert.
punchline: The vendor's onerous paperwork turns out to be optional and vanishes the moment the customer threatens to leave, showing the requirement was never really necessary.
summary: A customer discovers that a supplier's tedious forms disappear the instant he threatens to take his business elsewhere.

title: Motivosity Bucks Instead of Real Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks for working all weekend to get the project done, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I award you two Motivosity bucks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like real money better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That just cost you two Motivosity bucks.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss thanks Dilbert for working all weekend and rewards him with two Motivosity bucks, a fake employee-recognition currency. When Dilbert says he would prefer real money, the Boss punishes the complaint by taking the two bucks back.
punchline: The worthless token reward is immediately revoked as a penalty for pointing out that it is no substitute for actual pay, showing how hollow and controlling such recognition schemes are.
summary: A manager pays an employee for a weekend of overtime in a pretend currency, then fines him in that same currency for preferring cash.

title: Coworker Urges Maskless Freedom, Admits Doubt

transcript.speaker: Masked Coworker
transcript.text: That stupid coronavirus is no match for a healthy, young leader such as yourself.

transcript.speaker: Masked Coworker
transcript.text: Freedom demands that you go to crowded indoor spaces without wearing your mask.

transcript.speaker: Seated Employee
transcript.text: Are you trying to kill me?

transcript.speaker: Masked Coworker
transcript.text: I'd say there's reasonable doubt.

setting: Office break area with a table and coffee
situation: A coworker wearing a face mask flatters a seated colleague, telling them the coronavirus is no threat to a healthy young leader and that freedom means going maskless into crowded indoor spaces. The colleague asks if they are being set up to die, and the masked coworker coolly answers that there is reasonable doubt.
punchline: The coworker's flattering pro-freedom pep talk is a sarcastic cover for a possible attempt to get the colleague infected, and they all but admit it.
summary: A masked colleague sweet-talks someone into ditching their face mask, then casually concedes that murder might be the motive.

title: Plans That Can't Be Implemented

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow shirt
transcript.text: I'm a pragmatist. I like plans that are practical.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not me. I like plans that can't be implemented.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Way less work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow shirt
transcript.text: My way sounds stupid now.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Two coworkers walk along a hallway while one proudly calls himself a pragmatist who prefers practical plans. Wally, holding his coffee, says he prefers plans that can never be implemented. He explains that this means far less work, leaving the other man feeling foolish.
punchline: Wally's lazy logic is that an unimplementable plan means no work ever has to be done, which makes the earnest pragmatist's approach look foolish by comparison.
summary: A self-described pragmatist gets upstaged by a colleague who prizes plans that will never need to be carried out.

title: Muted Diversity Training Exposed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My records show you completed the online training for diversity and inclusion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently, you did not know we can detect it when you have the sound muted during the entire course.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can do that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but I can trick most of you idiots into confessing.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team that records show they finished the online diversity and inclusion training, then claims the system can detect when the sound was muted throughout the course. One coworker blurts 'Oops,' and Dilbert asks if that's really possible. The Boss admits he can't detect it but tricked them into confessing.
punchline: The Boss bluffed about being able to detect muted training, and the employees' guilty reactions proved the bluff worked, showing both their lack of engagement and his manipulative tactics.
summary: A manager bluffs about monitoring capabilities to expose which employees ignored their mandatory online course.

title: Free Morale Boosts: Punching and Kicking

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for ideas to improve morale without spending money.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We could take turns punching you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No punching!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any other ideas?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did anyone suggest kicking?

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss asks his team at a meeting for zero-cost ideas to improve morale. Alice suggests the staff take turns punching him, and he rejects it. When he asks for other ideas, Wally asks whether anyone has suggested kicking.
punchline: The employees' morale would obviously be improved by physically hurting their boss, and Wally cheerfully proposes an alternative form of violence once punching is ruled out.
summary: A manager hunting for free ways to cheer up his staff gets a hostile suggestion from Alice, and Wally follows it up with one of his own.

title: Dogbert Teaches Tech Support Stonewalling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dogbert, I need you to train Asok to fill in for you on tech support.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The goal of tech support is to convince the caller the problem is on their end.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I do this by recommending increasingly difficult things for them to try.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eventually, they give up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Watch and learn.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-huh... Uh-huh... Try rebooting your computer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now try it again while holding control-escape-space bar-delete for exactly 27.3 seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No luck? Try looking at your computer's binary code to find any zeros and ones that are out of order.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Aaand he's gone.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Genius!

setting: Tech support desk in the office
situation: The Boss asks Dogbert to train Asok to cover tech support. Dogbert explains his method and demonstrates it on a phone call, telling the caller to reboot, then to hold an absurd key combination for an exact time, then to inspect binary code for misplaced zeros and ones. The caller hangs up and Asok is impressed.
punchline: Tech support's real goal is not fixing problems but making tasks so absurd that callers give up and blame themselves.
summary: A dog schools a young colleague in the art of driving frustrated callers to abandon their support requests with ridiculous instructions.

title: Realizing You're Dumb, Too Late

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We need to make decisions based on real data!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who do you imagine disagrees with that obvious statement?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I just realized I'm dumb and never knew it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear it can sneak up on you.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with attendees wearing face masks
situation: A masked coworker declares in a meeting that decisions should be based on real data. Dilbert sarcastically asks who could possibly disagree with something so obvious. The coworker then realizes he may be dumb himself, and Dilbert deadpans that it can sneak up on a person.
punchline: Dilbert implies the coworker's idea of presenting an obvious statement as insight is itself a sign of ignorance, and that people often don't notice their own stupidity until it hits them.
summary: A man in a meeting proudly announces a painfully obvious principle, and Dilbert's sarcasm leads him to a belated, unflattering self-discovery.

title: Infected Callers Over the Phone

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Scientists say our smartphones can spread the coronavirus.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's why I no longer answer the phone. You never know if the caller is infected.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't think. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let it go.

setting: Conference room during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: Three masked coworkers sit at a meeting table. One reports that scientists say smartphones can spread the coronavirus, then explains he has stopped answering his phone because the caller might be infected. Another coworker starts to object, but Dilbert tells him to let it go.
punchline: The coworker misunderstands how contagion works, believing a phone call itself can transmit the virus, and Dilbert recognizes the logic is so absurd that correcting it isn't worth the effort.
summary: A masked colleague takes a warning about germy phones to an absurd extreme by refusing calls in case the caller is contagious, and a teammate is told not to bother correcting him.

title: Passion for Porcelain Frogs Isn't Career

transcript.speaker: Job candidate
transcript.text: I still live with my parents because I can't find a job that matches my passion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is your passion?

transcript.speaker: Job candidate
transcript.text: I collect porcelain frogs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That isn't a career.

transcript.speaker: Job candidate
transcript.text: How is that my fault?

setting: Office interview desk
situation: Dilbert is interviewing a bearded man who complains that he still lives with his parents because no job fits his passion. When Dilbert asks what the passion is, the man says he collects porcelain frogs. Dilbert points out that this isn't a career, and the man indignantly asks how that is his fault.
punchline: The candidate blames the world for not offering jobs in his absurdly impractical hobby, refusing to take any responsibility for his unemployment.
summary: A man living with his parents insists no job suits his passion for collecting porcelain frogs and resents being told that's not a career.

title: Medical-Grade Coffee Straight To Veins

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I drink so much coffee that I developed a tolerance for it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have any kind of medical-grade coffee that could take me to the next level?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Yes, but it has terrible side effects.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Skip the details and shove it in my veins.

setting: Doctor's examination room
situation: Wally sits on an exam table and tells his doctor he has built up such a tolerance to coffee that it no longer works on him. He asks for a stronger, medical-grade version, and when the doctor warns of terrible side effects, Wally insists on getting it intravenously anyway.
punchline: Wally's caffeine addiction is so extreme that he willingly ignores medical warnings and demands coffee injected directly into his bloodstream.
summary: A caffeine-dependent employee begs his physician for a stronger prescription-strength brew and waves off all safety concerns.

title: Karma Joins the Team

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think karma is real?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet the newest member of our team. His name is Karma.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be hiding.

transcript.speaker: Karma
transcript.text: I hear one of you has been bad.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether karma is real, and Wally dismisses the idea. A new employee whose name happens to be Karma is then introduced to the team. Dilbert nervously announces he will go hide, and Karma says he has heard that one of them has been bad.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally casually dismissed karma, and then a new coworker literally named Karma shows up and announces he's looking for whoever has been bad, so the concept comes to get them.
summary: After a casual chat doubting cosmic justice, the team is introduced to a new colleague whose name is the very thing they just scoffed at.

title: Hate-Edits Mock Colleague's Analysis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't like your analysis, so I made some hate-edits.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's a hate-edit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll see.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You changed "in my opinion" to "according to the squirrels in my skull."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There you go.

setting: Office, with face masks worn (2020), ending on an exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, hands a coworker a printed copy of his analysis and says he has made 'hate-edits' because he disliked it. The confused coworker asks what that means, then reads the page and finds that Dilbert has replaced a sincere phrase with an absurd, insulting one.
punchline: A hate-edit is a petty, sarcastic rewrite that mocks the author's reasoning, here by implying his opinions come from squirrels rattling around in his head.
summary: A man gets back his work with spiteful, silly rewrites that turn his confident opinion into a joke about rodents in his brain.

title: Zoom Masks and Hating People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't need a mask for a Zoom call.

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: Can you back up that claim with a randomized clinical study?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed it's a lot easier to hate people lately.

setting: Dilbert's home office during a video call
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker on a Zoom call that a mask isn't needed for video meetings. The coworker, wearing a mask on screen, demands a randomized clinical study to back up the claim. Dilbert, standing with his coffee next to Dogbert, responds by observing how easy it has become to hate people.
punchline: Dilbert's casual remark gets met with a demand for scientific proof, which tips him into admitting that pandemic-era arguments have made hating people easier.
summary: A simple comment about masks on video calls draws a pedantic demand for scientific evidence and leaves Dilbert feeling more misanthropic.

title: Medical-Grade Coffee Gives Superpowers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've had a lot of side effects since I switched to medical-grade coffee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On the plus side, I can see through plywood, and I no longer need a tool to open jars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You couldn't open jars before?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's not dwell on that point.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Wally walks alongside Dilbert holding a cup of coffee and boasts about the side effects of switching to medical-grade coffee. He lists gaining X-ray vision through plywood and the ability to open jars without a tool. Dilbert asks whether he couldn't open jars before.
punchline: Wally treats being unable to open a jar as a minor detail next to gaining X-ray vision, and his evasive reply admits he was always too weak to do it.
summary: A coworker brags about the strange superpowers his special coffee gave him, then dodges the embarrassing implication that he was previously unable to open a jar.

title: Wally Already Socially Distances

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to practice "social distancing" until the virus risk has passed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I already do that. I haven't hugged anyone since the eighties.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good job. High-five.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Back off.

setting: Office desk
situation: The boss tells Wally to practice social distancing during a virus outbreak. Wally replies that he already does, since he hasn't hugged anyone since the eighties. The boss congratulates him and offers a high-five, and Wally tells him to back off.
punchline: Wally's natural aversion to human contact makes him a social distancing expert, and the boss immediately violates the practice by offering a high-five.
summary: A manager asks his employee to keep his distance during a pandemic, only to discover the man has been doing so for decades and then break the rule himself.

title: Elbonian Factory Disaster Downplayed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have some problems in our Elbonian factory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How bad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They lost power on the main floor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The employees were scared.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They'll get over it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One of them tripped in the dark.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Big deal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He accidentally opened a gas line.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A little gas never hurt anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now there's a crater where the capital city used to be.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's keep an eye on that.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert reports a series of escalating problems at the company's Elbonian factory, starting with a power outage and ending with a gas line explosion. The Boss dismisses each new development as no big deal. Even when Dilbert reveals the capital city has been reduced to a crater, the Boss only says to keep an eye on it.
punchline: The Boss's indifference to the factory's problems is so complete that he casually shrugs off the destruction of an entire capital city as something merely to monitor.
summary: A manager waves away each worsening piece of news from an overseas plant, right up to a catastrophic explosion.

title: Boss Fakes Dilbert's Firing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Marketing is complaining that you're not using their ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because all of their ideas are moronic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told them I fired you. Don't leave your cubicle or use any digital devices until this blows over.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that Marketing is upset because he isn't implementing their ideas. Dilbert says the ideas are moronic, and the Boss does not argue. Instead, he announces he has told Marketing that Dilbert was fired and orders him to stay hidden in his cubicle and off all digital devices until it blows over.
punchline: Rather than defend Dilbert or confront Marketing's bad ideas, the Boss takes the cowardly route of lying that Dilbert is fired and making him pretend not to exist.
summary: Faced with a department angry that its poor suggestions are being ignored, the manager solves the problem by pretending his engineer no longer works there.

title: Consulting the Dumbest Person Deliberately

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ted is the dumbest human being in the known universe. His opinion can only make things worse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's how we do it here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't realize it was a strategy.

setting: Office, with workers wearing face masks
situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup tells Dilbert, who is working at his laptop, to get Ted's input before finalizing the plan. She then explains that Ted is the dumbest human being in the known universe and that his opinion can only make things worse. When Dilbert questions the logic, she says that is simply how they do things there.
punchline: The company deliberately seeks advice it knows is terrible, and Dilbert realizes this self-sabotage has been an unacknowledged strategy all along.
summary: A colleague casually admits that the office routinely consults its least capable person about plans, a habit that apparently counts as company policy.

title: Suspecting the Elbonian Spy Hire
