transcript.text: Is it you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but I don't see how that excuses you.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: In a masked meeting, a woman announces that data security has detected an Elbonian spy in the company. The Boss suggests it might be the Elbonian man someone hired, and Dilbert calls that super racist. The Boss then asks if the spy is Dilbert, who admits he is, but says that doesn't excuse the Boss's remark.
punchline: Dilbert condemns the Boss's stereotyping as racist, then admits he is the spy anyway, so the Boss's accusation was accidentally correct and his own indignation is hypocritical.
summary: A manager's prejudiced guess about who is the foreign spy gets rebuked, until the rebuker turns out to be the culprit himself.

title: Racists Follow You On Twitter

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting reports from your staff that you're a white supremacist.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But I'm not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have proof because you follow racists on Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What makes you think they are racists?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because they follow you on Twitter.

setting: Office hallway, with both characters wearing face masks during the pandemic
situation: The Boss tells an employee that staff reports claim he is a white supremacist. When the employee denies it, the Boss cites proof that he follows racists on Twitter. The employee asks how the Boss knows they are racists, and the Boss answers that they follow the employee.
punchline: The Boss's accusation rests on circular logic: the employee is guilty because of the racists he follows, and those people are racists only because they follow him.
summary: A manager tries to justify a damaging accusation with reasoning that chases its own tail.

title: Thanking The Boss For Leadership

transcript.text: Are you done?

transcript.text: I just want to thank you for all the leadership.

setting: Boss's office, with both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert reports to his boss, who is sitting at a desk looking at his phone, that he followed orders to gather input on his project from a range of people less capable than himself. He explains the result was that everything got worse. When the boss impatiently asks if he's finished, Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for the leadership.
punchline: Dilbert's thank-you for the boss's "leadership" is pure sarcasm, blaming the boss's order to seek input from less informed people for making the project worse.
summary: After being told to consult a crowd of less knowledgeable colleagues, an employee reports the predictable mess and sarcastically credits his manager's guidance.

title: Guessing Won't Hurt Your Career

transcript.text: I need a quick decision on this, but I don't have time to compile the relevant facts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Without facts, I would just be guessing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It won't affect your career average.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's change the subject.

setting: Office conference room, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: The Boss hands Alice a document and demands a quick decision without having gathered any facts. Alice objects that she would only be guessing, and he reassures her that a wrong guess won't hurt her career average. When she asks why not, he abruptly changes the subject.
punchline: The Boss implies that Alice's career average is already so poor that one more bad guess can't make it worse, then dodges the obvious follow-up question.
summary: A manager pushes his employee to decide on something with no supporting information, assuring her that a wrong call hardly matters and then evading her question about why.

title: Distracting Dilbert While He Designs Deadly Software

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you ever think about the fact that one small error in your software design could kill hundreds of people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All it would take is some kind of distraction while you are trying to concentrate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A real man could multitask in this situation.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss hovers behind Dilbert while he works on his laptop and ominously reminds him that a single software error could kill hundreds of people, and that a distraction while concentrating is all it would take. When Dilbert asks if he's finished, the Boss says a real man could multitask through it.
punchline: The Boss is the very distraction he describes, then insults Dilbert's masculinity for being unable to concentrate through his interruptions.
summary: A manager rattles an engineer by listing the lethal consequences of a coding slip, then mocks him for not being able to work through the interruption.

title: Spreadsheet Calculates Delay Replying to Boss

transcript.text: Seven.

transcript.text: You can wait 27 minutes before responding.

situation: Wally asks Dilbert how long he should wait before replying to a text from his boss. Dilbert asks a series of questions about workload, grudges and the timing of the next performance review, then feeds the answers into a spreadsheet. The result is a 27-minute wait, which disappoints Wally, who wanted five days.
punchline: Wally wants to wait five days to reply, but it turns out the boss's text arrived back in August, so he has already ignored it for months.
summary: A coworker consults a spreadsheet to decide how long to leave his boss's text unanswered, only to reveal he has already ignored it for months.

situation: Dilbert gets a text asking if he is available for a Zoom call and watches the typing indicator start and stop while he waits for a reply. He answers with a long list of times, including now, then grows frantic when the other person does not respond to his proposal. Thirty minutes later the other person finally asks if now works, and Dilbert angrily rejects it.
punchline: Dilbert offers 'now' as an option, then becomes so enraged by the delayed reply that he refuses the very time he proposed, showing how petty and irrational impatience over scheduling messages can be.
summary: A man's maddening wait for a text reply about scheduling a video call ends with him rejecting the slot he offered himself.

title: Boss Judges Performance By Heuristics

transcript.text: Do you even know what my job is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course I do. You're an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but do you know what projects I'm working on?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, various things, and some miscellaneous things, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you determine my job performance when you don't know what my job is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you heard of heuristics? You're bad at everything I've observed, so I assume you are bad at everything else as well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should have started with that.

setting: Boss's office, during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't give him a good performance review because he hasn't met expectations. Dilbert asks whether the Boss even knows what his job or projects are, and the Boss can only vaguely say 'various things.' The Boss then justifies the poor rating by claiming heuristics: Dilbert is bad at everything he has observed, so he must be bad at everything else.
punchline: The Boss admits he has no real knowledge of Dilbert's work and rates him poorly by generalizing from a few observations, a flimsy rationale Dilbert says he should have admitted from the start.
summary: A manager with no idea what his engineer actually does defends a bad evaluation by extrapolating from a few unflattering observations.

title: Solutions, Not Problems, Says Worthless Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to bring me solutions, not problems!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a funny way to call yourself worthless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I do plenty around here!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But in the interest of time, I will not list any examples.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: At a meeting table, the Boss demands that his staff bring him solutions rather than problems. Dilbert replies that this is a funny way for the Boss to call himself worthless, since the Boss himself only ever hands out problems. The Boss protests that he does plenty, and Dilbert politely declines to list examples, implying there are none.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss contributes nothing useful himself, and by refusing to list examples 'in the interest of time' he implies the Boss's accomplishments are nonexistent.
summary: When a manager insists on receiving only answers and never difficulties, an employee turns the demand around to expose how little the manager actually contributes.

title: Threatening Someone With a Stick

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: A wise person once said you can't boil an egg with a stick.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, but I can threaten you with a stick unless you boil an egg for me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why didn't the wise person think of that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He sounds overrated.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Asok holding a coffee cup quotes a wise saying that you can't boil an egg with a stick. Wally, also holding coffee, points out that he could instead threaten Asok with a stick unless Asok boils an egg for him. Asok asks why the wise person never thought of that, and Wally dismisses the sage as overrated.
punchline: Wally treats coercion and delegating work as a cleverer solution than the proverb's wisdom, concluding that the wise person must be overrated.
summary: A coworker's bit of proverbial wisdom gets undermined by a lazy colleague whose answer is to bully someone else into doing the work.

title: Threatening Sales VP Or Salesman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got feedback on the proposed package design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our VP of Sales says if we go with this design, he will "jump off the roof."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is he crazy or just good at selling?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No way to tell.

setting: Office, with characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert reports feedback on a proposed package design to a coworker, saying the VP of Sales threatened to jump off the roof if the design is approved. The coworker wonders whether the VP is actually unstable or just using a dramatic sales tactic. Dilbert admits it is impossible to tell.
punchline: The VP's threat is so extreme that it is indistinguishable from a persuasion technique, making it unclear whether he is unhinged or simply a skilled salesman.
summary: A sales executive's melodramatic objection to a product design leaves his colleagues unable to judge whether he is unstable or just persuasive.

title: Banana Versus Apple Argument

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not hungry today. Do you want my banana?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's an apple.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... No. This is a banana.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Clearly it is not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't believe you are making me do a Google search to prove I know what a banana is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See? Those are bananas. This looks just like the photos. This is a banana.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Those images are doctored.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are a million banana images! They are not all doctored!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know how I know you are wrong? Because you never admit you are wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gotcha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is not a thing!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's exactly what all the people who are wrong say.

setting: Office conference table, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert offers the Boss his banana, and the Boss insists it is an apple. Dilbert does a Google search to prove it is a banana, but the Boss claims the photos are doctored. The Boss then argues that Dilbert must be wrong because he never admits being wrong.
punchline: The Boss uses unfalsifiable circular logic in which any denial of being wrong is itself treated as proof of being wrong, so no evidence could ever convince him.
summary: A manager stubbornly denies obvious fruit facts and dismisses all evidence with a logic trap that makes disagreement itself proof of error.

title: Happiness No Longer Matters, Apparently

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that we used to talk about employee morale . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But now we talk about "engagement" and "workplace culture." Why is that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We found out it doesn't matter if you are happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me to never ask another question.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks during the pandemic
situation: Dilbert, standing in a mask, observes that the company has stopped discussing employee morale and now uses terms like engagement and workplace culture. A panel of the office building follows as he asks why. Alice, seated with a coffee, bluntly says management learned that employee happiness doesn't matter, and Dilbert wishes he hadn't asked.
punchline: Corporate buzzword changes reveal that management doesn't actually care whether employees are happy, only whether they are productive and engaged.
summary: A new vocabulary for talking about staff satisfaction turns out to hide the unpleasant fact that nobody in charge cares how workers feel.

title: Reducing Theft Isn't Eliminating It

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And by using this system, we will drastically reduce theft.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's the dumbest thing I have ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No one can stop theft everywhere in the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said we would reduce it, not eliminate it. And only for our own products.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So, in other words, it won't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It works to reduce theft.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But you admit there will still be theft.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What is wrong with you????

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not the one who is in favor of theft.

setting: Conference room in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert presents a system that will drastically reduce theft of the company's products, but a skeptical coworker keeps dismissing it because it can't eliminate theft everywhere. As Dilbert patiently clarifies, the coworker grows more irrational and eventually explodes in anger, moving from calling the idea dumb to demanding what is wrong with Dilbert.
punchline: By insisting that anything short of total elimination is a failure, the coworker ends up sounding like someone who favors theft, which Dilbert points out.
summary: A colleague rejects a plan because it can't achieve perfection, until his stubborn illogic gets turned back on him.

title: Guilt By Photo Association

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't be your friend because I saw a disturbing photo of you on social media.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You were in a group photo with a person whose opinions I abhor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you explain why that makes me a bad person?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sure. Duh.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When you appear in photos with other people, you acquire their bad characteristics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think that's how it works.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's exactly how it works! One photo with a jerk makes you a jerk! Case closed!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Smile.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No-ooo!!!

setting: Office conference table
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert she can't be his friend because she saw a photo of him on social media standing with someone whose opinions she despises. She insists that appearing in a photo with a bad person transfers their bad traits to you. Dilbert responds by holding up his phone to take a photo of the two of them together.
punchline: Dilbert turns her own guilt-by-association logic against her by threatening to photograph her with him, a supposed jerk, which terrifies her.
summary: A coworker's theory that photos spread bad character backfires when Dilbert offers to snap a picture of them together.

title: Fired Man Frames Alice Aloud

transcript.speaker: Fired Coworker
transcript.text: I have been unjustly accused of being a white supremacist, and my boss just fired me for it.

transcript.speaker: Fired Coworker
transcript.text: Alice is the obvious choice to take my job, so I assume you will hear something on that soon.

transcript.speaker: Fired Coworker
transcript.text: I wish I knew who had the motive to start that rumor and get me fired.

setting: Conference room during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: A coworker holding a box of his belongings tells Dilbert and Alice that he was fired over a false accusation of being a white supremacist. He points out that Alice is the obvious person to replace him, then says he wishes he knew who had the motive to start the rumor. Alice sits right there while he all but accuses her.
punchline: He claims not to know who started the rumor while loudly pointing out that Alice had the most to gain, so his supposed puzzlement is really a thinly veiled accusation.
summary: A newly fired man with a box of his things insists he cannot imagine who smeared him, while carefully pointing the finger at the woman who benefits from his dismissal.

title: Non-Credible Data Is Credible If Flattering

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I finished the data throughput tests, but the results are not credible because of a problem with the test.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Boss (offscreen, from the building)
transcript.text: Does the non-credible data make us look good?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Boss
transcript.text: Our name for that kind of data is "credible."

setting: Conference table in an office meeting, with a building exterior shown in the middle panel
situation: Alice, wearing a face mask, tells a manager across the table that her data throughput test results are unreliable because of a flaw in the test. The manager asks whether the flawed data makes the company look good. When Alice says yes, the manager declares that this kind of data is officially considered credible.
punchline: Management defines data as credible based on whether it flatters the company rather than whether it is accurate.
summary: A manager happily accepts a flawed test result as trustworthy the moment he learns it casts the company in a favorable light.

title: Training Replacement With Deliberate Omissions

transcript.speaker: Trainee
transcript.text: I can't shake the feeling that you are intentionally doing a bad job training me how to do your job functions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm omitting important steps, so you'll fail hard should I get fired and you are asked to fill in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called a "poison pill."

transcript.speaker: Trainee
transcript.text: You're a good planner.

setting: Office cubicle, sitting in front of a computer
situation: Dilbert is cross-training a co-worker on his job duties. The co-worker suspects the training is deliberately poor, and Dilbert cheerfully admits he is leaving out key steps so that the co-worker will fail if Dilbert is fired and the co-worker has to take over.
punchline: Dilbert sabotages his own cross-training as a self-protective 'poison pill', and the co-worker responds with deadpan admiration for his planning.
summary: An employee quietly undermines the handover of his duties so that anyone who replaces him is set up to stumble.

title: Proving Dilbert Doesn't Believe Safety

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ugh. Dilbert is on the project team? That guy doesn't believe in safety.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Just out of curiosity, what evidence of that extremely weird allegation have you seen?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What evidence do you have that you exist? See? Anyone can do that.

setting: Office conference room during the pandemic, with a video call on screen
situation: A colleague complains that Dilbert, shown on a video screen in a chef's hat, is on the project team and claims he doesn't believe in safety. A coworker in a face mask asks what evidence supports this odd accusation. She deflects by demanding he prove his own existence, claiming anyone can do that.
punchline: Instead of providing evidence for her baseless accusation, she turns the question around with an absurd demand, showing that anyone can dodge a request for proof with a ridiculous counter-challenge.
summary: A coworker slanders a teammate with an unsupported claim and, when pressed for proof, dismisses the challenge with a silly philosophical retort.

title: Destroyed Prototypes on Fired Employee's Word

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We destroyed all of the prototypes as you requested.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I never asked for anything remotely like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted said you did.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did he tell you that before or after I fired him last week?

setting: Office meeting room or desk, with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the team destroyed all the prototypes because the boss requested it. The boss denies ever asking for such a thing. Dilbert says Ted told him so, and the boss points out that he fired Ted last week.
punchline: Dilbert acted on an instruction relayed by a man who was already fired, so the prototypes were destroyed on bogus authority and the boss shrugs off any responsibility.
summary: A costly mistake is traced back to a secondhand order passed along by someone who no longer even works there.

title: Fear Itself Will Kill You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have nothing to fear from the coronavirus but fear itself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Obviously, the fear will increase your cortisol levels and depress your immune system so the virus can finish you off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dead man walking!

setting: Conference room table
situation: Dilbert reassures Dogbert that the only thing to fear from the coronavirus is fear itself. Dogbert explains that fear raises cortisol, weakens the immune system and lets the virus finish you off. Dilbert becomes visibly frightened, and Dogbert declares him a dead man walking.
punchline: Telling someone that being afraid will make the virus deadlier only makes them afraid, which by that logic makes them doomed.
summary: A comforting pep talk about not fearing a pandemic collapses when Dogbert points out that fear itself is what makes the virus dangerous.

title: Fixed It After Five Years

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote a software patch that will save three million dollars per year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel as if I deserve a bonus or a raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When did you do it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long did we have the problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Five years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you should have fixed it five years ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks like a gigantic failure to me. You should be ashamed of yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you try my strategy for keeping payroll expenses low?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Works like magic.

setting: The Boss's office, with a final scene in a purple-lit room
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he wrote a patch that will save three million dollars a year and asks for a bonus or raise. The boss learns the patch took a week to write for a problem that existed for five years, and turns it into a reason to shame Dilbert instead of rewarding him. Dogbert then asks the boss if his strategy for keeping payroll low is working, and the boss agrees it is.
punchline: The boss twists a valuable accomplishment into a failure to deny a raise, which is exactly Dogbert's cynical payroll-cutting strategy at work.
summary: A programmer asking for a reward for a money-saving fix is told he should be ashamed for not doing it years earlier.

title: Harvard Graduate's False Modesty Major

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What college did you go to?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'd rather not say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only people who answer that way are people who went to Harvard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do they teach you false modesty?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was my major.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with both characters wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks a masked coworker which college he attended, and the coworker evasively says he'd rather not say. Dilbert observes that only Harvard graduates answer that way, then jokingly asks if false modesty is taught there. The coworker replies that it was his major.
punchline: By proudly claiming 'false modesty' as his college major, the coworker reveals he is a Harvard graduate bragging about his school while pretending to be humble.
summary: A man who coyly refuses to name his alma mater is called out as a Harvard alum and cheerfully confirms it with a joke about his degree.

title: Empty Office Brings Flatulent Freedom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The office is a beautiful place when everyone else is working from home.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No distractions, private bathroom, and I no longer need to suppress my bodily noises.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Brraaap!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Freedom!

setting: An empty office, with an exterior view of the office building in the final panel
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, is alone in the office because everyone else is working from home. He enjoys the quiet and the private bathroom, then adds that he no longer has to hold in his bodily noises. The last panel shows the office building from outside as a loud burp or fart echoes out, followed by a cry of 'Freedom!'
punchline: The one thing Dilbert loves most about the empty office is that he can finally be as loud and gassy as he likes, and the noise is so loud it rings out of the building.
summary: With his coworkers all working remotely, a masked Dilbert revels in the deserted workplace and lets loose a bodily noise that echoes across the whole building.

title: Compilation Video of Incompetent Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You think I didn't do anything useful this year.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: So I made a compilation video of my co-workers being incompetent in meetings for comparison.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At least they are trying.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: As you can see, maybe they shouldn't.

setting: Office meeting room table
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker defends his usefulness this year by saying he made a video compiling clips of other coworkers being incompetent in meetings, to serve as a comparison. The Boss, sitting across from him, responds that at least those coworkers are trying. The coworker retorts that the video shows they would be better off not trying.
punchline: The coworker's only contribution is a mean-spirited video, and he turns the Boss's defense of effort on its head by claiming his colleagues' attempts are so bad they'd do less harm doing nothing.
summary: An employee justifies his year's work by filming colleagues flubbing meetings, then dismisses their effort as worse than idleness.

title: Odds Giver Refuses Any Blame

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I estimate the odds at a 70% chance things go well, and a 30% chance we lose money on the deal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we lose money, will you admit you were wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could I be wrong? I'm just telling you the odds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we lose money, that's on you for recommending it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no. I'm telling you the odds and letting you decide.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you're the one saying this is such a great deal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm only telling you the ODDS, you pea-brained ignoramus!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you won't admit you were wrong?

setting: Office meeting table, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert presents a risk estimate of a 70% chance of success and a 30% chance of losing money. The Boss keeps trying to pin responsibility on Dilbert for recommending the deal if it fails. Dilbert insists he only supplied probabilities and that the decision belongs to the Boss, and eventually loses his temper.
punchline: The Boss is so fixated on assigning blame that he cannot grasp the difference between stating odds and making a recommendation, and keeps asking for an admission of wrongness even after Dilbert has exploded at him.
summary: A manager insists his employee must own the outcome of a decision even though the employee only supplied the probabilities.

title: Sarcasm Earns Extra Safety Camp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear you were being sarcastic about safety.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Obviously, you don't take safety seriously, so I have to send you to a safety re-education camp for a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will totally fix this problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You just bought yourself an extra week.

setting: Office hallway, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert, who is holding a coffee cup, about being sarcastic regarding workplace safety. He announces Dilbert will be sent to a week-long safety re-education camp as punishment. Dilbert responds with more sarcasm, and the Boss adds another week to the sentence.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic reply proves the Boss's point that he doesn't take safety seriously, so the punishment gets longer, showing that sarcasm just gets punished harder.
summary: A manager sentences a sarcastic employee to safety re-education, then lengthens the sentence when the employee mocks it.

transcript.text: You might be lying about not changing your opinion.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And you might be hallucinating or lying or just stupid.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You might be trying to gaslight me right now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm glad we can have these honest talks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you plunge to your death in a freak elevator accident.

setting: Office, with a final exterior shot of the office building
situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert for supposedly changing his opinion since last week, and Dilbert insists he hasn't. The coworker keeps insisting, accusing Dilbert of lying, hallucinating, being stupid or gaslighting him. In the last panel, the two voices speak over a shot of the building: the coworker praises their honest talks while Dilbert wishes him a fatal elevator accident.
punchline: Dilbert's polite-sounding wrap-up is actually a sarcastic reply, as he says out loud the hostile wish he has been holding back during an argument in which the coworker claims to know Dilbert's opinion better than Dilbert does.
summary: A pushy coworker insists he knows Dilbert's own mind better than Dilbert does, and Dilbert answers with a darkly polite death wish.

title: Dogbert Hides Rent in DocuSign

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, for one thing, it's the only way you can pay your rent.

transcript.text: Rent? I own this house.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a blue armchair
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair with Dogbert, who is looking at a phone, and wonders aloud whether earning money is worth losing his soul. Dogbert replies that money is needed to pay rent. Dilbert is confused because he owns his house, and Dogbert reveals that Dilbert unknowingly signed documents electronically that changed that.
punchline: Dilbert has unwittingly signed away ownership of his own house by e-signing documents from Dogbert without reading them, so he now owes rent.
summary: A man questions the value of money, only to learn his dog has quietly turned him into a tenant in his own home through documents he never read.

title: Project Phase: Death Spiral Blame

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or is it in the middle phase, in which everyone is grinding away and hating the other team members?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's in the death spiral phase.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone is trying to assign blame to someone they already hate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They requested that I add you to the team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To save the project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... Okay, sure.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to a network redesign project, and Dilbert asks what phase it is in, suggesting hopeful early or grinding middle stages. The Boss admits it is in the death spiral phase where everyone is hunting for someone to blame. Dilbert assumes he was requested to save the project, and the Boss awkwardly goes along with it.
punchline: Dilbert was really added to the doomed project as a convenient scapegoat, but the Boss lets him believe he was brought in as the savior.
summary: A manager sends an employee to a failing project where the team is hunting for a scapegoat, and lets him think he's the rescuer.

title: Conflict Resolution By Insulting Everyone

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.text: Watch me use my conflict resolution skills to lower the temperature.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Okay, what were you idiots yammering about?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Solid start.

setting: Office hallway during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: Two coworkers are in the middle of a heated argument when Asok walks up and announces he will use his conflict resolution skills to cool things down. He then calls the two of them idiots and asks what they were yammering about. One of the arguers sarcastically calls it a solid start.
punchline: Asok's idea of conflict resolution is to insult the people arguing, which obviously inflames the situation, and the sarcastic reply 'Solid start' mocks his failed attempt.
summary: A confident peacemaker steps into a quarrel and promptly makes it worse by name-calling the participants.

title: Reorganized Lab, Ungrateful Co-Workers Cursing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Were your co-workers grateful?

transcript.text: Yes, assuming they show it by rummaging through the wrong drawers and cursing.

setting: Lunch table in a break room or office
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at a table eating lunch. Dilbert says he reorganized the tech lab, and Dogbert asks if his co-workers were grateful. Dilbert sarcastically replies that they were, if gratitude looks like searching the wrong drawers and swearing.
punchline: Dilbert's reorganization made things harder to find, so his co-workers' frustration is the only 'thanks' he gets, and he wryly calls it gratitude.
summary: After tidying up a shared lab, a man discovers that his colleagues can no longer find anything and are far from thankful.

title: Betting Lives on Either Outcome

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you sure?

transcript.text: I'd bet my life on it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd bet your life on it, too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd win either way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if we're agreeing.

setting: Conference room table in an office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, asks the Boss if he is sure about something. The Boss confidently says he would bet his life on it, and Dogbert replies that he would bet the Boss's life on it too. Dogbert then notes he wins either way, leaving the Boss unable to tell whether they agree.
punchline: Dogbert places a bet that costs only the Boss's life, so he profits whether the Boss is right or wrong, while the oblivious Boss can't even tell if they're in agreement.
summary: A consultant happily wagers his client's life on a claim, guaranteeing himself a win no matter what, while the client remains clueless.

title: Secretly Loving Pandemic Social Isolation

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Two masked coworkers chat while getting coffee. One asks the other how he coped with the lack of social contact during the pandemic. Dilbert says it was the best weeks of his life, and the coworker admits he felt the same but didn't want to say it first.
punchline: Both introverted coworkers actually enjoyed the pandemic isolation but were too embarrassed to admit it until someone else did.
summary: Two masked office workers sheepishly confess over coffee that being cut off from other people was something they secretly loved.

title: Stapler Safety Training Before Stapler Fight

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: But now you're fresh and ready for the fight?

transcript.text: Only if it's a stapler fight.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting room
situation: The boss asks Dilbert what he has accomplished since that morning's planning meeting. Dilbert explains that his only activity was a mandatory training class on stapler safety. The boss, apparently missing the point, asks if he is now ready for the fight, and Dilbert answers that he is only ready for a stapler fight.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic reply shows that his only newly acquired skill is pointless stapler safety, so he is useless for any real work.
summary: A manager demands progress hours after a planning meeting, but the employee has spent the time on irrelevant compliance training.

title: Hot Job Market Means Hiring Morons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The job market is so hot right now that we can only afford to hire morons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will we fill our critical technical jobs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just told you.

setting: Conference room meeting
situation: At a meeting table, the Boss explains that because the job market is hot the company can only afford to hire morons. Dilbert asks how the critical technical jobs will be filled, and the Boss replies that he has just answered that question.
punchline: The Boss's plan to fill critical technical jobs is to hire morons, which he thinks he has already explained, showing he sees no problem with putting unqualified people in important roles.
summary: A manager declares that budget limits mean only unqualified hires are possible, then is baffled that anyone would ask how skilled positions will get filled.

title: Too Many Dogberts, Read a Book

transcript.text: I'd bump it up to five Dogberts, but then we risk creating a singularity event.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't get it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Read a book.

setting: Conference room in the office
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells the Boss that three copies of himself are already on the marketing plan and it still isn't enough. He warns that adding two more would risk a singularity event. The confused Boss admits he doesn't get it, and Dogbert curtly tells him to read a book.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the Boss's ignorance of the technological singularity with a curt suggestion to educate himself instead of explaining.
summary: A consultant cloned several times over claims further duplication would trigger a runaway intelligence event, then brushes off his clueless client's confusion.

title: No Adapter For Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The hardware you ordered is not compatible with our network.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just buy an adapter.

transcript.text: I don't think anyone makes an adapter that can fix stupidity.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert walks up to a coworker holding a coffee cup and tells him the hardware he ordered won't work with the company network. The coworker casually suggests simply buying an adapter. Dilbert replies that no adapter can fix stupidity.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the real incompatibility is the coworker's poor judgment in ordering the wrong hardware, and no product can fix that.
summary: A technician delivers the bad news about mismatched equipment and answers a glib fix with a cutting insult about the buyer's intelligence.

title: Allergy Meds Make Dilbert Dumber

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I took allergy meds last night, and now I have brain fog.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My I.Q. is about 50% of normal capacity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoo-hoo! I'm smarter than an engineer!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not quite. I'm only down by 50%.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that allergy medication has left him with brain fog and only half of his normal IQ. The Boss gleefully claims that this makes him smarter than an engineer. Dilbert corrects him, saying he is only down by 50%, so he is still ahead.
punchline: Even at half his intelligence, Dilbert is still smarter than his boss, which means the Boss's pride at beating an engineer is misplaced.
summary: A drowsy engineer gets a bit of a dig in after his manager mistakenly thinks a drug-addled brain finally puts them on equal footing.

title: Assuming Common Sense Fills Specs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is, unless you gave me the wrong specs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assumed you would use your common sense to know what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did your common sense help you make that assumption?

setting: Office desk or conference table
situation: A manager complains that the deliverable Dilbert produced isn't what he wanted. Dilbert replies it matches the specs, so the manager says he assumed Dilbert would use common sense to figure out what he really wanted. Dilbert turns the argument around and asks whether the manager's own common sense guided that assumption.
punchline: The boss blames Dilbert for lacking common sense, but Dilbert sarcastically points out that assuming someone can read your mind is itself a failure of common sense.
summary: When a manager faults an employee for not guessing unstated requirements, the employee snidely questions the manager's own judgment in expecting that.

title: Thanking Everyone Except Slowing-Down Ted

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to thank everyone who made the project a huge success.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except for Ted, who made everything twice as hard as it needed to be.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I can hear you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're slowing us down again, Ted.

setting: Conference room table, during a video or phone meeting
situation: Dilbert sits at a laptop with coffee and thanks the team for a successful project. He then singles out Ted, who is apparently on a remote audio link, for making everything twice as hard as necessary. Ted replies that he can hear him, and Dilbert accuses him of slowing everyone down again.
punchline: Dilbert publicly insults Ted behind his back, forgetting or not caring that Ted is on the call, and then simply doubles down by blaming him for the delay of the conversation.
summary: A project wrap-up speech turns into a public dig at a remote colleague who is listening in the whole time.

title: Whisper Campaign Against Baby-Eating Rival

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm starting a whisper campaign against my rival in management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to tell people he buys babies from the poor and eats them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one is dumb enough to believe that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People will believe anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. I'll try it, but only to prove how wrong you are.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How many does he eat per day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a new planet.

setting: Office meeting room, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to start a whisper campaign claiming his management rival buys babies from the poor and eats them. Dilbert insists nobody would believe something so absurd, but the Boss insists people will believe anything. Dilbert tries it to prove him wrong, and a coworker promptly asks how many babies the rival eats per day.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to prove people are not gullible backfires instantly, as the coworker believes the absurd rumor and asks for details, leaving Dilbert to wish he could escape humanity.
summary: A manager's absurd smear rumor is tested by a skeptical employee, who discovers just how gullible his coworkers really are.

title: Stupidity Extinguishes Project, Transfer to Marketing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's your project going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was doing fine until a thick wave of stupidity swept over it and extinguished my spark of divinity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what will become of me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll transfer you to marketing. They're all like that.

setting: Conference room
situation: A manager with a topknot hairstyle asks Dilbert how his project is going. Dilbert dramatically laments that a wave of stupidity destroyed his project and his creative spark, and wonders what will happen to him. The manager casually offers to transfer him to marketing, where everyone is the same.
punchline: The manager's solution to Dilbert's complaint about stupidity is to move him to marketing, implying that department is full of exactly the kind of people who caused the problem, so Dilbert will fit right in.
summary: After a florid complaint that foolishness ruined his work, Dilbert is offered a move to marketing, a department said to be full of the same.

title: Self-Love Instead of Self-Improvement

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Philosophers say loving yourself is the greatest love of all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do philosophers really say that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All the good ones do.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: After years of trying, I have finally learned to love myself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm no philosopher, but instead of learning to love yourself the way you are . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be better if you learned how to stop being an evil, ignorant, selfish piece of garbage?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds a lot harder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In other words, you are lazy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I love that about me!

setting: Office cubicle
situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup announces that philosophers say self-love is the greatest love, and that he has finally learned to love himself. Dilbert suggests it would be better to stop being an evil, ignorant, selfish person instead. The coworker says that sounds harder, and when Dilbert calls him lazy, he happily embraces that too.
punchline: The coworker chooses accepting his flaws over the harder work of fixing them, and cheerfully loves his own laziness as well.
summary: A man proudly claims to have mastered self-love, but it turns out to be an easy excuse for never improving.

title: Talking To Avoid Listening

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work every day, and yet I am not feeling completely self-actualized.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's that mean?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know. It's something I heard.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are we even talking about it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because the more I talk, the less I have to listen to you.

setting: Office conference table
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a coworker and announces that despite working every day he doesn't feel self-actualized. When asked what that means, he admits he has no idea and only repeated a phrase he heard. When the coworker questions why they are discussing it, Dilbert reveals his real motive.
punchline: Dilbert doesn't care about the topic at all; he just keeps talking so that he doesn't have to listen to his coworker.
summary: A man babbles about a buzzword he doesn't understand purely to keep a colleague from getting a word in.

title: Lunch Suggestion Designed To Fail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do you want to go to lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want you to suggest a place so I can say yes but still make you feel bad about it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How about the Thai place?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pffft. Sure. I'm not that hungry anyway.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker where she wants to go for lunch, then openly explains that he wants her to suggest a place so he can agree while still making her feel bad about it. When she suggests the Thai place, he dismissively agrees with a sigh and says he isn't that hungry anyway, carrying out exactly the guilt trip he announced.
punchline: Dilbert announces his passive-aggressive plan in advance and then follows through with it, making the coworker feel bad even though she knows exactly what he is doing.
summary: A man asks a colleague to choose a lunch spot purely so he can grudgingly accept it and make her feel guilty.

title: Too Late to Start Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't seem to be working.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't want to start something new because it's almost the end of my work day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's ten o'clock in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And here comes the micro-managing.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The boss approaches Wally, who is leaning back in his chair with his feet up on the desk, and points out that he isn't working. Wally claims it's too close to the end of his day to start anything new. The boss checks his watch and says it's only ten in the morning, and Wally complains that this is micro-managing.
punchline: Wally treats a basic factual correction about the time as unreasonable micro-management, showing how shamelessly he avoids work.
summary: A slacking employee uses a ridiculous excuse for idleness, then accuses his boss of hovering when the excuse is debunked.

title: Promotion To Master Engineer, No Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting you to the position of "Master Engineer."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm already a Senior Engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you're a Master Engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With all of the rights and responsibilities that come with it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Such as...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, for example, you can do more kinds of work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For more pay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no, no!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're thinking of "Platinum Level" engineers. You're not one of those.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That comes next?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Optimism is not an attractive quality.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss announces he is promoting Dilbert from Senior Engineer to Master Engineer, but the only perk is permission to do more kinds of work. When Dilbert asks if it comes with more pay, the Boss says that is reserved for a higher 'Platinum Level' tier. Dilbert hopefully asks if that is the next step, and the Boss shoots him down.
punchline: The promotion is just a new title that adds work without any extra pay, and the Boss mocks Dilbert for being naive enough to hope for a real reward.
summary: A manager hands out a fancy new job title whose only benefit is extra duties, then dismisses any hope of advancement as unattractive optimism.

title: Thought Leader Won't Use Calendar

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ask my assistant to put it on my calendar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't you just put it on your calendar right now?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm more of a thought leader. I don't like to work with my hands.

setting: Office meeting table
situation: Dilbert is trying to schedule something with a coworker, who tells him to go through the coworker's assistant to get it onto the calendar. When Dilbert asks why the coworker can't simply add it right now, the coworker explains that as a 'thought leader' they avoid doing any hands-on work.
punchline: The coworker uses the pretentious title 'thought leader' to excuse laziness, claiming that even a trivial task like typing a calendar entry is beneath them.
summary: A self-important colleague refuses to schedule a simple appointment himself, insisting his lofty status means he doesn't do manual tasks.

title: Karma Strikes the Coronavirus Hoax Denier

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you keep saying the coronavirus is a hoax, you are practically begging the universe to infect you.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Don't be so superstitious. That's not how anything works, you moron.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Cough cough

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, karma! Not me!

setting: Office hallway by an elevator
situation: Two coworkers wait by an elevator. The masked one warns the bald coworker, who keeps calling the coronavirus a hoax, that he's tempting the universe to infect him. The bald coworker dismisses this as superstition, then immediately coughs, and the masked coworker cowers in fear.
punchline: The man who scoffed at superstition coughs right after dismissing it, and the masked coworker who also claimed karma isn't real panics that karma is about to hit him instead.
summary: A masked worker's warning about tempting fate is brushed off as nonsense, until a sudden cough sends everyone scrambling.

title: Dilbert Won't Read Emailed Article

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I get your thoughts on the article I emailed to you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. My thoughts are that I don't want to waste my time reading any articles you send to me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you dive a bit deeper?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I also don't like talking to you.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: A coworker stands beside Dilbert's desk and asks for his thoughts on an article he emailed. Dilbert bluntly says he won't waste time reading anything the coworker sends. When the coworker asks him to elaborate, Dilbert adds that he also dislikes talking to him.
punchline: Asked to dive deeper into his feedback, Dilbert simply doubles down on the insult, adding a second reason to avoid the coworker.
summary: A colleague seeking feedback on an emailed article gets an unvarnished refusal, followed by an even blunter explanation when he presses for more detail.

title: Armed Drones Meet Gazebo Neighbor

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For use by the military?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Good idea. I hadn't thought of that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's too dangerous for private use.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You sound just like my neighbor when he still had a gazebo.

setting: Office hallway
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert his company bought a start-up that builds autonomous drones armed with machine guns. Dilbert asks if they are meant for the military, and the coworker says he hadn't thought of that use. When Dilbert warns they are too dangerous for private use, the coworker likens him to a neighbor who complained before his gazebo was destroyed.
punchline: The implication is that the coworker has already tested the armed drones on his neighbor's gazebo, treating a lethal weapon like a petty neighborhood feud tool.
summary: A man casually reveals his company's armed robot drones and then hints he has already used them to destroy a neighbor's backyard structure.

title: Dilbert Refuses Handshake, Spreads Virus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry, I no longer shake hands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can practically see the viral load on that filthy paw of yours.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't "see" a virus.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee-hee! That's how we getcha.

setting: Office hallway
situation: A coworker extends his hand for a handshake, but Dilbert refuses, claiming he can practically see the viral load on the coworker's hand. The coworker points out that viruses are invisible, and Dilbert gleefully replies that this is exactly how viruses get you, as the coworker's hand is shown with a speckled, dirty look.
punchline: Dilbert's cheerful answer that invisibility is precisely how viruses infect people turns the coworker's rebuttal into an argument for Dilbert's own germophobia.
summary: A man's attempt to shake hands is rebuffed by Dilbert, whose paranoia about invisible germs proves unshakable.

title: Solid Analysis Built on Wild Guesses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How confident are you in your analysis?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Very confident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unless I used the wrong discount rate, which is hard to know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But otherwise, it's solid?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except for the installation and maintenance costs, which are wild guesses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we don't know if we sized the project right, so costs could be double or triple.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It sounds as if you applied math to a bunch of wild guesses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but I got the result you wanted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next time, just say that.

setting: Office, with masked employees (2020 pandemic era)
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how confident he is in his analysis. Dilbert says he is very confident, then keeps adding caveats: the discount rate may be wrong, the installation and maintenance costs are wild guesses, and the project may be sized wrong so costs could double or triple. The Boss summarizes it as math applied to guesses, and Dilbert admits it produced the result the Boss wanted.
punchline: The analysis is really just guesswork dressed up with math to reach the conclusion management wanted, and the Boss's only complaint is that Dilbert didn't say so up front.
summary: An engineer's confident-sounding analysis turns out to rest on a pile of guesses, but it delivers the answer his manager was hoping for.

title: Pandemic Income Survivor Guilt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I personally doubled my income during the pandemic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I have a bad case of survivor guilt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you expect to get much sympathy for that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't know until I try.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with coworkers wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: Three coworkers in face masks stand around with coffee while the Boss, looking at his phone, brags that he doubled his income during the pandemic. He then claims to be suffering survivor guilt. Dilbert asks whether he expects sympathy, and the Boss says he will only find out by trying.
punchline: The Boss shamelessly announces that profiting from a pandemic has left him emotionally burdened, then admits he is just testing whether anyone will feel sorry for him.
summary: A boss who got richer during the health crisis fishes for compassion over his supposed guilt, and his colleague calls out how absurd that request is.

title: Avoiding Work By Ignoring Messages

transcript.text: I rarely see you working. How do you get away with it?

transcript.text: For example, here's Alice asking if I can attend a meeting in an hour.

transcript.text: I'll answer her in the morning and say I didn't see her message.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And here's Dilbert asking me for some data.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tomorrow, I will text him to ask for clarification, and he will tell me he found the data on his own.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't you feel guilty?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah. They'd do the same to me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And do they?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They would if I didn't ignore them first.

setting: Office conference room
situation: A coworker asks Wally how he avoids doing any work. Wally explains that he waits a day before replying to texts and emails, so people either give up or solve their own problems. When asked if he feels guilty, he claims others would do the same to him.
punchline: Wally justifies his habit of ignoring colleagues by claiming they would ignore him too, but admits they only don't because he ignores them first.
summary: A slacker shares his foolproof method for dodging work: letting every message sit unanswered until the sender gives up.

title: Masked Meeting Insults the Boss

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: That is a dumb idea, you pointy-haired fool.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who mumbled that? I can't tell with your face masks.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Meetings just got a lot more fun.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who is saying that???

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: During a meeting where everyone wears face masks, someone mutters an insult calling the Boss a pointy-haired fool. The Boss cannot tell who said it because the masks hide everyone's mouths. The anonymous speaker realizes this and gleefully notes that meetings are now more fun, while the Boss angrily demands to know who is talking.
punchline: Face masks make it impossible to identify who is insulting the Boss, so employees can now trash his ideas with no consequences.
summary: Pandemic face masks give meeting attendees the perfect cover to insult their clueless boss without being identified.

title: Unwelcome Advice Gets Insulted Back

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I give you some helpful advice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Leave my personal life out of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's talk about the putrid quality of your work.

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: A coworker peeks around a cubicle wall, both wearing face masks, and offers Dilbert some helpful advice. Dilbert replies that the coworker's own life is too poor for them to give advice. When the coworker objects to the personal jab, Dilbert switches to criticizing the coworker's work instead.
punchline: Dilbert only agrees to drop the personal insults so he can substitute equally harsh insults about the coworker's professional performance.
summary: An offer of friendly guidance is answered with a cutting put-down, and a request for politeness only redirects the abuse toward the offender's job skills.

title: Height Advantage Vanishes on Zoom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl, I hired you because you are tall, but now it doesn't matter because everyone looks the same height on Zoom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your height advantage has disappeared, so today will be your last day with the company.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Maybe instead you could cut my pay to the same level as short people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That just might work.

setting: Office video call (Zoom) between the boss and an employee working remotely
situation: The Boss tells Carl, shown on his laptop screen, that he was hired for being tall, but on Zoom everyone looks the same height. He announces Carl is fired, but Carl offers a pay cut to the level of short people instead, and the boss readily agrees.
punchline: Carl's attempt to save his job by proposing a pay cut is accepted immediately, showing the boss is more interested in cutting costs than in fairness, and that hiring based on height was absurd to begin with.
summary: A boss decides a worker's tallness is worthless in video meetings, and the worker cheerfully negotiates his way into a salary reduction rather than a firing.

title: Novel Idea Meets Jealous Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking about writing a novel.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stay in your lane!

transcript.text: I'm not ambitious and I have intense hate-jealousy for anyone who is!

transcript.text: I was looking for some encouragement.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die!

setting: Office cubicle during the pandemic, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert, wearing a mask, tells a coworker he is thinking about writing a novel. The coworker, also masked, angrily tells him to stay in his lane and admits she is unambitious and bitterly jealous of anyone who is. Dilbert mildly notes he wanted encouragement, and she responds by shouting 'Die!' repeatedly.
punchline: Dilbert seeks support for his ambition but gets hostile envy instead, and the coworker's unhinged escalation to 'Die! Die! Die!' shows how badly she handles other people's drive.
summary: A man's creative aspiration is met with furious resentment from an unambitious colleague who has no interest in cheering him on.

title: Accused by Staff Who Want Job

transcript.text: Who gets to decide?

situation: Catbert, acting as human resources, tells a masked manager that staff members have complained he is a white supremacist. The manager denies it and asks who gets to decide, and Catbert replies that it is the people who want his job.
punchline: Accusations of misconduct are decided by the people who stand to gain from them, so the system is open to being used as a weapon for personal advancement.
summary: An HR cat informs a manager he has been accused of a serious offense and cheerfully admits the verdict is delivered by his own would-be replacements.

title: Pandemic Bonus Earned Wearing Socks

transcript.speaker: Catbert

setting: Executive office during the pandemic, both wearing face masks
situation: Catbert, acting as the HR director, tells the masked Boss that the company profited so hugely from the pandemic, purely by luck, that his bonus would be ten million dollars. The Boss insists he earned it. Catbert counters by pointing out his only contribution was attending Zoom calls wearing only socks.
punchline: The Boss claims credit for a windfall bonus, but Catbert deflates him by noting his sole contribution was embarrassingly minimal and silly, exposing how executive pay often rewards luck rather than merit.
summary: An HR chief questions whether a manager deserves a lucky pandemic windfall bonus when all he did was join video meetings in his socks.

title: Fired to Protect Boss's Career

transcript.text: I have to fire you because employees are saying you are a white supremacist.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But I'm not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Doesn't matter. I care more about my career than your life.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You're firing me just to look good?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells an employee he must be fired because coworkers are accusing him of being a white supremacist. When the employee denies it, the Boss says the truth is irrelevant because he values his own career over the employee's livelihood. He then adds that he also needs to punch the employee in front of witnesses to make the show of disapproval convincing.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that the firing is purely about appearances and self-interest, and cheerfully escalates to staging a public punch to maximize the reputational benefit.
summary: A manager sacks a worker over an unproven rumor, admits it is purely career protection, and plans to stage a public beating for good measure.

title: Risking Life for Network Latency

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going into the office to upgrade a server.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my boss, reducing network latency is more important than my life.

transcript.text: Can I depend on you to not change the locks while I'm gone?

setting: Dilbert's home living room, during the pandemic
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, tells Dogbert he must go into the office to upgrade a server because his boss values reduced network latency over his safety. He then asks Dogbert to promise not to change the locks while he is away. Dogbert agrees only on the condition that Dilbert sleep in the garage when he returns.
punchline: Dogbert deadpans that he won't lock Dilbert out only if Dilbert quarantines in the garage, mocking how little the boss's demands account for Dilbert's health or the risk of bringing infection home.
summary: A masked Dilbert grumbles about risking his health for a server upgrade, and Dogbert allows him back in only if he isolates in the garage.

title: Scheduling the Follow-Up Call Spiral

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's schedule a follow-up call.

transcript.text: Do you prefer Zoom, FaceTime, Signal, WhatsApp, or voice call?

transcript.speaker: Remote colleague
transcript.text: Zoom.

transcript.text: How about next Tuesday at 10 a.m. my time, which is 1 p.m. your time?

transcript.text: I'll be on the road then, so your 10 a.m. will be my noon.

transcript.text: But that's after the time change.

transcript.speaker: Remote colleague
transcript.text: And I can't remember if I'm going to a place that change their clocks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't we skip the whole thing because the call we are scheduling probably won't be any more useful than this one.

transcript.speaker: Remote colleague
transcript.text: Let us never speak of this again.

setting: Dilbert's office and the colleague's remote location, shown over a video call on laptops
situation: Dilbert tries to schedule a follow-up video call with a remote colleague. They get tangled in platform choices, time zone differences, travel plans and daylight saving time changes. Dilbert finally suggests skipping the call altogether, since it will be as pointless as this one, and the colleague readily agrees.
punchline: The scheduling conversation is so tedious and unproductive that both agree the future call it is meant to arrange would be equally useless, so they cancel it.
summary: Two coworkers get so bogged down arranging a remote call across time zones that they decide to drop the call entirely.

title: Data Is Unreliable, Guessing Wins

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When humans were primitive and dumb, they used their superstitions and biases to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eventually, science won out, and we evolved to use data and reason to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How'd that work out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It turns out that all of our data are unreliable and conflicting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we don't have the mental capacity to use reason.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's still better than guessing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are hard to talk to.

setting: Conference room table with coffee mugs and snacks
situation: Dilbert explains to Dogbert how humanity moved from superstition-based decisions to data and reason, then admits the results have been poor because data is unreliable and people can't reason well. Dogbert insists it's still better than guessing, and when Dilbert asks how he knows that, Dogbert dodges by complaining Dilbert is hard to talk to.
punchline: Dogbert's claim that data-driven decision-making beats guessing is itself unsupported, and he deflects with a personal insult when asked for evidence, proving the point about humans not using reason.
summary: After a quick history of human decision-making, Dilbert concedes that data and reason have disappointed, and Dogbert defends them with a claim he can't back up.

title: Fish Smell Sends Asok Janitor-Ward

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm working from home. Maybe you should check the cubicles for a rotting corpse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe I'll let the janitor do that.

setting: An office desk, then Asok's home couch, then an office hallway
situation: A coworker phones Asok to complain about the smell of microwaved fish in the office. Asok, sitting on his couch with a laptop, says he is working from home, so the smell cannot be his, and suggests checking the cubicles for a rotting corpse. The coworker, walking down the hallway, decides to leave that unpleasant job to the janitor.
punchline: The coworker blames the wrong person for the smell and, rather than investigate a possible corpse, passes the unpleasant task to the janitor.
summary: A smell complaint gets aimed at a remote worker who can't possibly be the source, and the caller shrugs the problem off onto someone else.

title: Lowering Expectations Equals Happiness, Says Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Asok, the key to happiness is lowering your expectations.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: For example, all I expect from work today is twelve cups of coffee and a humorous display of corporate dysfunction.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That sounds so sad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Try expecting excellence and see how that works for you.

setting: Office desk or conference table
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker advises Asok that happiness comes from lowering expectations, and explains that he only expects coffee and some entertaining corporate dysfunction from work. Asok says that sounds sad, and the coworker sips his coffee and tells him to try expecting excellence instead.
punchline: The coworker implies that expecting excellence at a dysfunctional company only leads to disappointment, so cynicism and caffeine are the rational way to cope.
summary: A jaded colleague teaches a young engineer that the secret to workplace contentment is expecting nothing good, and dares him to hope for better.

title: We're Definitely Not a Monopoly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government is threatening to regulate us like a monopoly.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are we not a monopoly?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We are simply a company that makes an essential product for modern life, and we have no real competition.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounds like a monopoly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, we are not a monopoly because other companies could compete with us if they wanted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if they tried?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as they got some traction, we'd buy them and shut them down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... they would fail every time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they could try.

setting: Office hallway, with employees wearing face masks
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that the government wants to regulate the company as a monopoly. He insists it isn't one, since rivals could theoretically compete, then admits the company would acquire and shut down any competitor that gained traction. Dilbert points out that means competitors always fail.
punchline: The Boss's claim that competition is possible is hollow, because the company destroys any competitor that tries, which is exactly how a monopoly behaves.
summary: A manager argues his company can't be a monopoly because rivals are free to try, while admitting that every successful rival would simply be bought and killed.

title: Termites in Clothes Learn Makeup

transcript.speaker: The Boss
