situation: Dilbert and the Boss, both wearing face masks, walk down a hallway and wait at an elevator. The Boss admits he is a poor judge of character because his last three hires were actually termite colonies dressed as people. Dilbert asks how the termites disguised their faces, and the Boss says they used YouTube makeup tutorials.
punchline: The Boss's terrible hiring judgment is explained by the absurd claim that termite colonies in clothes fooled him, helped along by online makeup videos.
summary: A boss blames his hiring blunders on insect colonies wearing human disguises complete with tutorial-based cosmetics.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

situation: Dilbert and his coworkers learn that Ted can't attend a meeting whose only purpose is to hear Ted's project update. Dilbert suggests everyone else leave so that coworker can also guess what the rest of them would have said, and the coworker is left alone doing exactly that.
punchline: The coworker is so committed to holding a pointless meeting that he ends up alone in the room imagining everyone else's contributions as well.
summary: A meeting that exists solely to hear from an absent colleague gets saved by a stubborn coworker who keeps it going by role-playing everyone.

situation: During a meeting, a man in a green sweater decides he must say something to look attentive. He offers a vague concern about the project reducing employee engagement. A colleague asks what that actually means, and he realizes he has no answer prepared.
punchline: He made a meaningless buzzword statement purely to look engaged, and he is caught out when someone expects him to explain it.
summary: A meeting participant blurts out an empty buzzword concern just to seem attentive, then panics when a coworker asks him to clarify.

punchline: The staff are so unfamiliar with the company's stated values that they can't even say whether theft is against them, showing that value posters have no real effect.
summary: A boss's break-room values poster goes unnoticed by his team, who can only speculate about what ethics the company actually demands.

title: Experts Recommend Horoscopes Over Data

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on the couch watching a news report on TV. The report claims a study found all data is wrong and that experts now recommend horoscopes and guesswork for decisions. Dilbert remarks that his co-workers already decide that way, and Dogbert says they were ahead of their time.
punchline: Dilbert's co-workers have always made decisions by guesswork and horoscopes, so the experts' new advice just proves them right, which is a sarcastic dig at poor workplace decision-making.
summary: While watching the news, Dilbert and Dogbert learn that experts now endorse star signs and hunches, which his colleagues have been doing all along.

title: Testing Fake Confidence on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it working?

situation: Asok walks up to Dilbert, who is seated at a table looking at his phone, and boasts that the room needs more of him. He sits down and keeps bragging. Dilbert, still on his phone, asks if he's trying out fake confidence, and Asok anxiously asks whether it's working.
punchline: Asok drops the confident act the moment he's called on it, nervously asking if his bluster is convincing, which shows how little real confidence he has.
summary: A young employee tries out an overblown boast about his own importance, only to seek reassurance when a coworker spots the act.

title: Boss Doesn't Know If 5G Dangerous

transcript.text: How would I know?

transcript.text: Maybe I should study it first.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Conference room, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to respond to a reporter who claims the company's 5G technology is dangerous. When Dilbert asks whether it actually is dangerous, the Boss admits he has no idea. Dilbert suggests studying it first, and the Boss dismisses him and says he'll find someone else to respond.
punchline: The Boss wants a rebuttal to safety concerns without caring whether the concerns are true, and he rejects Dilbert as soon as he proposes doing actual research.
summary: A manager demands a rebuttal to a safety accusation but abandons the employee who wants to investigate whether it's true.

situation: A coworker sits at a table and confidently declares the coronavirus is a hoax no worse than a common cold. Dilbert, wearing a face mask and looking at his phone, warns that he is tempting fate. The coworker panics and begs not to be jinxed, but Dilbert says it is already too late.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests the coworker has doomed himself by dismissing the pandemic, implying he will inevitably catch the virus.
summary: A pandemic skeptic brushes off the virus until a masked colleague dryly assures him his bravado has sealed his fate.

summary: A meeting participant fires off impressive-sounding blockchain buzzwords, then confesses to a skeptical coworker that it was all made up on the spot.

summary: A masked coworker presses Dilbert over a software testing commitment he insists never existed, and Dilbert calmly predicts the coworker will keep pushing.

title: Dogbert's Embezzling Clone Consultants

punchline: Dogbert learned the hard way that he is a thief, since his clones embezzled from him, and he treats this unflattering truth about himself as the end of his self-discovery.
summary: After filling his firm with copies of himself, Dogbert watched them all rob him and gained some unwelcome insight into his own character.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is working from home to avoid the coronavirus and will therefore be home 24 hours a day. summary: A man isolating at home during a pandemic discovers that his dog considers the arrangement a misfortune for the dog alone.

summary: A coworker proves her own brilliance with a loop of logic that Dilbert can't help but question, earning him an unmasked scolding.

summary: A worker demands a raise after years of service, only to learn his manager had no idea he existed and decides that anonymity is the better outcome.

title: Job Candidate's Disrespect for Authority

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say are your weaknesses?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I have a deep disrespect for authority.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: But... you don't act on it, right?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Let's not take the surprise out of it.

setting: Job interview in an office, with the interviewer wearing a face mask
situation: An interviewer wearing a face mask asks a job candidate to name his weaknesses. The candidate calmly says he has a deep disrespect for authority. When the interviewer hopefully asks if he doesn't act on it, the candidate refuses to promise anything and says he'd rather keep it a surprise.
punchline: The candidate implies he absolutely does act on his disrespect for authority and wants to keep the future insubordination a surprise for his new employer.
summary: A hiring manager's reassurance-seeking question about a candidate's rebellious streak is met with an ominous refusal to spoil the fun.

title: Brainstorming Drone Attack on Protesters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anti-gun advocates are complaining because we bought a start-up that makes drones with machine guns.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our best bet is to lure them into some sort of outdoor protest event and...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bad idea. Very bad!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Don't be judgmental during the brainstorming.

setting: Conference room
situation: Dilbert tells a colleague that anti-gun advocates are complaining about the company's acquisition of a start-up making machine-gun drones. Asok proposes luring the protesters to an outdoor event, clearly implying they would be attacked. Dilbert panics at the idea, and Asok scolds him for judging ideas during brainstorming.
punchline: Asok's brainstorming 'solution' is to massacre the protesters with the company's armed drones, and he treats Dilbert's horrified objection as a breach of brainstorming etiquette.
summary: A colleague's cheerfully sinister plan to deal with gun-drone critics is shut down in horror, only to be defended as a sacred part of the idea-generation process.

title: Boss Yells at Kids During Zoom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do you think you can get me that estimate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get off the couch with your shoes! No! No! No! Do not throw the iPad! Aaagh! I am going to strangle you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you like working at home?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm on a Zoom call! I said I'm on a call!!!

setting: Dilbert's home desk, on a video call
situation: Dilbert asks his boss over video when he can have an estimate. The boss, visible only on the laptop screen, ignores him and screams at unseen children misbehaving in his home. Dilbert then asks how he likes working from home, and the boss yells that he is on a call.
punchline: The boss's chaotic home life, which he is oblivious is audible to everyone on the call, shows how working from home blurs family and work, and his sarcastic-sounding yet sincere shouting about being on a call makes the point.
summary: A manager's video meeting is overrun by him shouting at his rowdy kids, turning a simple question into a vivid look at remote-work chaos.

title: Brain Fog, Halved IQ, Handsome

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have brain fog from the meds I took last night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My I.Q. is down by 50%, but I make up for it by being handsome.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sounds more like a 75% situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now, can someone remind me of my name?

setting: Office break area where coworkers stand holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells Alice and Wally that medication he took the night before has left him foggy. He claims his I.Q. has dropped by half but that his good looks compensate. Alice replies that the drop is closer to 75%, and Dilbert then asks someone to remind him of his own name.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic correction implies Dilbert is even dumber than he admits, and his forgetting his own name proves her point.
summary: A groggy engineer brags that looks offset his medication-induced mental slump, only for a coworker to mock the estimate and his own memory lapse to confirm it.

title: Underpaid Tech Writers Hate Everyone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is your writing so angry?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Tech writers are underpaid, so all of our envy and contempt spill out on the page.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you tech writers should drink less coffee and exercise more.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: This is exactly why we hate everyone.

setting: Conference room
situation: Dilbert, holding a document he has been reading, asks Tina why her technical writing sounds so angry. Tina explains that tech writers are underpaid, so their envy and contempt leak into their work. Dilbert responds with glib health advice about coffee and exercise, which proves her point.
punchline: Dilbert's condescending, oblivious advice to fix a pay-and-respect problem with lifestyle tweaks demonstrates precisely why tech writers resent everyone.
summary: A tech writer admits her bitterness comes from low pay, and the engineer's patronizing wellness tip only confirms her contempt.

title: Social Media Poisoning Diagnosis Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I have social media poisoning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It makes me feel defensive and angry all the time, but I can't quit.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've gained five pounds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You fat-shaming quack!

setting: Doctor's examination room
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, tells his doctor he thinks he has social media poisoning, explaining that it makes him constantly defensive and angry but he can't stop using it. The doctor calmly notes that Dilbert has gained five pounds. Dilbert immediately explodes in outrage, accusing the doctor of fat-shaming.
punchline: Dilbert's furious overreaction to a simple medical observation proves his own diagnosis of social media-induced defensiveness and anger.
summary: A patient complains that online platforms have made him perpetually touchy, then promptly demonstrates the symptom when his physician mentions a weight gain.

title: Dunning-Kruger Accusation Backfires on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: The Dunning-Kruger effect is strong in you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, you can't know if I am suffering from it or if you only think I am because YOU have it.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Only a narcissist talks that way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel as if I have no path to glory here.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper tells Dilbert that the Dunning-Kruger effect is strong in him. Dilbert replies that she can't be sure he has it rather than her projecting it. She then calls him a narcissist for saying so, leaving him stuck.
punchline: Any defence Dilbert offers is treated as proof of the accusation, so he is trapped in a no-win argument where she wins by default.
summary: A coworker's armchair psychology diagnosis leaves Dilbert unable to win, since every rebuttal is taken as further evidence against him.

title: Fired Vendor Replaced By Subsidiary

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We will no longer be using you as a vendor because you have not performed.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I already knew that because you replaced us with one of the subsidiaries of my parent company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, at least it isn't you.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Who do you think they subcontract that work to?

setting: Dilbert's office desk, on the phone
situation: Dilbert phones a vendor to tell them they are being dropped for poor performance. The vendor replies that Dilbert's company has already replaced them with a subsidiary of the vendor's own parent company. Dilbert takes comfort that at least it isn't the same vendor, but the vendor reveals the subsidiary subcontracts the work back to them.
punchline: Switching vendors accomplishes nothing when the replacement simply subcontracts the work back to the original underperforming vendor.
summary: A client thinks he has escaped a bad supplier, only to learn the new one quietly hands the job right back to them.

title: Customers Lost to Disinfectant Poisoning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our factories are back online, but we have no buyers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It turns out that our customer base overlaps with the people who recently poisoned themselves with household disinfectants.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Who could have seen that coming?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won a bet on it.

setting: Office meeting room, with masked employees during the 2020 pandemic
situation: Dilbert stands beside a screen showing revenue at $0 and explains that the reopened factories have no buyers. He says the customers are the same people who recently poisoned themselves with household disinfectants. A seated coworker holding a coffee asks who could have predicted it, and Dilbert replies that he won a bet on it.
punchline: Dilbert had predicted that the company's customers were the sort of people who would drink disinfectant, and he cashed in on the bet while the business collapsed.
summary: A company reopens its factories only to find its buyers have been wiped out by their own reckless pandemic behavior, which one employee had bet would happen.

title: Co-workers Are All Huge Liars

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What did you accomplish this week?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I helped several of my co-workers solve critical problems.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And if I asked them to validate your claim?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They're all huge liars.

setting: Conference room, with both people wearing face masks
situation: Alice, seen from behind at a conference table, asks Wally what he accomplished this week. Wally claims he helped several co-workers solve critical problems. When Alice says she could ask those co-workers to confirm it, Wally preemptively dismisses them all as liars.
punchline: Wally knows his claim is fabricated, so he discredits any potential witnesses in advance, revealing he made up his accomplishment.
summary: A worker pads his weekly achievements with a boast and then smears everyone who could contradict him.

title: Too Many Questions, One-Way Mars Trip

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our space division asked if you would accept the honor of being their first astronaut to Mars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't know they had even tested it for safety yet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He asked too many questions.

setting: Office, with masked employees
situation: A coworker tells the Boss that the company's space division wants him to be the first astronaut sent to Mars. The Boss responds that he didn't know the spacecraft had even been safety tested yet. In the last panel the coworker, now with Wally and Dilbert, explains the Boss is gone because he asked too many questions.
punchline: The Boss was volunteered for a dangerous Mars mission as punishment, because questioning the safety of the project made him a liability to management.
summary: A manager who probes whether a Mars spacecraft is safe finds himself drafted as its first passenger.

title: Designing Headphones to Frustrate Customers

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've designed these over-ear headphones for maximum customer annoyance.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The charging port is only on one side, so the user has a fifty percent chance of guessing wrong.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And the charger only fits if you put it in right-side up.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: To increase the frustration, I made the plug look the same on both sides.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Best of all, the plug is so poorly designed that half the time it doesn't seem to fit, even when you put it in correctly.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I made the headphones black, so you can't easily find the charger hole in low light.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Ninety percent of users will be cursing us every time they try to recharge.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Customers won't know any of this until after they purchase.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ship it.

setting: Conference room
situation: Ratbert presents a pair of over-ear headphones he has deliberately designed to be as annoying as possible, listing flaws like a one-sided charging port, a plug that looks the same on both sides, and black casing that hides the port in low light. The Boss listens throughout, then approves the product for release.
punchline: Customer frustration is treated as a design goal, and the Boss approves shipping because customers only discover the flaws after buying, mocking real products that seem designed to annoy users.
summary: A tiny designer proudly details every way his headphones will infuriate buyers, and his manager gives the go-ahead to sell them.

title: No Handshakes, Awkward Banter Instead

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: To avoid spreading viruses, there will be no shaking hands in the workplace.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That custom has been replaced by uncomfortable body language and awkward banter about not shaking hands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are high-fives still okay?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Yes, we don't care if those people live or die.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with masked employees
situation: Employees sit around a conference table wearing face masks while a new workplace rule banning handshakes is announced. A caption notes the rule just leads to awkward body language. Dilbert asks whether high-fives are still allowed, and the answer reveals management's callous attitude toward the people involved.
punchline: The reply that high-fives are fine because management doesn't care if 'those people' live or die exposes how arbitrary and half-hearted the pandemic safety rules are, and how little concern there is for employees.
summary: A new no-handshake policy is announced during the pandemic, and a question about high-fives draws an answer that reveals management's indifference to anyone's survival.

title: Trust Exercise Fails Immediately

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, team. We can get this done if we trust each other.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not a thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't trust any of you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe we can pretend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd need to pretend we're different people.

setting: Office building exterior, then a conference room table
situation: The Boss, speaking from offscreen over a shot of the office building, tells the team they can finish the project if they trust each other. Alice dismisses trust as nonexistent and Dilbert admits he trusts none of his coworkers. Wally suggests pretending to trust, and Dilbert says that would only work if they were different people.
punchline: The team's mutual distrust is so complete that even faking trust would require imagining their colleagues as entirely different people.
summary: A manager's call for teamwork based on trust is met with blunt admissions that nobody on the team trusts anyone.

title: Managing With Data, Without Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to manage with data!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we have any useful data?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not really.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... actually, we need to get data before we can use data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have time for your analysis paralysis!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you're taking both sides of the same argument.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You insist on using data, but you don't want to wait for data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called leadership. You wouldn't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, I think I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop being such a mask hole.

setting: Office hallway and conference room, with both characters wearing face masks; final panel shows the office building exterior
situation: The Boss announces that the team must manage with data, then admits there is no useful data. When Dilbert points out that data must be collected before it can be used, the Boss dismisses him for 'analysis paralysis.' Dilbert notes the contradiction, the Boss calls it leadership, and Dilbert calls him a 'mask hole' from outside the building.
punchline: The Boss demands data-driven management but refuses to wait for data, and Dilbert caps the argument by turning the Boss's pandemic-era mask-wearing into an insult.
summary: A manager insists on data-driven decisions while refusing to gather any data, and an employee answers his illogic with a pandemic-flavored insult.

title: Full-Length Mirror Coronavirus Risk Insult

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you worried about coronavirus because you're in a high-risk group?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why would I be in a high-risk group?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you own a full-length mirror?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, they make me look fat.

setting: Office cubicle area during the coronavirus pandemic
situation: Two coworkers in face masks chat at a cubicle. One asks whether the other is worried about coronavirus because he is in a high-risk group. When he asks why he would be, she sarcastically asks if he owns a full-length mirror, and he reveals he avoids them because they make him look fat.
punchline: The suggestion that he is high-risk is a veiled jab at his weight, and his reply that mirrors make him look fat confirms he is in denial about it.
summary: A masked coworker's question about pandemic vulnerability turns into a barbed hint about a colleague's weight that he cheerfully misses.

title: Spreading Coronavirus To Disliked People

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They say the best way to manage the coronavirus is to spread it to people you dislike.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The happiness you get from that will boost your immune system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll get my medical advice from an actual doctor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They leave out the good stuff.

setting: Conference room table with coffee mugs
situation: Dogbert, sitting across a table from Dilbert, offers dubious pandemic health advice, claiming the best way to handle the coronavirus is to give it to people you dislike. He adds that the resulting happiness will boost your immune system. Dilbert, holding a donut, says he'd rather consult a real doctor.
punchline: Dogbert admits that real doctors omit the 'good stuff', meaning the malicious, self-serving advice he is offering.
summary: Dogbert dispenses gleefully malicious pandemic wellness tips while Dilbert suggests asking a real physician instead.

title: Refusing Stupid Tasks: Field Tested

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you know you can just refuse to do things that are stupid, and it will be okay?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't believe that.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's true! I've been testing it all week.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice (from the office building)
transcript.text: Take a video next time you do it so I can see how.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice (from the office building)
transcript.text: No, that's stupid.

setting: Conference table in an office, with a final panel showing the office building from outside
situation: Asok, wearing a face mask, tells a skeptical Alice that he has discovered you can simply refuse to do stupid things without consequences. When Alice doubts it, he says he has been testing it all week. In the last panel, voices from the building ask for a video of him refusing, and someone else refuses that request as stupid.
punchline: Asking for video proof of someone refusing stupid tasks is itself a stupid request, so the voice immediately gets refused, which demonstrates the theory working.
summary: A young employee claims he has been successfully declining pointless assignments, and the building itself unwittingly provides the experiment's proof.

title: Donating to Violent Protesters' Cause

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All of our retail locations were destroyed by protesters last night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do they hate us?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They don't hate us. We donate to their cause.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I missing some context?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You should see what they do to the people they don't like.

setting: Office conference area
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that all of the company's retail stores were destroyed by protesters overnight. Dilbert asks why the protesters hate the company, and the coworker says they don't, since the company donates to their cause. The final panel shows an office building as the coworker explains that the protesters treat people they dislike even worse.
punchline: The company's donations to the protesters' cause apparently serve as protection money, since being supported still gets your stores destroyed and being disliked would be far worse.
summary: A company that funds a protest movement learns that even its allies trash its shops, and that its enemies fare far worse.

title: Empathy Sensor Is Just Stapler

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You did not have sufficient empathy when I told you my sad story.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could you possibly measure my internal feelings of empathy?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I used my empathy sensor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a stapler.

setting: Office conference room
situation: A coworker in a face mask complains that Dilbert did not show enough empathy when she told him her sad story. Dilbert challenges how she could possibly measure his internal feelings. She claims she used an empathy sensor, but the device she is holding is actually a stapler.
punchline: Her supposedly scientific proof of Dilbert's lack of empathy is a stapler, exposing the accusation as baseless and the measurement as absurd.
summary: A complaint about someone's missing sympathy rests on a bogus gadget that turns out to be ordinary office stationery.

title: Escaping Boring Meetings Via Bathroom Training

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That slide deck in yesterday's meeting was lethally boring.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Luckily, all of my training kicked in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that training taught you to...?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Go to the bathroom and never return.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers wearing face masks and holding coffee
situation: Three coworkers in face masks stand around with coffee. Wally complains that a slide deck in yesterday's meeting was deadly boring, then says his training kicked in. When Dilbert asks what the training taught him, Wally reveals it was to go to the bathroom and never come back.
punchline: Wally's 'training' is simply a technique for slipping out of a tedious meeting under the pretext of a bathroom break and never returning, a lazy way to dodge boredom.
summary: A coworker boasts that his survival training helped him endure a dreary presentation, only to admit it consisted of vanishing to the restroom for good.

title: Spring Cleaning Deletes Incriminating Server Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to do spring cleaning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Delete any data on our servers that make us look like white-collar criminals or drunken baboons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All that leaves is our birthday list.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Torch that too.

setting: Phone call between the Boss's home and Dilbert's living room
situation: The Boss, talking on a phone while walking through his house, orders Dilbert to do a 'spring cleaning' of the company's servers. He wants anything that makes the company look like criminals or drunken baboons deleted. Dilbert, working on a laptop on his couch, says that would leave only the birthday list, and the Boss tells him to destroy that too.
punchline: Everything on the company's servers is incriminating or embarrassing enough to delete, and the Boss would rather destroy even the harmless birthday list than risk any scrutiny.
summary: A manager orders a purge of company data that could make the firm look bad, and the cleanup ends up wiping out everything.

title: Making the World Worse, Honestly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want employees who are only working for the money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want employees who are working to make the world a better place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does working here make the world a better place?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Half of our products cause cancer, and the other half don't work at all.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We don't even pay taxes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: One could argue that every day we spend working here makes the planet a little bit worse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that why I never see you doing any work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When did it become a crime to care about people? Sheesh!

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team he wants employees motivated by making the world better rather than by money. Dilbert asks how the company does that and points out its products cause cancer or don't work, and Wally adds that the company dodges taxes and harms the planet. The Boss then asks if that's why Wally never works, and Wally claims he's just caring about people.
punchline: Wally twists the company's harmful reputation into a self-serving excuse for slacking, claiming his idleness is an act of caring about people.
summary: When the boss demands idealistic staff, the team lists the company's social harms, and Wally recasts his laziness as a moral stand.
keywords: make the world a better place

title: Social Distancing Golden Age for Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Social distancing has been a great upgrade to my life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the old days, women avoided me by at least ten feet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I often get within seven.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think it's because I'm better-looking with most of my face covered.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Especially if I wear a hat and sunglasses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I learned that women will talk to me if I walk the wrong way down a grocery aisle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They're usually complaining, but at least they make eye contact.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's sort of a golden age for people like me.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Wearing face masks, Wally chats with Dilbert over coffee and celebrates how pandemic social distancing has improved his dating prospects. He explains that women used to avoid him by ten feet but now come within seven, and that his masked face looks better. Dilbert silently listens while Wally describes being yelled at in grocery aisles as a form of social contact.
punchline: Wally treats being scolded by strangers for going the wrong way down a grocery aisle as a social win, showing how low his bar for female attention is.
summary: A masked Wally happily explains to Dilbert that the pandemic has made him more tolerable to women than ever before.

title: Learning to Hate the Developers

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I spent all week trying to sign into an app that stopped working for some reason.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But you got it to work in the end?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: No, all I did was learn to hate the developers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do you plan to solve that?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I don't need to. It isn't an app I need.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a bald coworker in a green shirt complains that he spent a whole week failing to sign into an app that suddenly stopped working. A colleague asks whether he got it working eventually, and he says all he gained was resentment toward the developers. Asked how he will fix that, he shrugs off the problem, saying he doesn't actually need the app.
punchline: After a week of wasted effort the only thing he fixed was nothing; the app turns out to be unnecessary, so the whole struggle was pointless and left him with only a grudge against the developers.
summary: A worker burns a week fighting a broken login, ends up resenting the programmers, and then admits he never needed the software at all.

title: Borrowing Money From Non-Distancers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard you are not practicing social distancing. Can I borrow some money?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: What does social distancing have to do with borrowing money?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I like borrowing money when I might not have to pay it back.

setting: Office conference table during the pandemic
situation: A coworker wearing a face mask approaches a bald colleague who is sitting at a table with a coffee. He asks to borrow money because he has heard the colleague is not practicing social distancing. When questioned about the connection, he admits he likes borrowing from people who might not survive to collect the debt.
punchline: The borrower is cynically betting that a person ignoring social distancing may catch the virus and die, so the loan would never have to be repaid.
summary: A masked worker tries to hit up a pandemic-ignoring colleague for cash, hoping the lender won't live long enough to be repaid.

title: Dogbert, Marketing Genius, Blushes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your products are shoddy, and your sales teams are incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But there is a theoretical amount of marketing genius that can fix all of that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you that genius?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please. You're making me blush.

setting: Office, across a desk during a consulting meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that his products are shoddy and his sales teams incompetent. He adds that enough marketing genius could fix everything, and the Boss asks whether Dogbert is that genius. Dogbert feigns modesty while clearly claiming the title.
punchline: Dogbert insults the client's whole business, then pretends to be bashful when the Boss assumes he is the genius who can save it, a smooth way of selling his own services.
summary: A consultant dog trashes a company's products and sales force, then coyly accepts the role of its saviour when the boss invites him to.

title: Bias for Action Over Verification

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss told us to scrap our prototype and start over from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was in that meeting and he said nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should verify what he wants.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Or . . . we could have a bias for action!

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: A coworker in a blue shirt claims the boss ordered the team to scrap their prototype and start over. Dilbert, who attended the same meeting, says the boss said no such thing and suggests checking what the boss actually wants. The coworker brushes this off, proposing that they simply act instead.
punchline: Spinning a wild misinterpretation as 'a bias for action' lets people charge ahead and destroy their work without bothering to confirm anything.
summary: A colleague wants to throw away a project based on instructions that were never given, and treats checking the facts as a lack of initiative.

title: Too Worried About Sweat

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: What do you think of my idea?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be honest, I didn't hear a word of it. I spent the whole time being worried about that bead of sweat on your forehead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's warm in here!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be a thousand yards in that direction.

setting: Office conference room during the pandemic
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, asks the Boss what he thinks of his idea. The Boss, also masked, admits he heard none of it because he was fixated on a bead of sweat on Dilbert's forehead. Dilbert protests that the room is just warm, but the Boss points away and says he'll keep a thousand yards' distance.
punchline: The Boss is so paranoid about COVID symptoms that he treats a drop of sweat as a threat and ignores the idea entirely, fleeing from Dilbert instead.
summary: A pandemic-era pitch collapses when the listener becomes so fearful of a single drop of perspiration that he bolts from the room.

title: Stop Assigning Me Homework

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you watch the video I sent?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a burden to know you because you keep assigning me homework.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm trying to be helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help my enemies instead?

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Asok, a coworker, asks Dilbert whether he watched the video he sent. Dilbert complains that knowing Asok is a burden because Asok keeps giving him homework. When Asok says he is only trying to be helpful, Dilbert asks him to go help his enemies instead.
punchline: Dilbert treats Asok's well-meant help as such a nuisance that he wishes it would be inflicted on his enemies instead.
summary: A coworker's eager stream of recommended videos so exasperates Dilbert that he suggests the coworker bother his foes rather than him.

title: Choosing the Impossible Option Deliberately

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I analyzed our only two options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One option costs too much, and the other option is impossible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's do the impossible one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you can explain your reasoning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to you, we will fail either way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But if we fail in a slow and inexpensive way, no one will even notice for months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With any luck, we'll have a corporate reorganization that forever hides our gross incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you done this before?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every six months.

setting: Office break area with a coffee machine, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert reports that his analysis of the company's only two options found one too expensive and the other impossible. The Boss chooses the impossible one because it will fail slowly and cheaply, and he hopes a reorganization will hide the failure. When Dilbert asks if he has done this before, the Boss admits he does it every six months.
punchline: The Boss deliberately picks a doomed plan because slow, cheap failure can be buried by a corporate reorganization, and he admits this is his routine every six months.
summary: A manager knowingly chooses a plan that can't succeed, counting on a company shake-up to cover his tracks, as he apparently always does.

title: Fixing a Moron With TED Talks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The labor market is so tight that I had to hire a moron just to fill a position.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to make him watch TED Talk videos until he smartens up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many will it take?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With any luck, fifteen to seventeen will get it done.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss admits that a tight labor market forced him to hire a moron to fill an open position. He explains his plan to have the new hire watch TED Talk videos until he becomes smarter. Dilbert asks how many videos it will take, and the Boss optimistically estimates fifteen to seventeen.
punchline: The Boss treats stupidity as something easily cured by a short run of TED Talks, showing both his naive faith in them and his low standards for hiring.
summary: A manager who settled for an unqualified hire expects a modest binge of inspirational online lectures to turn him into a smart employee.

title: Distracting Smart Employee With Instagram

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The moron I hired keeps watching TED Talks and getting smarter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He's only about three TED Talks away from taking your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There must be a way to slow him down.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll see if I can interest him in Instagram.

setting: Office, seated at a conference table
situation: The Boss complains that the unintelligent employee he hired keeps watching TED Talks and getting smarter. A coworker warns that the employee is only a few talks away from being able to take the boss's job. They decide to slow the employee down by getting him hooked on Instagram.
punchline: The boss is so threatened by a self-improving subordinate that he plans to sabotage him by steering him toward mindless social media, which also implies the boss himself is a barely competent manager.
summary: A threatened manager and his colleague scheme to keep a self-educating underling from advancing by tempting him with a time-wasting social media app.

title: Bribing Lawmakers Over Armed Drone Sales

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just learned it's illegal to sell armed drones to private citizens.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many orders did we get since we started selling them this morning?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seventy million.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll look into bribing someone to change the law.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert, working at his laptop, tells the Boss that selling armed drones to private citizens is illegal. The Boss ignores the legal problem and asks how many orders came in that morning. When Dilbert reports seventy million, the Boss decides to bribe someone to change the law rather than stop selling.
punchline: The Boss treats an illegal product as a legal obstacle to be bought off, because the huge sales numbers matter more than the law or any ethical concern.
summary: Upon hearing his product is illegal, a manager responds to a flood of orders by planning to buy a change in legislation.

title: Too Unimportant To Be Fired

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss isn't returning my messages. Do you think he plans to fire me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Phew! Good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're just totally unimportant to him.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes! That's where I want to be!

setting: Office meeting table, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A masked coworker worries that the Boss is ignoring his messages because he plans to fire him. Dilbert reassures him that he won't be fired, then explains it's because the Boss considers him completely unimportant. The coworker happily embraces being overlooked.
punchline: Being so unimportant to management that they don't even notice you is portrayed as the safest place to be in a company.
summary: A worried employee gets comfort from learning his boss ignores him because he doesn't matter at all, and he's thrilled about it.

title: Dilbert Argues He Is Right

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You argue with everything because you just have to be right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you tell the difference between someone who "has to be right" versus someone who IS right and you need therapy?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You're doing it again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or am I?

setting: Outdoor path with grass, apparently on a walk
situation: Dilbert and Tina, a coworker, are walking outside together. Tina accuses Dilbert of arguing with everything because he needs to be right. Dilbert responds by arguing that maybe he is simply right and she is the one who needs therapy, then answers her complaint by questioning it again.
punchline: Dilbert proves her point by turning her accusation into yet another argument, leaving it impossible to tell whether he is being stubborn or genuinely correct.
summary: A walking companion accuses Dilbert of compulsively needing to win arguments, and he responds with a debate about whether she's the one who needs help.

title: Meeting Purpose: Hugs Versus E-Cards

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there anything you plan to do in this meeting that we couldn't have done more easily by email?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hugs?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Send me an e-card.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Dilbert asks the people gathered around the conference table whether anything planned for the meeting couldn't have been handled by email. A coworker hesitantly suggests hugs as the one thing email can't do. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, immediately dismisses the idea and says an e-card would do.
punchline: Even the one thing that seems to require physical presence, hugs, gets dismissed by Dilbert's antisocial insistence that everything can be done electronically, so the meeting has no justification.
summary: A skeptical employee challenges the value of an in-person meeting, and even the lone suggestion of hugging gets waved off in favor of a digital greeting.

title: Dogbert Edits Dilbert's Health Data

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to your private data in the cloud, you have a mild case of asthma.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can see my personal health data?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: See it? Hahaha! I can do more than that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is more than that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can edit it. You have six new diseases now.

setting: Office desk with a laptop and a coffee mug
situation: Dogbert, working at a laptop, tells Dilbert that his private health data stored in the cloud shows he has mild asthma. When Dilbert is surprised that Dogbert can see his personal health records, Dogbert gleefully reveals he can also edit them, and promptly gives Dilbert six new diseases.
punchline: Cloud-stored personal data is not only visible to whoever has access, it can be altered at will, so a person's official medical record can be rewritten to give them diseases they don't have.
summary: A smug dog with a laptop shows that access to someone's online medical records means he can rewrite them and invent illnesses.

title: Criminally Unfunny Sexist Jokes Lawsuit

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've contacted my lawyer to sue you for your sexist jokes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your humor is not funny, and there's a good chance it is illegal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just learned that I am criminally unfunny.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're always the last to know.

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Alice stands arms crossed in front of a seated coworker and announces she has contacted her lawyer to sue him over his sexist jokes. She adds that his humor is not funny and may be illegal. Later, a coworker carrying a coffee cup says he has learned he is criminally unfunny, and Catbert, sitting on a desk, jabs that he is always the last to know.
punchline: The coworker only now realizes his jokes are so bad they might be criminal, and Catbert mocks him for being the last person in the office to figure out what everyone already knew.
summary: After a coworker is threatened with legal action over his offensive humor, he reports back that he has discovered he is criminally bad at comedy, and a spiteful cat confirms he was the last to notice.

title: Too Many Critical Tasks, No Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I did no work this week because I had too many critical tasks to do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No matter what I worked on, I would have failed to do the other 99% of tasks that were equally critical.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I rounded it off to 100% and enjoyed my week.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do I work here??? Why???

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Alice that he did no work all week because every task was critical and he could never finish them all. He argues that he would have failed 99% of the tasks anyway, so he treated it as 100% failure and enjoyed his week. Alice, who has been typing at her laptop, becomes furious and screams in frustration.
punchline: Wally twists 'everything is a priority' into a justification for doing nothing, and his smug laziness drives the hard-working Alice into a rage.
summary: Wally excuses a week of slacking by claiming that so many urgent tasks made any effort pointless, leaving his diligent coworker screaming in despair.

title: Facial Recognition Reveals Social Media Secrets

transcript.speaker: Stranger
transcript.text: Hi, I'm. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My facial recognition app has identified you and is now showing me your social media history.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems it would be unwise for me to touch your hand.

setting: Office lobby or corridor
situation: A coworker approaches Dilbert to introduce himself and offer a handshake. Dilbert stops him, points his phone at him, and uses a facial recognition app to pull up the man's social media history. After reading it, Dilbert decides he shouldn't shake the man's hand.
punchline: Instant access to someone's social media history reveals something so off-putting that Dilbert refuses even a simple handshake, implying the stranger's online posts are alarming or unsanitary.
summary: A quick phone scan of a new acquaintance's online past gives Dilbert enough dirt to refuse greeting him properly.

title: Faking Blockchain Expertise With Earpiece

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Later I have a meeting about blockchain and I don't understand anything about it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be wearing this earpiece, and I want you to feed me smart lines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to do something evil?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Say no more. I give me that.

setting: Office hallway, then Dilbert's living room
situation: The Boss admits he knows nothing about blockchain but has a meeting about it later. He plans to wear an earpiece and wants Dilbert to feed him smart-sounding lines. Dilbert instead asks Dogbert if he wants to do something evil, and Dogbert eagerly volunteers to take the earpiece job.
punchline: Dilbert hands the job of coaching the clueless boss to Dogbert, implying that feeding the boss deliberately misleading lines is an evil prank Dogbert will happily carry out.
summary: A manager with zero grasp of a trendy technology wants a hidden coach for his big meeting, and Dilbert hands the job to the one person who delights in mischief.

title: Karma Claims He Has No Parents

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why did your parents name you Karma?

transcript.speaker: Karma
transcript.text: I don't have parents. I am Karma.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I suppose we have lots to discuss.

transcript.speaker: Karma
transcript.text: Let's start with volume one.

setting: Office table, with both coworkers wearing face masks
situation: Wally asks a coworker named Karma why his parents gave him that name. Karma serenely replies that he has no parents because he is the actual cosmic force of Karma. Wally says they have a lot to discuss, and Karma produces a red book labeled with Wally's name, volume one, implying Wally's lifetime of misdeeds is catalogued.
punchline: Karma literally keeps a multi-volume record of Wally's bad behavior and is ready to settle the score, starting with volume one.
summary: A coworker who claims to be the embodiment of karma pulls out a thick ledger of Wally's wrongdoings to begin their conversation.

title: Fixing Inefficiency With Inefficient Task Force

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our internal processes are so inefficient that we can't get products to market before they are obsolete.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll create a multidisciplinary task force to look into it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You want to use an inefficient system to fix an inefficient system?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called fighting fire with fire.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Alice tells the Boss that the company's internal processes are so slow that products are obsolete before they reach the market. The Boss proposes creating a multidisciplinary task force to investigate. Alice points out that this means using an inefficient system to fix an inefficient system, and the Boss proudly reframes it as fighting fire with fire.
punchline: The Boss misuses the 'fighting fire with fire' idiom to justify fixing inefficiency with more inefficient bureaucracy, treating an obvious flaw as a clever strategy.
summary: A manager responds to a complaint about sluggish processes by forming a committee, then cheerfully rebrands the contradiction as a smart tactic.

title: Waiting for the Beak

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to people on social media, our 5G technology will "give you a bird head."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe we should study it a bit more.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nah. I'd wait until we see a beak.

setting: Conference room, with both men wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert tells a masked coworker that social media users claim the company's 5G technology will give people a bird head. The coworker first suggests more study, then decides against it and says he would rather wait until a beak actually appears.
punchline: The coworker's standard for taking a health risk seriously is waiting for visible, absurd physical proof, mocking how little diligence companies apply to safety concerns and conspiracy-laden rumors alike.
summary: Two masked colleagues weigh an internet rumor about their new wireless tech and settle on doing nothing until a physical deformity shows up.

title: Disbanding By Replacing Everyone

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why did you disband the technology task force? They were critical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't. I just replaced the people and changed the mission.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds a lot like disbanding it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? I was hoping it didn't.

setting: Office break area or meeting table, with both characters wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: A masked coworker confronts the Boss about shutting down a technology task force that was considered critical. The Boss insists he did not disband it, claiming he merely replaced all the members and changed its purpose. The coworker points out that this is effectively disbanding it, and the Boss admits he was hoping it wouldn't look that way.
punchline: The Boss uses a semantic dodge to deny disbanding the task force, then admits he only hoped nobody would notice that replacing everyone and changing the mission amounts to the same thing.
summary: A manager tries to claim a team still exists after swapping out every member and giving it a new purpose, then sheepishly hopes the trick would go unnoticed.

title: Wait for the Second Part

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: The company is considering no longer requiring employees to wear I.D. badges.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yes! Freedom!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too soon. Hold... hold...

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: ... in favor of permanent forehead tattoos.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Always wait for the second part.

setting: Conference room, with attendees wearing face masks
situation: Employees sit around a conference table wearing face masks while an announcement says the company may stop requiring I.D. badges. Asok cheers about freedom, but Dilbert tells him to hold off. The announcer then reveals the badges would be replaced by permanent forehead tattoos.
punchline: Management's good news always comes with a worse second half, so employees should never celebrate until the whole announcement is finished.
summary: A glimmer of workplace freedom is crushed when the company reveals its replacement for badges is something far more invasive.

title: Slide Deck Too Well-Designed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's no excuse for good design.

setting: Office desk or meeting room, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: The boss reviews a slide deck that Asok prepared and criticizes it for looking too polished, arguing it shows he wastes time on unimportant things. Asok points out that he is only given unimportant tasks, and the boss dismisses this as no excuse for good design.
punchline: The boss punishes an employee for doing quality work on the trivial tasks the boss himself assigned, so the employee can't win either way.
summary: A manager faults a subordinate for polishing a presentation too much, then brushes off the complaint that the work he hands out is unimportant.

title: What If I'm Actually Great?

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What if I'm actually great and I just don't know it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Office desk or conference table
situation: Asok, who admits to having low self-esteem, wonders aloud whether he might secretly be great without realizing it. Dilbert, looking at his phone and barely engaging, flatly tells him he is not.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly crushes Asok's hopeful self-reflection with a two-word dismissal, delivered without even looking up from his phone.
summary: A coworker with shaky self-confidence floats a hopeful theory about his hidden talent, and his colleague shoots it down in a heartbeat.

title: Becoming a Jaded Golem Employee

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I've noticed that the more experience I gain, the more cynical and jaded I become.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Am I doomed to become a golem-like creature with a bad attitude if I work here long enough?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No offense.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: None taken.

setting: Office break area, with both characters wearing face masks and holding coffee
situation: A young employee wearing a face mask tells an older, balding coworker that gaining experience is making him more cynical and jaded. He asks whether he is doomed to become a golem-like creature with a bad attitude if he stays long enough. He adds 'no offense,' and the coworker, who clearly fits that description, calmly says none was taken before sipping his coffee.
punchline: The older coworker is himself the embodiment of the jaded golem-like creature Asok fears becoming, and his deadpan 'none taken' shows he knows it and accepts it.
summary: A young worker frets about turning into a bitter, creature-like veteran while speaking directly to a bitter veteran who shrugs off the insult.

title: Boss Won't Call About Blockchain Class

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You haven't completed the mandatory class on blockchain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's an introductory class. I'm already an experienced blockchain developer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The class is mandatory. Every developer needs to check the box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just check the box for me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only the instructor can do that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I don't want to call him because he rambles on and on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to take a two-day class so you won't have to make a phone call???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I knew you'd understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if taking the class causes me to miss my deadlines?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem. I'll just cancel your bonus.

setting: Conference room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must complete a mandatory introductory blockchain class even though Dilbert is already an experienced blockchain developer. Dilbert asks the Boss to just check the box, but only the instructor can, and the Boss refuses to phone him because he rambles. Dilbert realizes he's being sent to a two-day class to spare the Boss a phone call, then learns missed deadlines will cost him his bonus.
punchline: The Boss will waste two days of an employee's time to avoid a brief phone call, then casually threatens to cancel the bonus when the lost time causes missed deadlines.
summary: A manager forces his skilled employee through a pointless two-day course simply because he dislikes talking to the instructor, and punishes him financially for the resulting delays.

title: Friend-Zoned Friends Were Insincere

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In hard times, you really find out who your friends are.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I assume you have hundreds of friends by now because of all the times you have been friend-zoned.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm starting to think they were insincere.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a window looking out on a snowy suburban street
situation: Dilbert stands by a window and remarks that hard times reveal who your real friends are. Dogbert, sitting on a dresser, sarcastically assumes Dilbert must have hundreds of friends because of all the times he has been friend-zoned. Dilbert glumly concludes those friends were probably insincere.
punchline: Dogbert's jab implies Dilbert has been romantically rejected countless times, and Dilbert's reply shows that he missed the sarcasm, or is resigned to it, as nobody has actually shown up for him in hard times.
summary: A lonely man's musing about true friendship is turned into a jab about his romantic rejections by his sarcastic dog.

title: Winning Arbitration Through Bribery

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was falsely accused of being a white supremacist and fired.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But I won in arbitration and got my job back!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How did you win?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Bribery. Once you realize the whole system is rotten, it's easier.

setting: Office cubicle area, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A masked coworker tells a woman at her desk that he was fired after a false accusation of being a white supremacist. He cheerfully announces he won in arbitration and got his job back. When she asks how he won, he casually admits he bribed his way to victory.
punchline: The triumphant story of vindication turns out to be corruption, and he treats bribery as the obvious, easy answer once you accept that the whole system is rotten.
summary: A man who was fired over a false accusation proudly reveals he regained his job by paying off the arbitration process.

title: Moonlighting Employee's Joke Misread

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Excuse me, I have to take a call from one of the other employers who also believes I work for them full time from home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell when he's joking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's probably for the best.

setting: Conference room during a video meeting
situation: During a video conference, a coworker announces he has to leave to take a call from another employer who also thinks he works for them full time from home. The Boss says he can't tell when the coworker is joking, and Dilbert replies that it's probably better that way.
punchline: The coworker is not joking at all: he is secretly holding multiple full-time remote jobs, and Dilbert dryly suggests the Boss is better off not realizing it.
summary: A remote worker casually reveals he's secretly employed full time by several companies, and his clueless manager assumes it's humor.

title: The Old Strategy Nobody Admits

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy is to make great products and sell them at a fair price.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was our old strategy?

transcript.speaker: Building
transcript.text: I'd rather not say.

setting: Conference room meeting, then an exterior shot of the office building
situation: In a meeting, the boss announces that the company's new strategy is to make great products and sell them at a fair price. Dilbert asks what the old strategy was. The final panel shows the company building, which answers that it would rather not say.
punchline: The company's previous strategy must have been something unsavory, such as making poor products and overcharging, so the building itself is too embarrassed to admit it.
summary: A grand new corporate plan that sounds like common sense makes a coworker wonder what the company was doing before, and the office building itself declines to answer.

title: Dogbert's Ultra-Short Safety Training

transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's corporate safety training.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't touch anything, don't move around, and don't talk to anyone. Ever!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks for coming.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: That's the whole class?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't blame me for being good at summarizing.

setting: A training room in an office, during the pandemic
situation: Dogbert, wearing a face mask, stands in front of a small group of masked employees, including Dilbert, and opens his corporate safety training. He sums up the entire course in a few prohibitions: touch nothing, stay put, and talk to no one. When an attendee asks if that's all there is, Dogbert says he is simply good at summarizing.
punchline: Dogbert squeezes an entire pandemic safety course into a few terse commands and then passes off his lazy, minimal effort as a skill in summarizing.
summary: A masked Dogbert reduces a whole workplace safety course to a handful of strict don'ts and brushes off complaints by crediting his concise style.

title: Business Lying Is Totally Acceptable

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it lying if I leave out important context from my project updates?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's called "business lying," and it is totally acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But it makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's how you know you are doing it right.

setting: Office, at a desk, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Alice asks Dogbert whether omitting important context from her project updates counts as lying. Dogbert, acting as a consultant, labels it "business lying" and says it is fine. When Alice says it makes her feel sick, Dogbert tells her that nausea means she is doing it correctly.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically reframes dishonesty as a professional skill and treats Alice's guilty conscience as proof she is performing it properly.
summary: A queasy employee is assured by her canine advisor that deceiving people through selective omission is standard professional practice, and that her guilt is a sign of success.

title: Screen Share Gone Horribly Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your Zoom call?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk and later in the living room
situation: During a video call, Dilbert starts to share his screen and realizes he has exposed something embarrassing. Panic ensues and he tries to make it disappear, then declares he quits. Afterward, Dogbert asks how the Zoom call went and Dilbert calmly says it was the best one ever.
punchline: Dilbert's meltdown over an embarrassing screen share contrasts with his calm claim that it was the best call ever, implying that the humiliation was either hilarious to others or he is in denial.
summary: A man accidentally exposes the wrong screen on a video call and spirals into panic, yet later insists the call went wonderfully.

title: Jealousy Accusation Backfires on Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Pffft. Of course you don't.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You read minds as well as you make plans.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thank you. Apology accepted.

setting: Office conference table
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he doubts the coworker's plan will work. The coworker dismisses the criticism, accuses Dilbert of sabotage out of jealousy, and then misreads Dilbert's sarcastic reply as a compliment and an apology.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcasm, implying the coworker is as bad at mind reading as at planning, goes over the coworker's head, and the coworker takes it as praise and an apology.
summary: A confident colleague waves off criticism as envy and then mistakes an insult for flattery.

title: Augmented Reality Reveals Your Social Media

transcript.text: My name is...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I hope it makes a good first impression.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My god, you are dumb!

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A woman wearing a face mask starts to introduce herself to Dilbert, but he stops her. His augmented reality glasses are pulling up her whole social media history. She hopes it makes a good impression, and he recoils in horror at how dumb her posts show her to be.
punchline: Instant access to someone's social media history means a first meeting can end in total judgment before the person even says her name.
summary: Smart glasses that dig up a stranger's online posts let Dilbert pass a harsh verdict on her before she can finish saying hello.

title: Working From Home Without Interruptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like working from home. I can do eight hours of work in one hour because no one is interrupting me.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to work here!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I tell you about my bowel problems?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Go away!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch holding a jar and praises working from home because nobody interrupts him. Ratbert, working on a laptop beside him, snaps that he is trying to work. Dilbert, unbothered, goes on to ask whether he has mentioned his bowel problems, and Ratbert yells at him to go away.
punchline: Dilbert brags about the lack of interruptions while being the one who constantly interrupts Ratbert, so the quiet he enjoys exists only because he doesn't realize he is the distraction.
summary: A man who loves the peace of remote work keeps pestering the little lab rat sharing his couch with unwanted personal medical chatter.

title: Experts Arrested, Opinion Unchanged

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Haha! You idiot! How dare you disagree with the foremost experts in this field!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a breaking story about those same experts being arrested today for falsifying data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a sane world, this information would serve to modify your strong opinion.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not how any of this works.

setting: Office desk, both wearing face masks
situation: A coworker in a face mask mocks Dilbert for disagreeing with the leading experts in their field. Dilbert pulls out his phone and shows a breaking news story that those very experts were arrested for falsifying data. He suggests that a sane person would reconsider, but the coworker replies that opinions don't work that way.
punchline: People cling to strong opinions and appeals to authority even when the evidence behind them is discredited, so new facts don't actually change minds.
summary: Dilbert confronts a smug coworker with news that his revered authorities are criminals, only to learn that the man's convictions are immune to evidence.

title: Refusing Demands Loses the Customer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't tell you to do that, you fool!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me to do exactly that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I never told you to lose our biggest customer!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me to refuse their demands.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I didn't tell you to lose the customer!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the same thing!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The important thing here is that it's your fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get it!!!

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert reports that he followed the Boss's instruction to refuse the biggest customer's demands, and the customer has canceled all its orders. The Boss denies ever telling him to do that and insists he never said to lose the customer. Dilbert points out that refusing the demands and losing the customer are the same thing, but the Boss simply declares it Dilbert's fault.
punchline: The Boss ignores the obvious consequence of his own instruction and assigns blame to Dilbert regardless of logic, leaving Dilbert frustrated and defeated.
summary: A manager disowns the predictable fallout of his own order and pins the disaster on the employee who obeyed it.

title: Forwarded Email Insulting Ted

transcript.speaker: Alice
