transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He needed to know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He did not need to know!

setting: Office hallway, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Alice, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert she forwarded his email to Ted. Dilbert is horrified because the email contained bad things he said about Ted and was meant to be private. Alice calmly insists Ted needed to know, and Dilbert angrily stomps off.
punchline: Alice justifies betraying Dilbert's private confidence with a flimsy claim that Ted needed to know he was being insulted, ignoring the obvious fallout for Dilbert.
summary: A coworker coolly exposes a colleague's secret gossip about a third person and refuses to see anything wrong with it.

title: Betting On Management's Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it reduce your confidence in our management that 100% of them got infected with coronavirus?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All I know is that I won $300 betting it would happen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How often do you bet on their stupidity?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Often enough to double my income.

setting: Conference room, with both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert and Wally sit at a conference table wearing masks. Dilbert asks whether it shakes Wally's faith in management that every one of them caught coronavirus. Wally replies that he won $300 betting it would happen, and admits he regularly wagers on management's stupidity, enough to double his income.
punchline: Wally's low-effort income is so reliably boosted by betting on management's foolish behavior that it doubles his pay, implying management's stupidity is highly predictable.
summary: A coworker cashes in on a wager that the company's leaders would all get sick, revealing that betting against their judgment is his steady side income.

title: How Hard Can It Be

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you finish the server migration by Monday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How hard can it be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ask that question every day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

setting: Conference table in an office, both wearing face masks
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to finish a server migration by Monday. When Dilbert refuses, the Boss asks how hard it can be, and Dilbert points out that he only says that about things he doesn't understand. The Boss admits he asks that question every day, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly confirms that he understands almost nothing about the work his team does, since he asks 'how hard can it be?' constantly.
summary: A manager's casual dismissal of a tough technical deadline backfires when he inadvertently admits he's clueless about nearly everything.

title: Accidentally Deleting the Unmarked Edits

transcript.text: I forgot to turn on the edit tracker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to accidentally delete your email.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's probably how I'd play it too.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he edited Dilbert's complex document and emailed it back. Dilbert finds no highlighted changes because the coworker forgot to turn on the edit tracker. Dilbert announces he will accidentally delete the email, and the coworker approves.
punchline: Dilbert plans to blame an 'accident' to dodge the tedious work of finding the untracked changes, and the coworker admits he would handle it the same way, showing how both treat such mistakes as convenient excuses.
summary: Faced with a colleague's untracked revisions to a tangled file, a man cheerfully plans a convenient 'accident' with his inbox, and the colleague respects the move.

title: Boss Threatens Replacing Employee With Robot

transcript.speaker: Employee

transcript.text: I just lost my will to live.

transcript.text: That is exactly why I plan to replace you with a robot.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: An employee offers to give his boss a status update on his project, and the boss, absorbed in his phone, says he doesn't want one. He explains he only assigns the employee projects he doesn't care about, and the employee says this has drained his will to live. The boss takes the remark as proof that a robot would be a better fit for the job.
punchline: The boss treats the employee's despair as a reason to replace him with a robot, since a machine can't lose the will to live.
summary: A manager waves off a project update from a worker, admits he hands out only unimportant work, and then cites the worker's despair as grounds for swapping him for a machine.

title: Stop Explaining Science To Me

transcript.text: Yes!!! I knew that!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you ever heard of the placebo effect?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAAA!!!

setting: Office meeting table, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, asks a masked coworker why he keeps explaining basic science when Dilbert already knows it. The coworker responds by asking if Dilbert knows that anecdotal evidence can be misleading, then whether he has heard of the placebo effect, while Dilbert grows increasingly agitated.
punchline: Dilbert's frustration at being lectured on basic science does not stop the coworker from continuing, and the exasperated outburst shows that being told things you already know is infuriating.
summary: A man who keeps being lectured on elementary scientific reasoning by a colleague finally loses his composure in a tiny, exasperated scream.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I created the culture that made it all possible.

transcript.text: I did the work!!!

setting: Conference room meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that although Dilbert's name is on a report, the credit should go to him because he ordered it to be done. Dilbert points out that the idea and the writing were his own, done on his own time. The Boss then claims credit for creating the culture that made it possible, and Dilbert angrily shouts that he did the work.
punchline: Managers will claim credit for any employee achievement by stretching their contribution to something as vague as 'creating the culture,' leaving the person who actually did the work with no recognition.
summary: A manager keeps escalating his justifications for stealing credit for a subordinate's report until the frustrated employee can only shout about doing the actual work.

situation: Dilbert, working from home at his laptop, complains that Dogbert's footsteps keep distracting him. Dogbert sarcastically offers to hover instead of walking, and Dilbert asks if he actually can. Dogbert then floats in the air, hinting at hidden abilities.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic offer to hover turns out to be literally possible, and his cryptic reply suggests Dilbert barely knows what his dog can do.
summary: A man working from home grumbles about his dog's noisy steps, and the dog responds by floating just above the floor.

situation: A masked coworker with spiky hair asks Dilbert for ten minutes to discuss the project timeline. Dilbert refuses to risk exposure to her germs by meeting in person. She replies that she will simply guess his input, and he agrees that this is the better option.
punchline: The coworker would rather invent Dilbert's feedback than have a face-to-face conversation, and Dilbert endorses it, showing how little real input matters to the project timeline.
summary: Pandemic fears lead two masked coworkers to replace a timeline discussion with one of them just imagining the other's answer.

title: Impostor Syndrome Confession Gets Brutal Reply

situation: The Boss confides to Dilbert that he suffers from impostor syndrome and fears being exposed as a fake manager. Dilbert, looking at his phone, deadpans that everyone already realized he is not a good manager.
punchline: The Boss's fear of being found out is moot because his incompetence was obvious to everyone long ago, and Dilbert offers this as sarcastic comfort.
summary: A manager worries his colleagues will discover he is faking competence, only to be told they already noticed.

situation: The Boss asks Catbert why people are so worried about coronavirus if only about 1% of those infected will die. Catbert checks his phone and calculates that 1% of Earth's population would be 77 million deaths. The Boss objects that the whole world won't catch it, and Catbert retorts that they will if they follow his advice.
punchline: Catbert sarcastically implies that the Boss's cavalier, uninformed attitude toward the pandemic would cause the virus to spread to everyone if people took his advice.
summary: A dismissive manager downplays a pandemic's fatality rate until his sardonic advisor points out the staggering death toll and the danger of heeding his casual attitude.

title: Duck Test Meets Deep Fake

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was going to say duck.

transcript.text: You might want to update your folksy sayings every century or two.

situation: A bald coworker begins reciting the classic duck-test proverb to Dilbert. Dilbert finishes it by suggesting the thing might be a deep fake, and the coworker says he meant to say duck. Dilbert then advises him to modernize his old-fashioned sayings.
punchline: In an age of deepfake technology, the old duck-test saying no longer proves anything is genuine, so folksy proverbs are outdated.
summary: Dilbert pokes fun at an old proverb by pointing out that modern fakes can imitate anything convincingly, making the saying obsolete.

summary: Faced with termination for being lazy, a slacker pitches his boss on deploying him as a saboteur against an unloved project and then angles for extra pay.

punchline: Dogbert's two predictions are both fatal, so the second 'alternative' is just a more drawn-out way of dying, making his foresight worthless as advice.
summary: A hat-wearing fortune-telling dog offers a client two forecasts that both end in his demise, differing only in how long it takes.

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert take a walk outdoors, both wearing masks. Dilbert says he is thinking of writing a book, and Dogbert doubts that a boring person could write an interesting one. summary: A man hoping his prose is livelier than his personality gets shot down by his dog's absurd, sarcastic comparison.

situation: Dilbert, watching from an upper floor, reports that protesters have surrounded the building. The Boss calmly assures him that a supportive sign in the lobby will show the protesters the company is on their side. Dilbert then reports that the nine lower floors are on fire, and the Boss merely wonders if a bigger sign was needed.
punchline: The Boss believes a token sign can placate angry protesters, and even as the building burns his only conclusion is that the sign was too small.
summary: A manager trusts a lobby sign to win over a hostile crowd, then responds to a fire with a complaint about signage size.

When Dogbert insists it is all legal, The Boss says he wasn't going to ask.
punchline: The Boss willfully avoids asking about the obviously unethical mind-control scheme because he is happy with the improved sales, showing his indifference to how results are achieved.
summary: A consultant dog cheerfully confesses to hypnotizing customers into overlooking terrible products, and his client is content to look the other way.

title: Nodding Feeds Endless Repetition Habit

summary: A man keeps restating his argument because his listener's agreeable nodding keeps encouraging him.

title: Software Price Haggling Backfires on Dilbert

summary: A buyer's flirty-sounding brush-off during a price negotiation is turned against him by the vendor, who uses the threat of an HR complaint to close the sale.

situation: Dilbert proudly reports that he worked all weekend to meet a deadline, only for the Boss to reveal he doesn't need the work for two more weeks. summary: A manager's secret padded deadline costs an employee his weekend and leaves him with the discovery that even his supposed importance was a fib.

summary: A coworker pushes an absurd bargaining tactic onto a colleague and happily admits he bears none of the embarrassment.

situation: The Boss tells his engineers that robots will eventually replace them and asks them to train a robot to do their jobs so the company is ready. summary: Management asks the engineering team to teach a robot their jobs, and the staff realize a machine wouldn't object the way they do.

title: Don't Jinx the Satellite Launch

A coworker idly wonders aloud about an alien spaceship appearing over the launch site, and Asok panics that he has jinxed them. The skeptic insists reality doesn't work that way, until radar shows something enormous over the rocket's path.
punchline: The coworker's insistence that speaking a possibility can't cause it is instantly disproved when a Belgium-sized object appears on radar, as if the jinx had worked.
summary: A confident launch crew tempts fate by imagining an alien invasion, and a gigantic radar blip promptly shows up above the rocket.

situation: A network vendor sits at a table with Dilbert and a coworker and gleefully announces that, because the installation is already half-done, the customers are trapped. punchline: The vendor openly admits to exploiting his locked-in customers because he enjoys watching them be powerless to stop it.
summary: A smug contractor cheerfully reveals his plan to overcharge clients who can no longer switch suppliers, simply because he finds it entertaining.

summary: A man tries to prove he emailed a request and ends up showing he sent a completely different message, then blames his colleague for arguing.

summary: An accusation of leaking company secrets collapses the moment the accused reveals he is watching his accuser's online habits too.

summary: A manager gleefully admits that his political contributions bought a legal change allowing weaponized drone sales, plus a tax break, to his employees' dismay.

punchline: Dilbert's use of sanitizer is so obsessive that he offers to share it, but the bottle itself is something Alice considers too contaminated to touch, ironically defeating the point of sanitizing.
summary: A masked office worker describes his creeping compulsion to sanitize ever more of his body, then offers to share his bottle with a coworker who finds it too germy to trust.

punchline: Dilbert's one remaining source of stress is his roommate Dogbert, whose illegal schemes (counterfeiting) threaten his peaceful isolation.
summary: A man relishing his solitary pandemic life realizes his lone worry is the dog who shares his house and his criminal hobbies.

situation: Dogbert sits at a table with a laptop and announces his new hobby of rewriting Shakespeare's plays to make them more sensible. Dilbert sips his coffee and sarcastically admires his confidence while the laptop shows Dogbert's 'improved' version of a famous line.
punchline: Dogbert's 'fixed' version of Juliet's famous line, 'Where are you, Romeo?', is a plain, unpoetic rewrite that is arguably worse, undercutting his arrogant claim that he can improve Shakespeare.
summary: A smug dog sets out to improve the Bard's writing and ends up flattening a legendary line into something bland.

summary: A manager brings in a patronizing science explainer to interrupt gatherings regularly, and when questioned, can only shrug that it is simply routine.

situation: Dilbert reports to the boss that the request-for-proposal process has finished and a vendor has been chosen. However, the process took so long that the vendor's technology is now obsolete. Dilbert asks whether to proceed anyway, and the boss encourages the foolish course.
punchline: The boss endorses proceeding stupidly because stupidity is what got the company through the whole process so far.
summary: A painfully slow vendor selection leaves the company with outdated technology, and the boss cheerfully approves continuing down the same foolish path.

title: Boss's Safety Record Claim Debunked

summary: A manager brags about a fictional industry-leading safety record, gets called out for the lie, and brushes past the criticism without a word of explanation.

summary: A worker who wants to telecommute agrees to ever-greater monitoring until his manager proposes outfitting him with a wearable camera.

transcript.text: It's more about the blame later.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A masked manager asks Dilbert whether he has tested everything to guarantee it is 100% safe. Dilbert explains that nothing can be completely safe, then guesses the manager wants him to say so anyway. The manager admits the request is really about assigning blame later.
punchline: The manager doesn't care whether the product is actually safe; he wants Dilbert's assurance so there is someone to blame if something goes wrong.
summary: A manager demands a safety guarantee from an engineer, not for safety's sake but to have a scapegoat in reserve.

title: Cooties Symptom Is Denying Science

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The news says there's a major outbreak of cooties in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think cooties is a real thing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Experts say one of the symptoms of cooties is "denying science."

setting: Office, with coworkers wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: A masked coworker reads a news story on his phone about a cooties outbreak in Elbonia. Dilbert, also masked, says he doesn't believe cooties are real. The coworker responds that experts list denying science as a symptom of cooties.
punchline: The experts have defined the disease so that anyone who doubts it is by definition infected, a circular argument that makes skepticism itself proof of the illness, satirizing pandemic-era science denial.
summary: A made-up outbreak comes with the convenient diagnosis that anyone who questions it is showing signs of the sickness.

title: Dogbert Monitors Dilbert, Accepts Bribes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did more work from home today before 10 a.m. than I could do in the office all day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could take a nap for the rest of the day, and no one would be the wiser.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your employer pays me to watch you at home, but I wouldn't say no to a well-considered bribe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can work with that.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert brags that he got more done working from home before 10 a.m. than in a full day at the office, then muses that he could nap all afternoon undetected. Dogbert, who has been hired by Dilbert's employer to monitor him at home, reveals he is open to a bribe, and Dilbert agrees to negotiate.
punchline: The home-surveillance hired to keep remote workers honest is itself corruptible, so Dilbert can simply pay off the monitor and slack off.
summary: A remote worker discovers that the person hired to spy on him from his couch can be bought off.

title: Boss Dislikes Employees Learning Things

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'd like to help on the blockchain project to build my skills in that area.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like it when people learn new things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I... don't know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Oh, good. It worked.

setting: Boss's office
situation: An employee with big curly hair asks the boss to be assigned to the blockchain project so she can build her skills. The boss, seated at his desk with a laptop, says he dislikes it when people learn new things. A final panel of an office building shows the boss speechless and the employee saying her ploy worked.
punchline: The employee uses reverse psychology, tricking the boss into speechless confusion, and the joke highlights that management is hostile to employee development.
summary: A worker asking for training on a trendy tech project meets a boss who openly opposes learning, leaving him with nothing to say.

title: Everyone Can't Outwork Everyone Else

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only way to succeed in this company is by working harder than everyone else.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wouldn't that mean only one person in the company can be successful?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might need to rethink my motivational messages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe save those for your dumber employees.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team during a meeting that the only way to succeed is by working harder than everyone else. Alice points out the logical flaw: only one person could ever be the hardest worker. The Boss admits he may need to rethink his motivational messages, and Dilbert suggests he reserve such messages for less intelligent employees.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the Boss's illogical motivational slogan only works on people too dim to notice the flaw in it.
summary: A manager's inspirational slogan collapses when an employee points out its basic logic, prompting a dig at his motivational skills.

title: Sciencesplainer States the Obvious

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Sciencesplainer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't have any data yet, but we are hearing good reports.

transcript.speaker: Sciencesplainer
transcript.text: Those reports are anecdotal. You need a controlled study to be certain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Literally everyone already knows that.

transcript.speaker: Sciencesplainer
transcript.text: Sure, but did you know accurate data are better than bad data?

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: At a meeting, Dilbert says there is no data yet but the reports are good. A coworker, labeled the Sciencesplainer, lectures him that anecdotal reports are not enough and a controlled study is needed. When Dilbert says everyone already knows that, the Sciencesplainer smugly adds that accurate data beats bad data.
punchline: The Sciencesplainer keeps condescendingly explaining obvious points, escalating to the absurdly self-evident claim that accurate data is better than bad data.
summary: A know-it-all coworker patronizingly lectures his colleagues on basic scientific principles that everyone already understands.

title: Timely Beats Right, Says Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got your email, but I didn't have time to include your upgrades on my analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better to be timely than right because our boss can't judge the quality of our work, but he knows when it's late.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why is it that everything true is also sad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's how the truth works.

setting: Office cubicle, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she skipped his suggested upgrades because she ran out of time. Dilbert explains that deadlines matter more than quality because their boss can only tell if work is late, not whether it is good. Alice wonders why every true thing is sad, and Dilbert says that is simply how truth is.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical observation that management can only measure lateness, not quality, is true and depressing, which he deadpans is just how truth works.
summary: Two coworkers conclude that rushing out mediocre work beats delivering good work late, since their manager can only recognize missed deadlines.

title: Teamwork Through Public Humiliation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's the B.R.A. on that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You look dumb in front of everyone for not knowing B.R.A. stands for Business Risk Assessment.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We'll probably mock you behind your back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think your teamwork exercises are working.

setting: Conference room meeting table
situation: At a meeting, a coworker asks Dilbert about the B.R.A. and Dilbert doesn't know the acronym. The coworker bluntly explains that Dilbert looks dumb for not knowing it and that the group will mock him behind his back. Dilbert responds that their teamwork exercises aren't working.
punchline: The coworker's blunt, insulting description of how the team will treat Dilbert is the opposite of teamwork, so Dilbert sarcastically notes the teamwork exercises have failed.
summary: A colleague spells out exactly how the group will ridicule Dilbert for missing a piece of jargon, undermining any claim of team spirit.

title: 5G Test Opens Demon Portal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our 5G test accidentally opened a doorway to the demon world.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's keep that to ourselves so we don't spook the public.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't tell me. Tell Daryll.

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: Hey, nice world you have here.

setting: Office, with employees wearing face masks and holding coffee
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that a 5G test accidentally opened a portal to the demon world. The coworker suggests keeping it secret so the public isn't frightened. Dilbert points at a green demon standing beside them, who cheerfully remarks on the nice world.
punchline: The secrecy plan is pointless because a demon has already crossed over and is standing right there, casually admiring Earth.
summary: A technical mishap lets a demon into the office just as two colleagues agree to hush the whole thing up.

title: Loneliness Beats Co-Workers, Thank Goodness

transcript.speaker: Video call voice
transcript.text: How do you like working at home all the time now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was delighted to discover that a crushing sense of loneliness is better than spending time with my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Video call voice
transcript.text: No offense taken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And don't get me started about the splendor of the mute button.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, working from bed on a laptop during a video call
situation: Dilbert sits in bed with his laptop on a video call while a co-worker asks how he likes working from home full time. Dilbert cheerfully says that crushing loneliness beats spending time with his co-workers. The co-worker on the call says no offense taken, and Dilbert adds that he loves the mute button.
punchline: Dilbert prefers the misery of isolation to his colleagues' company, and he is so cheerfully blunt about it that he even praises the mute button, which he uses to silence them.
summary: Working remotely, Dilbert tells a colleague on a video call that crushing isolation is an improvement over their company, then gushes about the mute button.

title: Emergency Excuses Avoid Boring Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any emergencies for me to work on?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perfect! I needed an excuse to avoid working on the boring parts of my job.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I also need your status report by end of day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would totally do that if not for this darned emergency.

setting: Office cubicle area, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, asks a masked coworker whether there are any emergencies he can work on. When she hands him one, he cheerfully says it gives him an excuse to skip the boring parts of his job. She then asks for his status report by end of day, and he blames the emergency for being unable to do it.
punchline: Dilbert actively hunts for emergencies as a convenient excuse to dodge routine tasks like status reports, and then uses the emergency as cover for not doing them.
summary: An employee eagerly requests a crisis to tackle so he has a ready-made reason to neglect his dull paperwork.

title: Going to War With Bad Data

transcript.speaker: Caller (from computer)
transcript.text: Is this data accurate?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't go to war with the data you need. You go to war with the data you have.

transcript.speaker: Caller (from computer)
transcript.text: Did you just make it sound noble to use bad data?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And heroic.

setting: Dilbert's home office, on a video call with a headset
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask and a headset, is on a remote video call where a colleague asks whether the data is accurate. Dilbert responds by borrowing a war-style maxim about fighting with the data you have rather than the data you need. When called out for making bad data sound noble, he adds that it is also heroic.
punchline: Dilbert dresses up the use of inaccurate data as a noble, heroic act instead of admitting the data is bad.
summary: Questioned about unreliable figures, a remote worker spins his use of flawed information into a brave military virtue.

title: Platinum Service Changes the Future

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired you to predict the future of our industry, but everything you say makes me sad.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't blame me. I only predict the future. I don't make the future.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless you buy my special platinum-level service.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice upsell.

setting: Office meeting table
situation: The Boss complains to Dogbert, whom he hired as a consultant to predict the future of the industry, that the forecasts are depressing. Dogbert says he only predicts the future and cannot change it. He then adds that he can change it if the Boss buys his premium platinum-level service.
punchline: The consultant claims he can't influence the future, then reveals that a pricier service tier will do exactly that, turning the bad news into a sales pitch.
summary: A gloomy-forecast consultant disclaims any power over the outcomes he predicts, then offers to alter them for an extra fee.

title: Boss Recoups Losses By Underpaying Staff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I used to be rich, but I lost it all in the stock market crash during the pandemic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily, I can make up the difference by working you idiots to death while underpaying you.

transcript.speaker: Employee (voice from video call)
transcript.text: We thought you didn't have a strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just don't like to talk about it.

setting: Home office during a video conference
situation: The Boss sits at his computer on a video call with his team and explains that he lost his fortune in the pandemic stock market crash. He announces cheerfully that he will recover his money by overworking and underpaying the staff. An employee remarks that they thought he had no strategy, and he replies that he just doesn't like discussing it.
punchline: The Boss's cruel plan to exploit his employees turns out to be a genuine strategy that he was simply too embarrassed to mention, undermining the usual assumption that he is clueless.
summary: A manager on a remote meeting reveals he will fix his market losses by squeezing his staff, then claims it was a plan all along.

title: Context Is for Humans, Apparently

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When you schedule the Zoom call with the customer, be sure to include me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you plan to use up all of our time talking about yourself?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: People enjoy context.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's as if you have never met a human.

setting: Office, with both people wearing face masks
situation: A coworker holding a coffee asks Dilbert, who is typing at his laptop, to include him on the upcoming Zoom call with a customer. Dilbert suspects the coworker will spend the whole call talking about himself. The coworker replies that people appreciate context.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically says the coworker's belief that people enjoy lengthy background about him shows he has never actually met a human, since nobody wants to hear it.
summary: A colleague wants to join a customer video call and defends his self-focused chatter as helpful background, which Dilbert mocks as being out of touch with how people actually behave.

title: Dilbert Refuses Stupid Task, Feels Powerful

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday I refused to do something I had been asked to do because it was stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it worked out fine.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't let the power go to your head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am off the leash!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office hallway, with both men wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker, who looks like Wally, that he refused a stupid request and nothing bad came of it. The coworker warns him not to let the power go to his head. Dilbert immediately declares he is off the leash and strides away aggressively.
punchline: Dilbert takes the warning about power going to his head as an invitation, instantly turning one successful refusal into a belief that he is now unrestrained.
summary: After discovering that saying no to a pointless task carried no consequences, a mild-mannered engineer leaps straight to feeling liberated and unstoppable.

title: Seventeen TED Talks Make Genius

transcript.speaker: Coworker in blue shirt
transcript.text: I used to be a moron, but then I binge-watched seventeen TED Talks on YouTube.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in blue shirt
transcript.text: Now I'm the smartest person in the room.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should we do something about this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know. I've only watched six TED Talks.

setting: Office break area where coworkers stand holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker in a blue shirt boasts that he used to be a moron until he binge-watched seventeen TED Talks, and now considers himself the smartest person in the room. Wally asks Dilbert if they should do something about it. Dilbert hesitates because he has only watched six TED Talks himself.
punchline: Dilbert measures his own authority to challenge the braggart by TED Talk count, implying that watching a few online talks is a ridiculous basis for claiming intelligence, and that he himself is not yet 'qualified' to argue.
summary: A smug colleague credits online lectures for his newfound brilliance, and his peers doubt whether they've watched enough of them to push back.

title: Reimagining Ted's Job for Higher Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, we need to reimagine your job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I hope that means you will replace the boring parts of my job with exciting new projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't mean that.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Does it mean doing the same work for higher pay?

setting: Office, at Ted's desk
situation: The Boss tells Ted that his job needs to be reimagined. Ted hopefully guesses it means swapping dull tasks for exciting projects, and when the Boss says no, Ted tries a second guess: the same work with a raise. The Boss never confirms what the reimagining actually means.
punchline: Ted's optimistic guesses about a job 'reimagining' are hopeful but unrealistic, implying that management buzzwords like this usually mean the same or more work with no benefit to the employee.
summary: A worker hopes a management makeover of his role will bring perks, but the boss's vague announcement offers nothing of the sort.

title: Labeling Disagreeing People Idiots

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell the difference between good ideas and bad ones.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: There are smart people on both sides of every idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What rational process do you use to determine who is right?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I label people who disagree with me "idiots" and call it a day.

setting: Office hallway, with both characters wearing face masks and holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert admits to a masked coworker that he can't distinguish good ideas from bad ones. The coworker observes that smart people can be found on both sides of any idea. When Dilbert asks how he decides who is right, the coworker reveals he simply calls anyone who disagrees with him an idiot.
punchline: The coworker's supposedly rational decision process is just dismissing anyone who disagrees with him as an idiot, which is no process at all.
summary: A colleague's method for settling who is right turns out to be insulting everyone who disagrees with him.

title: Boss Shows Interest, Employee Explodes

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have a doctor appointment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's wrong with you?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's none of your stinkin' business! Stay out of my life!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Didn't you advise me to show interest in my employees?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I was pranking you. They hate that.

setting: Office hallway
situation: An employee tells the Boss she has a doctor appointment, and the Boss asks what is wrong with her. She furiously tells him to stay out of her life. The Boss confusedly complains to Catbert, who admits his advice to show interest in employees was a prank.
punchline: Catbert's advice that managers show interest in their employees was a deliberate prank, because employees resent having their personal lives pried into.
summary: After taking a feline adviser's tip to care about his staff, a manager gets screamed at for a harmless question and learns he was tricked.

title: Judging Projects by Jerky Faces

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: I can't support this project because you're all a bunch of corrupt, godless communists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just out of curiosity, where did you get your education?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: I learned everything I need to know on social media.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does that help you evaluate a technical proposal?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: It's simple. I take one look at all of your jerky faces, and I know everything I need to know.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: I mean, look at this guy's face. He's obviously a grifter.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Lucky guess.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: This one obviously has anger issues.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I demand a larger sample size!

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: Whatever, geekface.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: A coworker in a yellow shirt announces he won't support a project because the team are corrupt, godless communists. When Dilbert asks about his qualifications, he says he learned everything from social media and judges people by their faces. He then labels one colleague a grifter and another an angry person, and when Dilbert asks for a larger sample size he insults him.
punchline: The man who judges people by their faces as if it were science rejects Dilbert's call for rigor with an insult, showing that his 'facial analysis' is just prejudice and that social media is a poor basis for technical decisions.
summary: A meeting attendee rejects a project based on snap judgments of his colleagues' faces, a skill he claims to have picked up online.

title: Never Coming Back After Dropping Off

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have a minute to help me?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Absolutely. I'll be right back after I drop off something at my desk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll never see you again, will I?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Don't take the mystery out of it.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: A seated coworker asks a colleague holding a coffee cup for a minute of help. The colleague cheerfully agrees but says he must first drop something off at his desk. The coworker correctly guesses he will never return, and he sips his coffee and tells her not to spoil the mystery.
punchline: The colleague pretends to agree to help but implicitly admits he has no intention of returning, preferring to keep up the polite fiction.
summary: A polite promise to return soon is exposed as a thinly veiled brush-off when the asker calls it out and the dodger shrugs it off.

title: Offer of Help Taken Literally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need any help at all, just let me know.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need a lot of help. Be here at 8 AM and plan to work late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is awkward, but I didn't mean a word of what I said.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert stands over a seated coworker working on a laptop and offers to help with anything he needs. The coworker takes him at his word and asks for a lot of help, including coming in at 8 AM and working late. Dilbert then admits he didn't mean the offer.
punchline: Dilbert's offer of help was an empty social pleasantry, and he honestly admits he never intended to follow through when it is taken seriously.
summary: A casual offer of assistance gets called in by a coworker, forcing the offerer to confess it was just politeness.

title: Baker Eats His Embalming Mistakes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's hard to find qualified engineers in this job market, so I'm casting a wider net.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says here you have experience as a mortuary assistant and a baker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not exactly like being an engineer, but I want to stay open-minded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell me about a time you had to deal with failure and what you did about it.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: Well, one time I totally botched an embalming.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: So I used a chainsaw to reduce the corpse to flushable parts.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: I told the family he came back to life and ran away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooookay. And why did you become a baker?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: So I could eat my mistakes.

setting: Job interview in an office
situation: Dilbert interviews a candidate for an engineering position, widening his search because qualified engineers are scarce. The candidate's resume lists mortuary assistant and baker, and when asked about handling failure, he describes disposing of a botched embalming with a chainsaw and lying to the family. When Dilbert asks why he became a baker, the answer implies he bakes his mistakes into food.
punchline: The candidate's answer that he became a baker so he could eat his mistakes darkly implies the corpse parts ended up in baked goods.
summary: A desperate interviewer hears a grisly tale of cover-up from an applicant whose career change to baking has a horrifying motive.

title: Pandemic Profits Need Insincere Gesture

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We doubled our income during the pandemic, and it isn't a good look.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to make some sort of insincere gesture of support for people who are suffering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we could actually help people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm thinking more along the lines of a sign in the foyer.

setting: Conference room during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: At a meeting, a masked boss admits the company doubled its income during the pandemic and that this looks bad. He proposes an insincere gesture of support for people who are suffering. Dilbert suggests actually helping people, but the boss prefers putting up a sign in the foyer.
punchline: The boss chooses a cheap, meaningless sign over real help, because the goal is to improve appearances rather than to help anyone.
summary: A company that profited hugely from a crisis opts for a token lobby sign instead of genuine aid.

title: Finishing Early Means Overpaid, Says Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I finished my project in half the projected time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means I'm paying you twice as much as you deserve.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't think it means that at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You look dumb arguing with math.

setting: Boss's desk in an office, with both wearing face masks
situation: An employee proudly tells his masked boss that he completed a project in half the estimated time. The boss responds that this proves the employee is being overpaid by double. When the employee objects, the boss claims the employee looks dumb for arguing with math.
punchline: The boss twists an efficiency win into a pay-cut justification and falsely claims his illogical reasoning is mathematics, shutting down any objection.
summary: A worker expecting praise for finishing early is instead told the quick turnaround proves he is overpaid, and his protest is dismissed as foolish.

title: Refusing the Pie Chart Request

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Put this on a pie chart instead of a line graph.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that's stupid. I'm not going to do that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh. Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is this working?

setting: Office hallway during the pandemic, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: A coworker holding a printed graph tells Dilbert to present the data as a pie chart instead of a line graph. Dilbert flatly refuses and calls the idea stupid. The coworker simply accepts it, leaving Dilbert to wonder in a thought bubble why bluntly saying no worked. The strip ends with 'Continued...'.
punchline: Dilbert tries the unthinkable tactic of directly refusing a pointless request, and is stunned that it succeeds without any pushback.
summary: A worker bluntly turns down a silly formatting demand and is baffled when nobody argues.

title: T-Shirt Two Sizes Too Small

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you like my new T-shirt? It's two sizes too small, but that's all they had.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be better to buy shirts that you like that are also the right size?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In theory, yes. But I have been buying T-shirts for years, and I don't recall seeing that option.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home, with a blue couch
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert a new T-shirt that is far too tight, explaining it was the only size available. Dogbert suggests buying shirts he likes that also fit. Dilbert replies that in all his years of buying T-shirts, he has never seen a shirt that is both appealing and the right size.
punchline: Dilbert dryly implies that shirts he likes are never available in his size, so he always ends up settling for whatever is left.
summary: Dilbert shows off an ill-fitting shirt and shrugs off his dog's sensible advice by claiming that a good shirt in the right size simply doesn't exist.

title: Endless To-Do List, Never Winning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I accomplished fifteen tasks on my to-do list today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That leaves only seven hundred tasks, not counting the twenty-three I added today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder what winning feels like.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's great.

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office, then walking past Dogbert
situation: Dilbert sits at his desk with a laptop and phone, thinking about the fifteen tasks he finished on his to-do list. He realizes hundreds remain, and he keeps adding new ones faster than he completes them. Carrying a bag, he wonders aloud what winning feels like, and Dogbert, sitting on a blue couch, tells him it is great.
punchline: Dilbert adds tasks nearly as fast as he completes them, so his list never shrinks and he can never win, while Dogbert, who doesn't play that game, smugly says winning feels great.
summary: A man celebrates finishing a pile of chores only to admit his backlog is enormous and still growing, leaving his smug dog to describe the victory he'll never taste.

title: Hired Complainer Says No Strategy

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got him cheap because that's all he does.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some would say we don't need him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe they're jealous of his wisdom.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No strategy.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with masked attendees
situation: In a meeting where everyone wears face masks, a manager explains she hired a cheap employee whose only job is to announce "we have no strategy" at every meeting. Dilbert remarks that some would say he's unnecessary, and she replies that people may be jealous of his wisdom. A coworker silently thinks the same phrase, "No strategy."
punchline: The hired complainer is redundant because everyone already knows the company has no strategy, and the coworker's thought bubble confirms it.
summary: A manager proudly pays someone just to point out the obvious: that the organization lacks any real plan.

title: Ted's Fatal Bear Selfie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. Where can I see that picture?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'd need to ask the bear. It didn't go well.

setting: Office, at a desk, with coworkers wearing face masks
situation: Two masked coworkers sit at a desk while the bald one tells Dilbert that Ted took a selfie with a wild bear. Dilbert eagerly asks where he can see the photo. The coworker replies that only the bear has it, implying the encounter ended badly for Ted.
punchline: The photo can only be found with the bear because the bear presumably killed Ted and kept his phone, a dark joke about risky selfie-taking.
summary: A casual office chat about a coworker's wildlife photo takes a grim turn when it becomes clear the bear ended up with the evidence.

title: Not Fired Until Laptop Returned

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Or else what? You'll fire me twice?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's say you're not officially fired until you return the laptop.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: And if I don't bring it back, will I never be fired?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um. . .

setting: Office, at Ted's desk with a box of his belongings
situation: The Boss tells Ted it's his last day and asks for his company laptop back. Ted, already packing his things into a cardboard box, asks what the consequence could be. The Boss says he won't be officially fired until the laptop is returned, and Ted realizes this means he could keep his job indefinitely by keeping it.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to force the laptop's return backfires by creating a loophole where withholding the laptop means Ted can never be fired.
summary: A manager's threat to delay a firing until equipment is returned hands the departing employee a perfect way to stay employed forever.

title: Two Random Guesses Make a Range

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which of your two projections do you think is more accurate?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They are both random guesses. I made two of them to create the illusion of a credible range.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... would it be reasonable to pick the midpoint?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's as reasonable as your other decisions.

setting: Office, at a desk
situation: The Boss is holding a printout of Dilbert's two projections and asks which one is more accurate. Dilbert admits both are random guesses, made in pairs just to make the estimate look like a credible range. The Boss then proposes choosing the midpoint, and Dilbert says that is as reasonable as the Boss's other decisions.
punchline: Dilbert's backhanded reply implies the Boss's decisions are every bit as arbitrary as picking the midpoint of two made-up numbers.
summary: An engineer confesses that his paired forecasts are pure invention, and when his manager suggests splitting the difference, he sarcastically says that fits the manager's usual decision-making.

title: Fake Video Believer Proves Point

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see the shocking claims in the video I emailed to you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. The video is so obviously fake that only a raging moron would think any of it is true.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think it's all true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Welp, that's one data point in my favor.

setting: Office hallway
situation: A masked coworker asks Dilbert if he watched the shocking video he emailed. Dilbert says the video is so obviously fake that only a raging moron would believe it. The coworker replies that he thinks it's all true.
punchline: By admitting he believes the fake video, the coworker has just confirmed Dilbert's claim that only a moron would believe it, handing Dilbert a data point supporting his insult.
summary: A man who shares a conspiracy video unwittingly proves a colleague's insulting theory about its believers.

title: Cloud Manager Snoops Recreationally

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The best part about my new job managing the cloud is that I get to laugh at everyone's personal information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not supposed to be looking at anyone's personal data.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm fairly sure it's legal if I only do it recreationally.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that the best perk of his new job managing the cloud is laughing at everyone's personal information. Dilbert, working at his computer, objects that he shouldn't be looking at anyone's personal data. Dogbert replies that it is probably legal as long as he does it only for fun.
punchline: Dogbert treats snooping on private data as a harmless hobby, claiming that doing it recreationally makes it legal, which is a flimsy excuse for abusing his access.
summary: Dogbert gleefully admits to spying on other people's private data from his new cloud admin role and justifies it as a leisure activity.

title: Alice Rejects Creepy Corporate Reassurance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I want you to know that I hear you and I value you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's terrific. Maybe you could stop talking to me in that super-creepy and condescending way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, Queen.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who broke you?

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: A male manager sits across from Alice and delivers a scripted assurance that he hears and values her. Alice, scrolling on her phone, tells him to drop the creepy, condescending tone. He responds with another patronizing line, calling her 'Queen', and she asks who broke him.
punchline: Trying to fix a condescending manner by switching to a different patronizing phrase shows he has absorbed buzzword-style empathy without understanding the problem, so Alice wonders what damaged him.
summary: A manager's rehearsed gesture of appreciation backfires when Alice calls out his tone and he answers with an even more patronizing nickname.

title: Hoarded Copier Paper at Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're running low on copier paper.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I know. I hoarded it all at my house when someone said we might have a shortage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you bring some of it back?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That would defeat the point of hoarding.

setting: Office cubicle area during the 2020 pandemic, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that the office is running low on copier paper. She admits she hoarded the supply at her own house after hearing a shortage might occur. When Dilbert asks her to bring some back, she refuses, insisting that would defeat the purpose of hoarding.
punchline: Alice created the office's paper shortage by hoarding supplies, and she treats giving any of it back as contrary to the whole idea of hoarding, mocking pandemic panic-buying logic.
summary: A coworker who stockpiled the office's printer paper at home refuses to return any of it because sharing would undermine her stockpiling.

title: Reimagining Your Unnecessary Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I say we need to reimagine your job, it means we no longer need anyone to do what you have been doing.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Do you mind if I ask when you first realized that my job was totally unnecessary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was four years ago, but you seemed happy, and we had the budget to pay you, so...

setting: Office cubicle
situation: A manager explains to an employee that 'reimagining' his job really means the work is no longer needed. The employee asks when the manager first realized the job was unnecessary. The manager admits he knew four years ago but kept him on because he seemed happy and the budget allowed it.
punchline: The company paid for a pointless job for years simply because it could afford to and the employee seemed content, revealing how arbitrary and wasteful staffing decisions can be.
summary: A boss uses buzzwords to announce a job is obsolete, then casually admits he has known for years but let it slide because money was available.

title: Borrowing a Stapler During Pandemic

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I borrow your stapler?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not with your bare hands. But I can wrap it in plastic and leave a hole for the staples to come out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you can just lend me a paper clip.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll throw it to you.

setting: Office cubicle during the coronavirus pandemic
situation: A masked coworker asks to borrow Dilbert's stapler. Dilbert, also masked and wearing gloves, says he would only lend it wrapped in plastic with a hole for the staples. The coworker gives up and asks for a paper clip instead, and Dilbert says he will throw it to her.
punchline: Dilbert's germ paranoia is so extreme that lending even a simple office supply becomes an absurd hazmat procedure, and even a paper clip must be tossed from a distance.
summary: A germ-wary Dilbert makes sharing office supplies so cumbersome that his coworker settles for a paper clip tossed across the room.

title: Dilbert Yells Through Zoom Call

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop using your speakerphone! I'm trying to make a Zoom call!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can still hear you! Go in the other room! I said go in the other room!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Being married sounds fun.

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: I can still hear you!

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk with a laptop during a work-from-home video call
situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop shouting at someone in his home to stop using speakerphone because he is trying to make a Zoom call. It turns out he is yelling at the woman on the laptop screen, who can hear him just fine. She shouts back that she can still hear him.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically remarks that being married sounds fun while the woman he is arguing with is actually on the other end of the video call, showing he is bickering with her through the laptop.
summary: A man furiously demands that a speakerphone user move rooms, only for the exchange to reveal he is quarrelling with a woman through his laptop, which prompts a dry crack about marriage.

title: Working Through Vacation Days Out of Guilt

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I come to work on my vacation days?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate being scolded for being behind in my work more than I enjoy taking vacations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It seems I have trained you well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm just broken.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks his boss if he can come in to work on his scheduled vacation days. He explains that being scolded for falling behind bothers him more than he enjoys time off. The Boss, glancing at his phone, takes it as proof of his good management, but Dilbert says he is simply broken.
punchline: The Boss congratulates himself for training Dilbert to be so dedicated, but Dilbert points out that the real result is a worn-down employee who can no longer enjoy time off.
summary: An employee who would rather work than face criticism during time off is praised by his manager for being well trained, only to say he is actually just broken.

title: Quarantine Required Before Dinner Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to go to dinner with me?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Only if you self-quarantine for two weeks first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can do!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, it seems I underestimated your desperation.

setting: Office, with both people wearing face masks during the pandemic
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, asks a female coworker typing at her laptop to go to dinner with him. She says she will only go if he self-quarantines for two weeks first, expecting that to put him off. Dilbert cheerfully agrees, and she realizes he is more desperate than she thought.
punchline: The coworker's absurd condition was meant as a polite refusal, but Dilbert accepting it instantly exposes how desperate he is for a date.
summary: A masked engineer's date request meets an unreasonable pandemic condition, and his eager acceptance shows how lonely he really is.

title: Honest Feedback About Moronic Goals

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: That's because my goals are totally unrealistic and were created by a moron.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't expect you to ACT on it!

setting: Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Alice she failed to meet her quarterly goals. Alice replies that the goals were unrealistic and set by a moron, then reminds him he asked for honesty. The Boss objects that he never expected anyone to actually take him up on it.
punchline: The Boss claims to want honest feedback from employees, but he is offended the moment someone is truthful about his own poor goal-setting.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for missing targets, then recoils when she bluntly blames his flawed planning after he invited candor.

title: Dilbert Has No Project Involvement

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an office building exterior shown in the last panel
situation: A manager tells a man who has questions about a project that Dilbert can answer them, then leaves for another meeting. Dilbert admits he has no involvement in the project and was only told to follow the man to the room. The man calls the situation awkward, and Dilbert offers to go to the restroom and never return.
punchline: Dilbert, dragged into a meeting he has no part in, responds to the awkwardness by offering to escape for good, which is the sarcastic way out of a situation created by a manager's careless delegation.
summary: A manager hands off a questioner to a coworker who knows nothing about the project, leaving both of them stranded in an uncomfortable silence.

title: App That Escapes Meetings

situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, tells a boss seated at the table that he has invented an app that makes your phone ring so you can get out of meetings. The boss asks how it fits the company's strategic direction. Dilbert's phone starts ringing, and he says he needs to take the call and walks away.
punchline: Dilbert answers the boss's question by demonstrating the app, using it to escape the meeting on the spot.
summary: A new gadget meant to rescue people from tedious meetings gets a live demonstration the moment a manager questions its business value.

transcript.text: And so it begins.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll text you if I'm running late.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he might stop by her neighborhood on Saturday. She says she won't fall for the trick of giving an estimated time and then repeatedly pushing it back until canceling. He promises to stick to a time, but when asked what the time is, he says it depends on how his day goes.
punchline: Dilbert's promise to be punctual is immediately undercut by his refusal to commit to any actual time, so the exact delay-and-cancel routine he denied is already underway.
summary: A man swears he won't dodge a visit with shifting arrival times, yet cannot name any time at all.

title: Denying Words, Then Retracting Them

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Will we now proceed as if you didn't hear me say that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They are NOT the wrong people.

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: A coworker with a large dark bob haircut confronts Dilbert, accusing him of telling the boss that her project has the wrong people on it. Dilbert denies saying it and points out he doesn't even know what her project is. When she asks that they pretend he never heard the accusation, he quickly flips and declares the team members are not the wrong people.
punchline: Dilbert is so eager to avoid conflict that he instantly agrees to disown his own opinion, saying whatever she wants as if he had never been accused, which shows how office politics rewards backing down over honesty.
summary: Accused of badmouthing a colleague's team, a man first claims ignorance and then hastily endorses her staff when she offers him a way out.

title: Wally's Camera Shortens Zoom Call

situation: Alice is on a video call and warns a colleague that his camera is on. She reacts in horror to something she sees on screen and says she can't unsee it. Afterward Dilbert asks Wally how his Zoom call went, and Wally says he found a way to shorten it by an hour.
punchline: Wally deliberately shortened the meeting by leaving his camera on while doing something so disturbing that everyone fled, implying he does it on purpose to escape long calls.
summary: A colleague's accidentally or deliberately live webcam horrifies a coworker, and it turns out to be Wally's trick for cutting meetings short.

transcript.text: And then we can begin construction?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how construction of the new lab is progressing. Dilbert explains that absurd local building codes, such as guaranteeing no rain touches the roof, are blocking the project. He says a donation to the mayor's campaign would get the roof reclassified as a wall, but the Boss's hope that construction can then start is dashed.
punchline: Even bribing a politician to get around the ridiculous regulations only starts a 'false hope phase' of further delays, showing how hopeless dealing with bureaucracy is.
summary: A manager learns that bizarre permit rules and a campaign donation workaround are merely the first stage in a long run of bureaucratic disappointment.

title: Self-Diagnosed Antibodies From Throat Tickle

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was wondering the same.

setting: Office, at a desk
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, asks a coworker why he isn't wearing one. The coworker claims he has antibodies because he thinks a throat tickle last January was the virus. Dilbert sarcastically suggests test kits are unnecessary if you can just ask people, and the coworker agrees without noticing the sarcasm.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic remark that medical testing is pointless if people can just self-report is taken sincerely by a coworker who relies on a vague hunch as proof of immunity.
summary: A maskless coworker cites a minor sore throat months earlier as proof of immunity, and a sarcastic jab about testing goes right over his head.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Then why can I think of only one?

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Asok stands holding a printout and confidently announces that the data can mean only one thing. Dilbert, seated at his laptop, corrects him that it could mean about seventeen things. Asok asks why he can only think of one, and Dilbert declines to answer.
punchline: Dilbert's refusal to answer implies that Asok can only think of one interpretation because he lacks imagination or intelligence, and Dilbert is too polite to say so.
summary: A coworker jumps to a single conclusion from some data, and when he asks why he can't see any others, his colleague tactfully declines to explain.

title: Ted's Implausible Tweet Excuses

setting: Conference room in the office
situation: The Boss tells Ted he must be fired for having liked an unacceptable tweet seven years earlier. Ted nervously blames a hacked account or a slipped finger. The Boss, plainly not believing either, asks which lie he should record in Ted's file, and Ted asks whether either sounded believable.
punchline: Both the boss and Ted openly acknowledge that Ted's excuses are lies, so the firing is a foregone conclusion and only the paperwork cover story is left to settle.
summary: A man is dismissed over an old social media endorsement, and his flimsy excuses are treated as fiction to be neatly filed away.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Office doorway and hallway
situation: Dilbert proudly tells his boss he stayed up all night finishing a presentation for this morning's meeting. The boss casually reveals the meeting was canceled, and when Dilbert demands to know when he found out, the boss refuses to say.
punchline: The boss's refusal to answer implies he knew about the cancellation long before Dilbert pulled the all-nighter and didn't bother to tell him.
summary: A worker's overnight effort turns out to be pointless, and his manager's evasive reply hints that the news could have saved him the trouble.

title: Low-Cost Phone Safety Testing

setting: Conference room, then Dogbert's low-cost testing desk
situation: Alice, seated at a meeting table, says she is nervous about sitting near the Boss's 5G phone prototype because it might fry her eggs. The Boss insists the phone was thoroughly tested by qualified experts. He then hands the phone to Dogbert, who runs a 'Low-Cost Testing' business and merely glances at it before declaring it fine.
punchline: The 'extensive testing by qualified experts' was really just Dogbert eyeballing the phone and calling it fine, revealing that the safety assurance is worthless.
summary: A manager brushes off a worry about phone radiation by citing expert testing, but the only testing consists of a cheap consultant giving the device a quick glance.

title: Blame the Client for Believing

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert, acting as a contractor, meets with a client who now says the network upgrade will take three months. Dilbert points out that the client's own bid claimed thirty days. The client responds that if blame is being assigned, it belongs to whoever was foolish enough to believe his original estimate.
punchline: The speaker admits his own estimate was unreliable and shifts the blame onto the person who trusted it, a twisted way of dodging accountability.
summary: A man defends a blown schedule by arguing the fault lies with anyone gullible enough to have trusted his original promise.

title: Software Upgrade Deaths Dismissed

transcript.text: But we don't think it means anything because all of them had underlying health issues.

transcript.text: Version 1.0 had some rough edges, too.

setting: Conference room during a masked presentation
situation: A masked presenter in a green jacket points at a slide showing a 100% figure with a downward arrow and reports that every user who upgraded to version 2.0 died the same day. He dismisses this as irrelevant because they all had underlying health issues. When a seated colleague asks how they could all have been unwell, he reveals that version 1.0 also had 'rough edges', implying the earlier release harmed them.
punchline: The company dismisses lethal side effects of its software as pre-existing conditions, then casually admits the previous version was probably what made everyone sick.
summary: A presenter shrugs off a batch of post-upgrade fatalities as unrelated, then inadvertently blames the earlier release for the victims' poor health.

title: Sarcasm Beats Good Arguments

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound like a productive thing to do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Office break area near a refrigerator
situation: Dogbert, sitting on a chair, announces that he has abandoned good arguments in favor of sarcasm because it is more effective. Dilbert, wearing a face mask, points out that this doesn't sound productive. Dogbert responds with a sarcastic jab at Dilbert's sudden productivity expertise, proving his own point.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his sarcasm-over-reason philosophy by answering a valid criticism with a mocking retort instead of an actual argument.
summary: After declaring that mockery works better than reasoning, a canine pal proves it by sneering at a coworker's perfectly sensible objection.

title: Systems Over Goals, Not Answers

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: What are your goals for the year?
