transcript.text: I prefer systems over goals.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay, what are your systems?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: None of them involve answering questions.

characters: Bald man with glasses in green shirt
setting: Office meeting room table
situation: A woman asks a coworker in a meeting about his goals for the year. He dodges by saying he prefers systems over goals, and when she asks what his systems are, he says none of them involve answering questions.
punchline: The man uses the popular 'systems over goals' idea as an excuse to evade questions, making his own system a built-in refusal to answer anything.
summary: A man deflects a goal-setting question by championing systems, then reveals his system is simply never answering questions.

title: Imagining Coworker Unmasked, Reporting Self

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you wear makeup under the mask where no one can see it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or do you leave your snout area all pale and pimply?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop imagining me unmasked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll report myself to Human Resources.

setting: Office meeting table during the pandemic, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert and Alice sit at a table wearing face masks. Dilbert idly wonders aloud whether Alice wears makeup under her mask or leaves the lower half of her face pale and pimply. Alice angrily tells him to stop picturing her unmasked, and Dilbert responds by saying he will report himself to HR.
punchline: Dilbert realizes his invasive musing about a coworker's face is the kind of inappropriate behavior HR handles, so he cheerfully volunteers to turn himself in.
summary: A masked Dilbert speculates about what his coworker's hidden face looks like, gets scolded, and promptly resolves to file a complaint against himself.

title: Layers of Carl's Defenses

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I almost got some information from Carl.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I stalked him to his cubicle and penetrated his outer defense of rudeness.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I never broke through his mumble layer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait until you get to his ignorance layer.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Asok tells Dilbert about his failed attempt to get information from a coworker named Carl. He followed Carl to his cubicle and got past his rudeness, but Carl mumbled and Asok couldn't get any further. Dilbert warns him that an even bigger obstacle awaits beyond the mumbling.
punchline: Even if you get past Carl's rudeness and mumbling, he has nothing useful to tell you because he doesn't actually know anything.
summary: A young intern describes the defensive layers he fought through to question a coworker, only to be told the final layer is that the man knows nothing.

title: Artificial Dumbness Software Invention

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My new software invention is called "Artificial Dumbness."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It acts dumb so humans will think they are talking to one of their own.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That couldn't possibly work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's phone
transcript.text: That couldn't possibly work.

setting: Office meeting room, with characters wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert pitches his new software invention, 'Artificial Dumbness,' to the Boss while holding a phone. The software is meant to act dumb so people believe they are talking to another human. When the Boss says it couldn't possibly work, Dilbert's phone repeats the exact same sentence in bold type.
punchline: The software perfectly mimics the Boss's dim response by parroting it back, proving that acting dumb is very convincing and that the Boss is the benchmark for human stupidity.
summary: A pitch for software that fakes human-like stupidity gets its demonstration when the device simply echoes the skeptical manager's own words.

title: Cloud Manager Redistributes Wealth Upward

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now that I'm managing the cloud, it's time to make some social changes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll transfer any remaining money from low-income people to the rich.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That feels wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm just adding efficiency to the inevitable.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert at a laptop on a stool and Dilbert in a bathrobe holding a coffee mug
situation: Dogbert announces that since he now manages the cloud he will make social changes, then types a command to move leftover money from poor people to the wealthy. Dilbert, in a red robe with a mug of coffee, objects that it feels wrong. Dogbert replies that he is simply making an existing trend more efficient.
punchline: Dogbert cynically justifies siphoning money from the poor to the rich by claiming it only speeds up what would happen anyway, a jab at wealth inequality and at the idea that efficiency excuses unethical outcomes.
summary: Having taken charge of the cloud, Dogbert quietly reroutes funds from the poor to the wealthy and shrugs off Dilbert's moral objection as mere optimization.

title: Wally Spits Coffee at Tweet Disclaimer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I object to your Twitter profile. It says. . .

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "My tweets are smart and useful, so obviously they do not represent my employer."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Smorph!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now see what you did to Wally.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Alice reads her phone and objects to a colleague's Twitter profile, quoting its disclaimer that his smart and useful tweets obviously don't represent his employer. While Wally is drinking coffee, the line makes him spray it out in laughter. Dilbert then blames Alice for what happened to Wally.
punchline: The Twitter disclaimer implies the employer is neither smart nor useful, and the insult is so blunt it makes Wally spit out his coffee.
summary: A coworker's social media bio accidentally insults the company, and the reading of it leaves another employee choking on his drink.

title: Employee Dumps Her Own Conscience

transcript.speaker: Laptop (voice from device)
transcript.text: "No one on the project team could have foreseen the problem that..."

transcript.speaker: Conscience (off-panel voice)
transcript.text: You are a lying piece of garbage.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Who said that?

transcript.speaker: Soul (off-panel voice)
transcript.text: It's your soul. We can't hang out anymore.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Fine. You were slowing me down.

characters: Woman (employee with bob haircut and face mask)
setting: Office cubicle, with the employee working at a desk on a laptop
situation: A masked employee sits at her laptop writing a statement claiming nobody on the project team could have foreseen a problem. A disembodied voice calls her a lying piece of garbage, and she asks who said it. The voice reveals it is her soul, ending their relationship, and she dismisses it as something that was slowing her down.
punchline: She cheerfully ditches her conscience because it interferes with her ability to lie and shift blame, showing that ethics are a hindrance to career advancement.
summary: A worker drafting a dishonest excuse for a failed project gets scolded by her own soul and happily lets it walk away.

title: Out-of-Context Quote Backfires on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't like what you wrote about my project, so I took one of your quotes out of context, to make you look dumb, and sent it to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That won't work, because once I explain the proper context, he will see there is nothing to it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So, as you can see, that quote was out of context.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Liar!!!

setting: Conference room, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: A coworker, annoyed by Dilbert's critique of his project, admits he sent a misleading out-of-context quote of Dilbert's to Dilbert's boss. Dilbert confidently says he can easily clear it up by explaining the context. When he tries, the boss simply accuses him of lying.
punchline: Dilbert assumes that explaining the real context will clear him, but the boss has already believed the misleading quote and treats the correction as a lie, showing how hard it is to undo a smear once it has landed.
summary: A colleague deliberately misquotes Dilbert to the boss, and Dilbert's confidence in a simple explanation is crushed when the boss calls him a liar.

title: Changing Minds With Data Seems Suspicious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday someone disagreed with me, and I changed his mind using data and reason.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That isn't possible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't think so either, but it happened.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Smells like a trap.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't sleep all night.

setting: Office break area or meeting table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker over coffee that he persuaded someone who disagreed with him by using data and reason. The coworker says that's impossible, and Dilbert admits he thought so too. The coworker suspects a trap, and Dilbert confesses the incident kept him awake all night.
punchline: Being persuaded by facts is so unheard of that Dilbert finds the success itself unsettling and suspects something sinister, suggesting rational persuasion almost never works.
summary: A man who won an argument with facts is so unnerved by the rare success that he lost sleep over it.

title: Auditor Depends On Not Being Questioned

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a reasonable fee, I will audit your company and find any fraud or crime if it exists.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: What's to stop you from taking bribes from the fraudsters and reporting that everything is fine?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My business model depends on you not asking that kind of question.

setting: Client's office, at a desk with a laptop
situation: Dogbert pitches his services as a company auditor who will uncover any fraud or crime for a fee. The skeptical client asks what would prevent Dogbert from simply accepting bribes from fraudsters and declaring everything fine. Dogbert replies that his business depends on clients never asking that question.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits that his auditing business only works if clients are naive enough not to question his integrity, implying he would indeed take bribes.
summary: A prospective client challenges a self-styled fraud auditor about corruption and gets an unashamedly cynical answer.

title: Wearing a Wire Against Idea Thieves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a great idea. Let's create a Google document that we can all update.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is exactly the idea I suggested to you yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't prove that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was only true until I learned to wear a wire.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces a great idea of creating a shared Google document for everyone to update. Dilbert points out it is the very idea he suggested to the Boss the day before. When the Boss smugly says Dilbert can't prove it, Dilbert reveals he is now secretly recording conversations with a wire.
punchline: The Boss has been stealing employees' ideas and relying on a lack of proof, but Dilbert has now armed himself with recording equipment to catch him.
summary: A manager passes off an employee's suggestion as his own brainchild, only to find the employee has started secretly recording him.

title: Ghostwriter Fingers Through the Keyboard

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: You should hire a ghostwriter to write your autobiography.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's dumb. A ghost's fingers would go right through the keyboard.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Then how do their clothes stay on?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fair point.

setting: Dilbert's workspace, with a laptop on a desk and a ghost perched on a stool
situation: A small ghost sitting on a stool suggests that Dilbert hire a ghostwriter for his autobiography. Dilbert dismisses the idea, arguing that a ghost's fingers would pass through a keyboard. The ghost counters by asking how ghosts' clothes stay on if they are intangible, and Dilbert concedes.
punchline: Dilbert's literal-minded objection to a ghost typing is undercut by an equally literal rebuttal about clothing, and he accepts that the logic is sound.
summary: A ghost pitches a spectral author for a memoir, and a pedantic debate about ghost physics ends with the skeptic conceding defeat.

title: Elbonian Consultant Recommends Executing Distributors

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an Elbonian consultant because we couldn't afford anyone local.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever consulted in this country?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: No, but people are people, so I assume it isn't that different from Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's enough chitchat.

transcript.text: Tell us what we should do about the problems in our distribution system.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I recommend executing one of your distributors as a warning to the others.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to need a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: My second opinion is that your barber must hate your guts.

setting: Conference room in the office
situation: The Boss introduces a cheap Elbonian consultant, who admits he has never worked in this country but assumes people are all alike. Asked how to fix distribution problems, the consultant recommends executing a distributor as a warning to the others. When the Boss asks for a second opinion, the consultant insults the Boss's haircut instead.
punchline: After a shockingly brutal recommendation, the Boss's request for a second opinion is answered with a mocking comment on his ridiculous hair, implying the consultant's advice is as dubious as the Boss's judgment.
summary: A bargain-basement foreign consultant proposes a murderous fix for supply chain trouble, then answers a request for another view by mocking the boss's haircut.

title: Word Salad Triggers Cognitive Dissonance

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You think you made a good argument, but...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You are failing to consider the overall implications of the long-term ramifications with regard to strategic priorities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That big bowl of word salad suggests I triggered you into cognitive dissonance.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Tuna carpet!

setting: Office, with both characters wearing face masks
situation: Asok starts to rebut Dilbert's argument and then strings together empty business jargon about long-term ramifications and strategic priorities. Dilbert points out that this rambling word salad shows he has been pushed into cognitive dissonance. Asok responds with the nonsensical phrase 'tuna carpet', proving Dilbert right.
punchline: Asok's complete breakdown into nonsense ('tuna carpet') confirms that Dilbert's argument has short-circuited his thinking, and that the jargon was only a cover for having no real counterargument.
summary: When a coworker loses a debate, he flails with empty corporate buzzwords and then collapses into gibberish.

title: Boss Ignores Incompatible Hardware Complaint

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't even know what conversation I'm in right now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The extended warranty is second to none.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the new hardware he purchased won't work with the company network. The Boss, absorbed in his phone, responds with irrelevant sales points about price, reliability and the extended warranty, none of which address the compatibility problem.
punchline: The Boss answers a compatibility complaint with unrelated purchasing talking points, showing he isn't really listening and has no solution, leaving Dilbert confused about what conversation he's even in.
summary: A manager brushes off a complaint about unusable equipment by praising its bargain price and warranty while staring at his phone.

title: Calling 4G Service '5G' Marketing

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The boss announces the launch of a new 5G wireless service. Dilbert points out the company has no 5G technology, and the boss admits it is really 4G relabeled because nobody wants 4G. When Dilbert warns that customers will complain, the boss says that is fine because they are also making the company impossible to reach by phone.
punchline: The company deceptively rebrands old technology as new and then shields itself from the resulting customer complaints by making its support line unreachable.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits to relabeling old wireless technology as the latest generation and has already arranged to dodge any angry customers.

title: Voice-Only Call Because No Makeup

situation: Dilbert texts a colleague asking to set up a Zoom call. She replies that she prefers voice-only because she isn't wearing makeup at home. Dilbert asks how hideous she looks without makeup, and she answers that FedEx has asked her to stop answering the door in person.
punchline: The colleague's deadpan reply implies her appearance without makeup is so frightening that delivery drivers have begged her not to greet them, turning her self-deprecation into a joke at Dilbert's blunt question.
summary: A coworker dodges video calls because she skips makeup at home, and jokes that couriers are too scared of her face to let her take deliveries.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has started doing telemedicine on the side. When Dilbert points out that this requires being a doctor, Dogbert explains his workaround is simply claiming to be one. A video patient then describes a thigh pain, and Dogbert diagnoses a rake and gives absurd advice.
punchline: Dogbert's fake medical practice is exposed as ridiculous when his only diagnosis is a rake, and his remedy is to pick up leaves by hand instead of using the rake.
summary: A dog with no medical training passes himself off as a physician online and dispenses a laughably silly diagnosis.

title: Early Arrival Invites Dreaded Chitchat

situation: Dilbert checks his watch and realizes he has arrived at the meeting room too early, dreading small talk. He sits at the table predicting that someone will bore him with their diet preferences. A coworker then walks up and announces he only eats figs, confirming his fear.
punchline: Dilbert's gloomy prediction about diet chitchat comes true almost instantly, and he silently begs for death.
summary: A man who arrives early to a meeting dreads small talk, and his worst prediction is fulfilled the moment a coworker speaks.

title: Try Unreasonable Assumptions To Save Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Have you tried "unreasonable" assumptions?

transcript.text: Why would I do that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, to keep your job, for example.

setting: Office meeting room, both wearing face masks
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that he has run the numbers and the boss's plan fails under any reasonable set of assumptions. The boss suggests he try unreasonable assumptions instead. When Dilbert asks why he would do that, the boss implicitly threatens his job.
punchline: The boss wants the analysis rigged with unreasonable assumptions to justify his plan, and he backs the request with a veiled threat to fire Dilbert if he refuses.
summary: A manager's flawed plan gets a failing grade from the numbers, so he pressures his analyst to fudge the inputs or lose his position.

title: Innocent People Say I Didn't Do It

transcript.text: On one hand, Carl is an idiot and a known liar.

transcript.text: On the other hand, it is common for guilty people to say they are innocent.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: What do innocent people say when you accuse them of stuff?

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: Who knows? Just don't do it again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't do it once!!!

setting: Conference room
situation: A coworker accuses Dilbert of telling the boss that the prototype needs more testing. Dilbert denies it and questions why the coworker would trust Carl, who wasn't in the room. The coworker muses that Carl is a liar, but guilty people also claim innocence, and then asks what innocent people say when accused.
punchline: The coworker's circular reasoning makes it impossible for Dilbert to prove his innocence, since any denial could be a guilty person's denial, leaving him frustrated and shouting that he never did it at all.
summary: A colleague uses unfalsifiable logic to convict Dilbert of an accusation, warning him not to repeat an act he insists he never committed.

title: Bureaucracy Against Incompetence: Yin and Yang

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yin and yang.

setting: Office desk with a coffee cup between the two
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that the company's employees all seem incompetent. The Boss proposes a maze of bureaucratic rules that will keep them from accomplishing anything. Catbert questions whether inefficiency can guard against incompetence, and the Boss dismisses the doubt with 'yin and yang'.
punchline: The Boss treats deliberately crippling the workforce with red tape as a balanced philosophy, using 'yin and yang' to justify a fix that makes the underlying problem worse.
summary: Faced with a workforce of incompetents, management decides the cure is a thicket of red tape that prevents any work at all, and calls it cosmic balance.

title: Badge Tracking Convenient Excuse Coincidence

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: That sounds like a convenient excuse to do something you've always wanted to do anyway.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with everyone wearing face masks
situation: The Boss announces that tracking chips will be added to employee badges to monitor social distancing. Dilbert points out that this seems like a convenient pretext for surveillance management has always wanted. The Boss brushes off the accusation, calling it a coincidence.
punchline: The Boss's feeble 'probably a coincidence' effectively admits that the pandemic is just a handy cover story for the employee tracking he has long wanted.
summary: Management uses a pandemic safety measure as cover to start monitoring staff through their ID badges, and barely bothers to deny it.

title: Social Distancing Sends Dilbert Over Bridge

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. A human being is walking in my direction.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Unseen person

setting: Outdoor stone bridge over a pond or stream
situation: Dilbert walks along a path beside a stone bridge wall and spots another person approaching. Panicking about proximity, he leaps backward away from them and tumbles over the bridge wall. In the last panel he is floating in the water below, and the other person calmly tells him from above to back up six feet.
punchline: Dilbert's fear of getting close to other people was so extreme that he backed himself right off the bridge, and the other person still insists he keep six feet away.
summary: A jumpy pedestrian avoiding a stranger retreats so hastily that he plunges into the water beneath a bridge.

title: Detailed List You'll Hopefully Forget

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With any luck, you'll forget you asked for it.

setting: Office meeting table
situation: Wally tells his boss he will meet his targets by doing a variety of complicated things. When the boss asks for specifics, Wally promises to send a detailed list. The boss worries he might forget, and Wally says he hopes the boss forgets he ever asked.
punchline: Wally has no real plan and is counting on his boss's poor memory and inattention so he never has to produce the promised list.
summary: An employee brushes off a manager's questions about his goals by promising paperwork he hopes everyone will forget about.

title: Futurist Predicts Doom for Everyone Else

situation: The Boss announces he has hired a futurist to predict the industry's direction. Dogbert, wearing a striped futurist hat, tells the Boss he can leave and enjoy his remaining time, then tells the rest of the staff, including Dilbert, that they face hard work with no rewards.
punchline: The futurist's grand prediction is just a cynical description of the status quo, hinting the Boss will be fired while employees keep toiling for nothing.
summary: A hired futurist delivers a bleak forecast that doubles as an insult to everyone at the table.

title: Recommending Something That Already Exists

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's why I recommend creating a 5G format called orthogonal frequency division multiplexing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That will never work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Dilbert recommends inventing a 5G format called orthogonal frequency division multiplexing, and the Boss immediately declares it will never work. Dilbert reveals it is already an industry standard and that he was joking. The Boss complains about being tricked, and Dilbert says he may not be able to stop.
punchline: The Boss reflexively rejects any technical idea without knowing anything about it, so Dilbert can trick him into dismissing an existing standard, and Dilbert can't resist doing it again.
summary: Dilbert pitches a technology that already exists, the Boss rejects it out of hand, and the prank proves too fun for Dilbert to give up.

title: Criticizing Methods Becomes Hating Safety

transcript.text: Your method of calculating the safety statistics is flawed.

transcript.speaker: Safety Manager
transcript.text: Wow. Wait until I tell everyone you don't think safety matters.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... didn't say that. I'm talking about the way you measured it.

transcript.speaker: Safety Manager
transcript.text: It's too late to walk it back now!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not "walking it back." I'm clarifying.

transcript.speaker: Safety Manager
transcript.text: There's nothing to clarify. You hate safety.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop putting words in my mouth!!! I'm a better authority on what I think than you are!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What was all that yelling about?

transcript.speaker: Safety Manager
transcript.text: Dilbert thinks safety doesn't matter.

setting: Office meeting room and hallway
situation: Dilbert points out that the safety manager's method of calculating safety statistics is flawed. The safety manager twists this into an accusation that Dilbert doesn't care about safety and refuses to accept his clarifications. When Dilbert finally loses his temper, the safety manager tells a curious coworker that Dilbert thinks safety doesn't matter.
punchline: The safety manager deliberately mischaracterizes a legitimate criticism as hostility to safety, and Dilbert's justified outburst only confirms the false narrative for onlookers.
summary: A man defending his own flawed numbers recasts a technical critique as an attack on safety itself, then uses the resulting argument as proof.

title: Dilbert Craves Touch During Quarantine

transcript.text: I haven't had any human contact for months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People need physical contact to keep their oxytocin at healthy levels.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Get away from me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe if we both close our eyes.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask and sitting on his couch, complains that he hasn't had human contact in months and explains that people need touch to keep their oxytocin levels healthy. Dogbert, sitting beside him, tells him to get away. Dilbert suggests that if they both close their eyes, Dogbert might pass as a human.
punchline: Desperate for human touch, Dilbert suggests they close their eyes so he can pretend the dog is a person to cuddle with.
summary: A lonely, masked Dilbert tries to talk his unwilling dog into a pretend cuddle to satisfy his need for touch during lockdown.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has upgraded the company's A.I. prototype so it can make management decisions. The device on the desk announces 'Slay the weak,' and Dilbert says that must be a bug. The Boss, intrigued rather than alarmed, wants to hear the A.I. out.
punchline: The A.I.'s ruthless advice is likely a bug, but the Boss is tempted to follow it, implying that management already leans toward cruelty and that the machine is simply being honest.

transcript.speaker: Alice

summary: A chief executive expects praise for sharing the cubicle life of regular staff, but an employee flatly calls the habit foolish and then uses that same verdict to explain his misery.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, politely asks Alice, who is also masked and working at her laptop, if she would like to have lunch with him. Alice harshly says she wants to stay far away from his diseased mouth, then adds 'no offense,' and Dilbert calmly accepts the insult.
punchline: In the pandemic era, an insulting rejection is delivered with a polite 'no offense' and accepted without complaint, because avoiding someone's germs has become normal and reasonable.
summary: A masked coworker turns down a lunch invitation by bluntly insulting the inviter's germs, and the insult is accepted with total calm.

situation: The Boss finds Alice slumped back in her chair with a coffee, not working, and asks why. She says her brain is full, so he offers to check back later. Alice replies that she won't remember him by then.
